method: 33 search units + 14 adversarial verification batches, all Opus/Sonnet subagents. Strategy deliberately shifted away from the package-partition reading sweeps of rounds 1-3, which had already been run twice: (A) regression review of the never-reviewed 12k-line fix wave d281e2e2~1..HEAD, 4 partitions; (B) ground truth instead of self-consistency - Go string literals against the real device universe (godevccu fleet data, openccu-data, aiohomematic); (D) scripted cross-artefact consistency (openapi/router/generated types/SPA, wsapi, MCP, surface registry, i18n); (E) seven whole-tree lenses none of the prior rounds ran (resource lifetime, persistence+migrations, time/DST/clock, numbers+units, authz matrix, upgrade path, SPA depth); (F) cache coherency, secondary binaries, dependency-failure injection, Matter behaviour vs matter.js, south-wire robustness, persisted-blob drift; (G) DYNAMIC - a running daemon against the godevccu simulator for REST, WS/MCP and lifecycle chaos, plus read-only measurement against the two live CCUs; (H) re-triage of the prior round's 47-item unresolved tail; (I) comment-claims sweep and mutation testing of the standing guards; (J) HA discovery validated against Home Assistant core's own schemas, and every cfg leaf checked for a production reader. Every critical/high was then handed to an independent Opus agent instructed to refute it.

baseline.make_race: 0 data races; the first run's failure was a 10-minute test timeout under load 17, re-run at a 40-minute timeout -> all green (tests/contract 2139s)
baseline.make_licenses: fails locally only - go-licenses cannot resolve stdlib when the toolchain is a module download; CI installs a real SDK and the gate is green there. Environment artefact, not a defect.

note_on_severity: severity is the post-verification value: where a verifier re-rated a finding, its value wins. The refutation pass moved 26 findings (mostly downward), raised one (A1-central-diff-4) and dropped 5 outright, including one that turned out to be a measurement artefact.

findings.title: Both operator-triggered MQTT reload paths bind the rebuilt stack's reconnect loop and health probe to a short-lived context, so after a reload the bridge never reconnects again
findings.claim: `mqttSupervisor.buildSwap(ctx, cfg)` binds the whole new MQTT stack to the ctx it is handed: `sw.lifecycle.Start(ctx)` (cmd/openccu-loom/mqtt_supervisor.go:595) and `sw.cancelHealth = mqtt.StartHealthProbe(ctx, cs, s.healthTracker, mqtt.DefaultProbeInterval)` (:601). go-mqtt's `Lifecycle.Start` derives `runCtx, cancel := context.WithCancel(ctx)` and runs the reconnect loop on it (GOMODCACHE/github.com/!sukram!j/go-mqtt@v1.3.0/lifecycle.go:166, :222-225 `go func(){ l.loop(runCtx) }()`), and `loop` returns on `case <-ctx.Done()` (lifecycle.go:277-279). Its own doc-comment states the contract: 'ctx governs the WHOLE reconnect loop ... never a short-lived timeout context, or the loop silently dies with it' (lifecycle.go:154-159). `mqtt.StartHealthProbe` likewise derives `pctx` from ctx and returns on `pctx.Done()` (internal/north/mqtt/health_probe.go:53, :62). The boot path is correct — `si.mqttSup.Start(ctx, cfg)` passes the daemon-lifetime ctx (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_infra.go:192) — and the boot-connect retry loop was already fixed for exactly this bug, with the rationale spelled out in a comment (mqtt_supervisor.go:422-431: 'Rebuild on the daemon-lifetime ctx, NOT retryCtx: Swap installs a lifecycle whose whole reconnect loop (and its health probe ...) is governed by the context handed to it'). But both remaining `Swap` callers still hand over a short-lived context: (1) REST — `MQTTReload` handler calls `svc.Reload(r.Context())` (internal/north/rest/handlers/admin_mqtt_reload.go:46), mounted at `POST /api/v1/admin/mqtt/reload` (internal/north/rest/router.go:1354), which forwards straight to `a.sup.Swap(ctx, cfg)` (mqtt_supervisor.go:723); net/http cancels `r.Context()` the moment ServeHTTP returns. (2) config-file watcher — `swapCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)` then `err := sup.Swap(swapCtx, swapCfg); cancel()` (cmd/openccu-loom/reload.go:124, :142-143). Nothing re-arms the loop afterwards: `retryInitialConnect` is only called from `Start` (mqtt_supervisor.go:336), and `Lifecycle.Start` refuses a second call while `started` is true (lifecycle.go:161-164). The REST path is reachable from a prominent SPA button (`api.reloadMQTT()` → assets/ui/src/lib/api/client.ts:1774, wired to the 'Reload MQTT' button in assets/ui/src/routes/Settings.svelte:193,632).
findings.failure_scenario: An operator edits MQTT settings in the SPA and presses 'Reload MQTT' (or edits north.mqtt in the YAML and lets the watcher apply it). The swap succeeds and MQTT keeps working — for as long as the TCP session happens to survive. The reconnect loop is already dead. The next time the broker restarts (Mosquitto add-on update, container restart, Wi-Fi blip) the session drops and nothing reconnects: every Home Assistant entity goes `unavailable` via the LWT and stays that way, every raw-plane publish is dropped, and inbound MQTT commands stop being delivered — permanently, until the daemon process is restarted. There is no log line saying so. Secondary effect from the same root cause: the `mqtt` health component stops being sampled, so `health.Tracker.applyStaleLocked` downgrades it to UNKNOWN after `staleAfter` (internal/health/tracker.go:298-309), which drags `Overall()` to UNKNOWN (:318-342) and the system-health score down (:486-505) for the rest of the process lifetime.
findings.verified_by: code trace end-to-end (handler → adapter → Swap → buildSwap → Lifecycle.Start/StartHealthProbe → go-mqtt loop) plus a measured reproducer at $S/repro/E1/main.go, which drives the real go-mqtt v1.3.0 Lifecycle with a fake connector: with the ctx kept alive two simulated broker drops produce 16 reconnects; with `cancel()` called right after `Start` (the reload.go:143 shape) they produce 0.
findings.fix_sketch: Give the supervisor a daemon-lifetime context captured in `Start` (or in `newMQTTSupervisor`) and have `buildSwap` use that for `lifecycle.Start` and `StartHealthProbe`, keeping the caller's ctx only for the bounded build/connect work — exactly what `retryInitialConnect` already does. Pin it with a test that Swaps under an already-cancelled ctx and asserts the new lifecycle still reconnects after a simulated drop.
findings.verify_reasoning: Re-derived independently. mqttSupervisor holds no daemon-lifetime context field at all (struct at mqtt_supervisor.go:39-84) — buildSwap uses whatever ctx it is handed, and Swap passes its caller's ctx straight through (mqtt_supervisor.go:486). go-mqtt v1.3.0 Lifecycle.Start derives runCtx from that ctx and spawns loop(runCtx), which returns on ctx.Done(); its own doc-comment forbids a short-lived ctx (lifecycle.go:154-159, :166, :222-225). I checked for the guards a finder could have missed: (a) no context.WithoutCancel anywhere on this path (grep over cmd/ + internal/ shows 8 hits, none in the MQTT supervisor or REST middleware); (b) no other re-arm — retryInitialConnect is called only from Start (:336) and Lifecycle.Start refuses a second call; (c) TCPClient has no internal reconnect, it only signals ConnectionLost and the Lifecycle drives the redial (adapter_tcp.go:229-232, :806, pump.go:392); (d) the two Swap callers are the only ones in non-test code and both are short-lived — svc.Reload(r.Context()) via POST /api/v1/admin/mqtt/reload (admin_mqtt_reload.go:46, mounted router.go:1354, adapter forwards verbatim at mqtt_supervisor.go:723) and context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30s) with cancel() fired immediately after Swap returns (reload.go:124,142-143). StartHealthProbe binds the same way (health_probe.go:53,62), so the mqtt health component also stops being sampled. Reachability confirmed: the SPA has a Reload MQTT button (Settings.svelte:632 -> client.ts:1774). The project already fixed exactly this shape once for the boot retry path, with the rationale in a comment (mqtt_supervisor.go:422-431) and a regression test (mqtt_supervisor_test.go:548-608) — the same defect simply survives on the two remaining Swap callers. Consequence as written holds: the link keeps working until the next broker drop, then never reconnects and nothing logs it.

findings.title: A central adopted at runtime starts its scheduler on the HTTP request context, so every periodic job for that CCU dies the instant the response is written
findings.claim: `centralOrchestrator.adoptCentral(ctx, cc)` calls `unit.Start(ctx)` with the caller's context (cmd/openccu-loom/central_adopt.go:469). `central.Unit.Start` forwards it verbatim to `u.Scheduler.Start(ctx)` (internal/central/central.go:628). `Scheduler.Start` makes that context the governing context of every job goroutine — `ctx, s.stopFunc = context.WithCancel(ctx); s.runCtx = ctx; ... go s.runJob(ctx, j)` (internal/scheduler/scheduler.go:193-200) — and `runJob` returns on `case <-ctx.Done()` (:262-264). Every caller of `adoptCentral` supplies a request-scoped context: (a) `liveCentralAdmin.Put(ctx, row)` → `l.orch.adoptCentral(ctx, cc)` (central_adopt.go:829), reached from `handlers.CreateCentral`/`UpdateCentral` via `svc.Put(r.Context(), row)` (internal/north/rest/handlers/admin_centrals.go:209 and :270), mounted as `POST /api/v1/centrals` / `PUT /api/v1/centrals/{name}` on the decorated service (internal/north/rest/router.go:1349-1350, wired at cmd/openccu-loom/daemon.go:610 `newLiveCentralAdmin(rw.centralAdmin, centralOrch, logger)` and daemon.go:836 `centSvc: centralAdminSvc`); and (b) the first-run onboarding wizard — `finalizeSetup(r.Context(), s, &req)` (internal/north/rest/handlers/setup.go:151) → `s.Centrals.Put(ctx, row)` (setup.go:294), where `Centrals` is the same decorated service (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_rest_mount.go:362). No middleware detaches the request context (`grep -rn WithoutCancel` over internal/ + cmd/ shows no wrapper on this path), and net/http cancels `r.Context()` as soon as ServeHTTP returns. Nothing restarts the scheduler afterwards: `Scheduler.Start` rejects a second call (`s.started` → 'scheduler: already started', scheduler.go:188-191), and `reg.StartAll(ctx)` runs once at boot only (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon.go:182). The jobs registered immediately before that dead `Start` (central_adopt.go:466 `registerStandardJobsFor` / :467 `registerFirmwareJobsFor`) are: central.health_heartbeat, central.check_connection, central.reconcile, central.refresh_client_data, central.firmware_check, central.firmware_delivery_check, central.firmware_updating_check, hub.connectivity_refresh, hub.bidcos_interfaces_refresh, hub.last_event_age_refresh, hub.program_refresh, hub.sysvar_refresh, hub.inbox_refresh, hub.service_messages_refresh, hub.alarm_messages_refresh, hub.system_update_refresh, hub.install_mode_refresh (internal/central/jobs.go:363-733, cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_jobs.go:62-83). Note this is precisely the CLAUDE.md 'bracketing test' shape: every adopt test calls `orch.adoptCentral(ctx, ...)` directly with a test-lifetime ctx (cmd/openccu-loom/central_adopt_boot_parity_test.go:96 and 11 sibling files), so the wiring the REST surface actually uses is never exercised.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator completes the first-run wizard, or adds a second CCU from Settings → CCUs. The CCU comes up, devices load, push events flow (the south-bound bring-up correctly runs on the manager's own parent context). But from the moment the HTTP 201 is written, that CCU's system variables, programs, inbox, service messages, alarm messages, system-update state and install-mode never refresh again — they stay frozen at their bring-up values — the periodic firmware checks never run, the reconcile pass never runs, and `central.health_heartbeat` never fires, so `unit.Health`'s `central` component goes stale and the CCU's health tile decays to UNKNOWN. Everything looks correct right after onboarding and silently stops being maintained; only a daemon restart (which runs `reg.StartAll` with the daemon context) fixes it. Live CCU adopt is explicitly a restart-free operation (central_adopt.go:26 and the ADR-0042 wiring), so nothing prompts the operator to restart.
findings.verified_by: code trace end-to-end (REST handler → liveCentralAdmin.Put → adoptCentral → Unit.Start → Scheduler.Start → runJob) plus a measured reproducer at $S/repro/E1/reqctx/main.go, which starts the same scheduler-shaped loop from a real httptest handler using `r.Context()`: 0 job ticks in the 200 ms after the handler returns, versus 17 for the identical loop on a daemon-lifetime context.
findings.fix_sketch: Give `centralOrchestrator` a daemon-lifetime context (it already has `bringUp.parentCtx` for exactly this reason) and pass that to `unit.Start` in `adoptCentral`, keeping the caller's ctx for the bounded persistence/validation work only. Then add a black-box pin in `tests/e2e/` that adopts a CCU over REST and asserts the new central's scheduler still reports running jobs after the response has been read — an in-process test that calls `adoptCentral` itself gets to choose the context and will choose the working one.
findings.verify_reasoning: Re-derived independently and the chain is unbroken: adoptCentral passes its caller ctx to unit.Start (central_adopt.go:469) -> Unit.Start forwards it verbatim to u.Scheduler.Start(ctx) (central.go:628) -> Scheduler.Start makes it the parent of every job goroutine (scheduler.go:193-200) -> runJob returns on ctx.Done() (scheduler.go:262-264). I looked hard for the reason it is not a bug and found the opposite: adoptCentral has exactly ONE production caller (grep: central_adopt.go:829, liveCentralAdmin.Put), which is reached only from svc.Put(r.Context(), row) in CreateCentral/UpdateCentral (admin_centrals.go:209,270; routes router.go:1349-1351, decorator wired daemon.go:610 + daemon_rest_mount.go:352) and from finalizeSetup(r.Context(), ...) -> s.Centrals.Put(ctx, row) (setup.go:151,294). No middleware detaches the request context — RequestID and RequestContext only WithValue (middleware.go:42, reqcontext.go:58) and middleware.Timeout ADDS a deadline (middleware.go:168-172, applied router-wide via timeoutExceptStreaming), so the scheduler dies at the WriteTimeout even if the handler blocked. Nothing re-arms: Scheduler.Start rejects a second call (scheduler.go:188-191) and reg.StartAll runs once at boot (central_registry.go:298). The strongest corroboration is two lines below the defect: the southbound bring-up deliberately runs on the manager's own daemon-lifetime parentCtx (central_adopt.go:497 nolint + central_bringup.go:39,237,289), which is why the CCU comes up, devices load and the failure is completely silent — only the periodic plane (health_heartbeat, reconcile, refresh_client_data, the firmware jobs and every hub.*_refresh) is dead until restart.

findings.title: Reconciler.EmitNotReady publishes a synthetic "every interface unreachable" burst on every CCU outage, which now reaches the alarm engine's central-loss policy and can fire a siren on a routine CCU reboot
findings.claim: 0.61.3 added `reconcileRun` (internal/central/jobs.go:298-307): while `!isOperational(unit)` - i.e. the central's state is neither RUNNING nor DEGRADED (jobs.go:250-256), which for a total CCU outage means FAILED (internal/central/central.go:1300-1301: no client connected -> FAILED) - the reconcile job runs `Reconciler.EmitNotReady` instead. `emitNotReadyConnectivity` (internal/central/coordinators/reconciler.go:390-408) walks the connectivity aggregate and, for every entry still marked reachable, calls `conn.OnStateWithInterface(..., false)` AND publishes `hmevent.ConnectivityChangedEvent{Reachable:false}`. This directly contradicts the deliberate design documented 90 lines above it in the same file: `reconcileVanishedInterfaces` (reconciler.go:246-262) refuses to derive down-events from an empty probe answer precisely because "Reading either as 'every interface went down' would run the alarm domain's central-loss escalation on every CCU restart". The escalation is real and reachable: `alarm.Service.onConnectivity` (internal/alarm/inputs.go:199-230) recomputes `allEnrolledDownLocked` and, on the whole-central transition, calls `s.engine.HandleCentralConnectivity(ctx, centralName, false)` (inputs.go:230); `Engine.HandleCentralConnectivity` (internal/alarm/engine/engine.go:1097-1104) triggers the zone (`e.trigger(..., causeKindCentralLost, ...)`, engine.go:1101) when the zone is armed and `cfg.CentralLoss == hmenum.AlarmCentralLossTrigger`, and journals a fault otherwise. `HandleCentralConnectivity` has exactly one production caller (that one), and before 0.61.3 the only two producers of `Reachable:false` were `reconcileConnectivity` (reconciler.go:228) and `reconcileVanishedInterfaces` (reconciler.go:301) - both of which require a *successful* probe against a reachable CCU. A total CCU outage therefore could not reach the central-loss policy at all before this change.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator with an armed alarm zone configured `central_loss = trigger` reboots the CCU for a firmware update. The central goes FAILED; on the next 5-minute reconcile tick EmitNotReady publishes reachable=false for every interface, the alarm service sees all enrolled interfaces down and the engine triggers the zone - the siren sounds and an incident is opened for what is a planned maintenance reboot. On the default policy (`alert`) the same reboot now writes a `central_lost_while_armed` fault to every armed zone's journal on every CCU restart. Neither behaviour existed in 0.61.2, and the 0.61.3 release notes describe the change only as "system_health and per-interface connectivity report 'unknown' during a CCU outage".
findings.verified_by: code trace of the whole chain: jobs.go:298-307 + 250-256 -> central.go:1279-1301 -> reconciler.go:390-408 -> internal/alarm/inputs.go:199-230 -> internal/alarm/engine/engine.go:1064-1105; exhaustive grep confirming the three ConnectivityChangedEvent producers and the single HandleCentralConnectivity caller
findings.fix_sketch: Either keep the demotion local to the state the fix was about - update the connectivity aggregate and the retained MQTT/REST view without publishing ConnectivityChangedEvent (e.g. a distinct `ConnectivityUnknownEvent`, or a flag on the event that the alarm subscriber ignores) - or make the alarm side deliberate: decide (and document) that a FAILED central drives the central-loss policy, and gate it behind the same carenz the reconciler's vanished-interface logic uses so a short reconnect cannot escalate.
findings.verify_reasoning: Every link holds and there is no guard anywhere between them. (1) reconcileRun (internal/central/jobs.go:298-308) runs notReady whenever isOperational(unit) is false; isOperational (jobs.go:250-256) accepts only RUNNING/DEGRADED, and a total CCU outage leaves no client CONNECTED, which EvaluateCentralState (internal/central/central.go:1279-1301) maps to FAILED. RECOVERING never appears (ConnectionRecoveryCoordinator.sm is deliberately nil, connection_recovery.go:320-327), so FAILED is the reachable non-operational state. (2) The daemon wires jobs.ReconcileNotReady = u.Reconciler.EmitNotReady unconditionally (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_jobs.go:145); the reconcile job ticks every defaultReconcileSlot = 5 min (jobs.go:193, 726-738). (3) emitNotReadyConnectivity (coordinators/reconciler.go:390-409) walks conn.List() and, for EVERY entry still Reachable, publishes ConnectivityChangedEvent{Reachable:false}. No reason code, no debounce, no consecutive-failure counter, no grace period. (4) The ids line up: observeProbeLatency (adapter/hub_wiring.go:494-512) rewrites every probe entry's InterfaceID to the wire form <central>-<iface>, which is exactly the space the alarm dpIndex is keyed in (alarm/inputs.go:41-45). (5) alarm.Service.onConnectivity (inputs.go:199-231) recomputes allEnrolledDownLocked and calls engine.HandleCentralConnectivity(ctx, central, false) on the whole-central transition; the engine (alarm/engine/engine.go:1064-1105) triggers when the zone is armed and cfg.CentralLoss == trigger, else journals central_lost_while_armed. The subscriber cannot distinguish 'not ready' from 'lost' — the event carries only Reachable. I built the missing half of the chain as a test: EmitNotReady alone, with no probe and no CCU, journals central_lost_while_armed under the default 'alert' policy and drives the zone to TRIGGERED with an incident under 'trigger'. The pre-0.61.3 claim also survives: the probe errors out against a down CCU (adapter/connectivity_probe.go:55-57) so reconcileConnectivity emits nothing, and reconcileVanishedInterfaces explicitly refuses to read an empty answer as a down burst (reconciler.go:247-276) for this exact reason. Severity: not medium. Default policy is 'alert' (engine/config.go:288-289), so the default-config damage is a fault journal entry per armed zone plus every sensor of the central marked unavailable on every CCU reboot that outlives a reconcile tick — annoying but honest-ish. With the documented 'trigger' policy a routine firmware-update reboot fires the siren and opens an incident. A physical false alarm on planned maintenance, with no operator-visible knob between the reboot and the siren, is high.

findings.title: The new socket-aware logout no longer revokes an OIDC user's server-side session, so the session id stays a valid credential for its full TTL after an explicit logout
findings.claim: The fix replaced logout's revoke-by-cookie-id with revoke-by-subject. internal/north/rest/handlers/auth.go:313-321: `subject` is taken from the resolved identity and, when a revoker is wired, the handler takes `case revoker != nil && subject != "": revoker.RevokeBySubject(subject)` — the `default:` branch that still calls `d.Sessions.Revoke(c.Value)` is now unreachable in production, because cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_rest_mount.go:343 always wires `d.credentialRevoker()` and every authenticated request carries a non-empty subject. That composed revoker (internal/north/rest/ws/credential_revocation.go:53-60) delegates to `SessionStore.RevokeBySubject`, and internal/auth/session.go:190-211 skips federated sessions outright: `if sess.Identity.Scheme.Federated() { continue }`. internal/auth/auth.go:38 defines `Federated()` as `s == SchemeOIDC`, internal/auth/oidc/client.go:408 stamps every OIDC identity with `Scheme: auth.SchemeOIDC`, internal/north/rest/handlers/oidc.go:230 issues the session from that identity, and internal/auth/session.go:263-271 deliberately preserves SchemeOIDC when the session is resolved. Net: for an OIDC principal RevokeBySubject evicts zero sessions; only `auth.ClearSessionCookie(w)` (auth.go:326) runs, which clears the browser cookie and nothing server-side. The old code path (`d.Sessions.Revoke(sid)`, session.go:166) deleted by id and was scheme-agnostic, so this is a regression introduced by the fix, not a pre-existing gap.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator signs in through OIDC (Keycloak/Authelia) and clicks Logout in the SPA. The browser cookie is cleared and the SPA shows the login page, but the session row survives in the in-memory store and in SQLite until its TTL expires. Any copy of that cookie value — a shared/kiosk browser where the value was read before logout, a reverse-proxy access log, a captured request, a restored backup of the auth_sessions table — still authenticates as that principal with its full role. Logging out is the operator's only means of ending a session; there is no admin 'revoke session' surface for a federated principal either, since every subject-keyed control skips federated rows by design.
findings.verified_by: code trace: handlers/auth.go:310-327 -> router.go:720 -> daemon_rest_mount.go:343 -> ws/credential_revocation.go:53-60 -> auth/session.go:190-211 (federated `continue`) -> auth/auth.go:38 -> auth/oidc/client.go:408 + handlers/oidc.go:230 + auth/session.go:263-271. No test covers a federated logout: handlers/auth_test.go's new TestLogout_WithRevoker_ClosesSocketsBySubject asserts only that RevokeBySubject was called, and router_test.go's TestRouter_Logout_ClosesSocketsBySubject uses a stub revoker, so neither reaches the SessionStore's federated skip.
findings.fix_sketch: Keep the by-subject revocation for the socket teardown, but always also revoke the presented cookie session by id: read the session cookie and call `d.Sessions.Revoke(c.Value)` unconditionally (not in an exclusive switch arm). Pin it with a test that issues an OIDC-scheme session, logs out, and asserts `store.Lookup(sid) == nil`.
findings.verify_reasoning: Measured, not just traced. I wrote a reproducer that drives the real Logout handler against a real auth.SessionStore for both schemes: scheme=session -> session gone after logout; scheme=oidc -> 204 returned and store.Lookup(sid) still resolves the session. The mechanism is as claimed and I found no second revoke path: the switch in Logout is exclusive (auth.go:310-325) and the default arm is unreachable in production because credentialRevoker() is nil only when d.sessions is nil (daemon_rest_mount.go:343,638-643); revokeBySubject skips every federated row by design (session.go:200-205) and Federated() is exactly SchemeOIDC (auth.go:38), which SessionMiddleware deliberately preserves on resolve (session.go:262-271). There is only one logout route (router.go:720) — no OIDC-specific server-side logout exists — and git -L confirms the pre-3914578d handler revoked unconditionally by cookie id, so this is a 0.61.3 regression, not a pre-existing gap. Two corrections in the finding's favour: the damage is broader than stated — Hub.CloseBySubject skips federated identities for the same reason (hub.go:148-171), so an OIDC user's logout also fails to tear down their open WebSocket, which keeps full command authority; and the socket teardown that the fix was written to deliver therefore does not happen for OIDC principals either.

findings.title: CUxD addresses were added to the central-scoped routing-key family without a migration, a golden fixture, a parity case or a doc update, so every existing install's CUxD entity identities change on upgrade and the documented cross-backend contract the HA drop-in implements now disagrees with the daemon
findings.claim: needsCentralPrefix gained `strings.HasPrefix(address, "CUX")` (internal/routingkey/uniqueid.go:35 const, :118 test). That function is the whole of NeedsCentralScope (:105) and the central-prefix decision inside GenerateUniqueID (:145), which CanonicalUniqueID wraps (internal/routingkey/canonical.go:61-63). Three consequences, all unconditional on the number of configured CCUs: (a) internal/north/mqtt/discovery.go:1462-1465 (scopedUniqueID) now emits `loom_<serial10>_cux2801001_1_state` where 0.61.2 emitted `loom_cux2801001_1_state`, and additionally withholds every CUxD entity while the CCU serial is unresolved; (b) internal/north/mqtt/discovery.go:1302 (physicalDeviceIdentifier) now emits the HA device-block identifier `openccu-loom_<central-slug>_cux2801001` instead of `openccu-loom_cux2801001`; (c) every REST/WS payload `unique_id` built through routingkey.CanonicalUniqueID (internal/central/adapter/eventbridge.go:1246, internal/north/rest/handlers/devices.go:943, internal/north/rest/ws/hub_events.go:260, ...) changes the same way. The MQTT discovery TOPIC does NOT change — it is built from naming.PathData (discovery.go:489-490), not from the unique_id — so the boot orphan sweep never sees an orphan and the retained config is simply overwritten with a different identity. Nothing migrates the old key: `docs/external-clients/ha-unique-id-migration.md:92-98` specifies the client-side rewrite as `entry_suffix`-prefixed keys -> serial-prefixed, everything else -> bare `loom_<old>`; `docs/external-clients/ha-unique-id-migration.md:44-49` and the schema exporter (script/export_schemas.go:244-247, which exports only the four hub pseudo-addresses) both still enumerate the scoped families as hub roots + INT000* + virtual remotes only, with no CUxD. The golden fixtures the package doc calls the contract of record (tests/contract/testdata/routing_key/*.json) carry no CUX case, and script/routing_key_parity.py only replays those fixtures, so the Go<->Python guard cannot see the divergence. The change's own comment calls it 'a deliberate multi-CCU divergence from the ... Python reference', but notes/parity/by_design.md has no entry for it (grep: no CUX/cuxd routing-key entry).
findings.failure_scenario: An existing (even single-CCU) install with CUxD devices — the common Homematic setup for Sonos/exec/system pseudo-devices — upgrades to 0.61.3. On the next discovery pass every CUxD entity's retained config is republished on the SAME topic but with a new `unique_id` and a new device `identifiers` value, so Home Assistant re-registers each entity under a new key: the previous registry entry (its entity_id, history, area, customisations, automations referencing it) is orphaned and the new entity typically appears as `<name>_2` under a second, empty device card beside the old one. Independently, a drop-in client (homematicip_local / py-openccu-loom-client) that rebuilds the key per the published contract computes `loom_cux2801001_1_state` while the daemon's payload `unique_id` says `loom_11a0001234_cux2801001_1_state`, so its rebuild path routes CUxD value changes to an entity that does not exist. Secondary: on a central whose serial is not yet resolved, scopedUniqueID now suppresses all CUxD entities where it previously published them.

findings.title: resolveScheduleDomain classifies only 3 of the 7 real *_WEEK_PROFILE channel types, so HmIP-RGBW/LSC/DRG-DALI and HmIP-HDM1/HDM2 get an empty schedule domain and MQTT reports them as switches
findings.claim: Ground truth (godevccu device+paramset descriptions, extracted to $S/repro/B1/channel_type_by_device.json) says exactly seven channel types end in WEEK_PROFILE on real devices: SWITCH_WEEK_PROFILE (25 devices), BLIND_WEEK_PROFILE (5), DIMMER_WEEK_PROFILE (6), DIMMER_OUTPUT_BEHAVIOUR_WEEK_PROFILE (3), UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_WEEK_PROFILE (3: HmIP-RGBW, HmIP-LSC, HmIP-DRG-DALI), SHADING_WEEK_PROFILE (2: HmIP-HDM1, HmIP-HDM2), WATER_SWITCH_WEEK_PROFILE (1: ELV-SH-WSM). domainFromWeekProfileType (schedules.go:532-549) tests twelve prefixes; only SWITCH_WEEK, DIMMER_WEEK and BLIND_WEEK match anything real. Nine prefixes -- LIGHT_WEEK, COVER_WEEK, SHUTTER_WEEK, LOCK_WEEK, DOOR_LOCK_WEEK, VALVE_WEEK, WATER_WEEK, HEATING_WEEK, CLIMATECONTROL_WEEK -- match no channel type in either godevccu's 399-device fleet or openccu-data's 234-entry OCCU channel-type table, so they are dead branches. UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_WEEK_PROFILE does not start with LIGHT_WEEK and SHADING_WEEK_PROFILE matches nothing, so both fall through to the actor-type fallback at schedules.go:521-526; that fallback scans the device's other channels with domainFromActorType (schedules.go:553-572), and those devices carry only MAINTENANCE plus UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_RECEIVER / SHADING_RECEIVER, neither of which matches any prefix there either. resolveScheduleDomain therefore returns "". Simulated over the whole fleet by $S/repro/B1/sim_schedule_domain.py: 5 of the 45 schedule-capable devices resolve to no domain. Two consumers are affected. (a) REST: GetClimateSchedule (schedules.go:446-454) puts that empty string into ClimateSchedule.Domain; the SPA's SimpleScheduleEditor.svelte derives `domain` from it (line 30-40) and dispatches the level widget on it -- domain "" hits the `{:else}` generic branch at line 501-515 and renders a bare 0..1 numeric input instead of the percent slider, the ramp_time field at line 628 is gated on `domain === "light"` and is hidden even though UNIVERSAL_LIGHT_WEEK_PROFILE really carries <NN>_WP_RAMP_TIME_BASE/_FACTOR, and the cover position+slat controls at line 356-393 are gated on `domain === "cover"` so HmIP-HDM1/HDM2's real <NN>_WP_LEVEL_2 (slat/shading angle) has no editor at all. (b) MQTT: EventBridge.scheduleDomainForChannel (eventbridge.go:3094-3107) treats an empty result as unresolvable and falls back to the literal "switch", which is published as the Zeitplan sensor's `schedule_domain` attribute at eventbridge.go:3173. The doc comment at schedules.go:113-119 compounds the drift: it names HEATING_WEEK_PROFILE (HmIP-FALMOT, HmIP-eTRV-CL) and COVER_WEEK_PROFILE (HmIP-BBL, HmIP-BROLL) as "examples observed on real CCUs"; ground truth says HmIP-BROLL carries BLIND_WEEK_PROFILE and no device anywhere carries HEATING_WEEK_PROFILE or COVER_WEEK_PROFILE.

The domain badge is absent, every switch point shows a raw '0.4'-style number box instead of a brightness slider, and the ramp-time field the device supports is not offered. In Home Assistant the same device's Zeitplan sensor carries attribute schedule_domain='switch'. On an HmIP-HDM1 shading actuator the slat/second-level control is missing entirely, so the operator can read but not edit the shading angle of a switch point.

findings.title: Blind.SetPosition/SetTilt re-send a permanently stale staged target for the axis the caller did not touch, because hasTgt/hasTgt2 are never cleared
findings.claim: Blind stages the commanded axis into b.target/b.target2 and sets b.hasTgt/b.hasTgt2 = true (blind.go:176-178 in SetPosition, :209-210 in SetTilt, :342-345 in SetCombined). A repo-wide grep over internal/model/custom/cover/*.go (non-test) shows these two flags are set in exactly those three places and cleared nowhere — not on CCU confirmation, not on Stop, not on teardown. SetPosition then reads `tilt, hasTilt := b.target2, b.hasTgt2` (blind.go:178) and only falls back to the currently observed LEVEL_2 `if !hasTilt` (blind.go:180-187). Once any tilt command has ever run, hasTgt2 stays true for the lifetime of the DP, so every later SetPosition writes the ancient staged tilt. sendCombined then emits COMBINED_PARAMETER = "L2=<stale>,L=<new>" (blind.go:301) or LEVEL_COMBINED (blind.go:296). The reference does the opposite: CustomDpBlind._set_level (cover.py:497-540) reads self._target_tilt_level, which is defined (cover.py:322-338) as the *unconfirmed* optimistic value only — it returns None once the CCU has confirmed — and then falls back to self._group_tilt_level, i.e. the currently observed slat position (cover.py:305-313). The same defect applies symmetrically to SetTilt reusing the stale b.target for LEVEL (blind.go:211-220). Reachable from production: custom_dp_dispatcher.go:631 'set_position' -> Blind.SetPosition; the MQTT cover component and the REST/WS command surface both route through it. Secondary effect of the same never-cleared flags: `wasMoving := b.hasTgt || b.hasTgt2` (blind.go:175/208/341) is true for every command after the first, so a STOP is emitted before every subsequent move (blind.go:284-286) whereas the reference only stops when a target is genuinely in flight (cover.py:534-540).
findings.failure_scenario: HmIP-BBL (BlindKindIP). Operator sets the slats to fully open: SetTilt(1.0) -> COMBINED_PARAMETER "L2=100,L=<pos>", target2=1.0, hasTgt2=true. Hours later the slats are closed from the wall switch or a CCU program, so LEVEL_2 = 0.0 is the observed state. Operator now drags the position slider to 50 %: openccu-loom writes COMBINED_PARAMETER = "L2=100,L=50" and the slats snap back to fully open, which the operator never asked for. aiohomematic would write "L2=0,L=50".
findings.verified_by: code trace: blind.go:170-189 / 194-222 / 266-307 / 340-347 plus `grep -rn 'hasTgt' internal/model/custom/cover/*.go` (no reset site outside those three setters); reference cover.py:305-313, 322-338, 497-540
findings.fix_sketch: Treat target/target2 as unconfirmed-command state, not permanent state: clear hasTgt/hasTgt2 when the corresponding LEVEL / LEVEL_2 echo confirms the staged value (and on Stop), so the fallback to the observed TiltPosition()/Position() takes over exactly as _target_tilt_level -> _group_tilt_level does in the reference. That also restores the reference STOP condition.
findings.verify_reasoning: Both halves reproduced against the production Blind. hasTgt/hasTgt2 are written in exactly three places (blind.go:177/210, :209/210, :344-345) and cleared nowhere in the package. Scenario driven end to end: observed LEVEL 0.30 / LEVEL_2 0.20 -> SetTilt(1.0) -> CCU confirms both -> LEVEL_2 later observed 0.0 (wall switch) -> SetPosition(0.50) emits COMBINED_PARAMETER "L2=100,L=50" instead of the reference's "L2=0,L=50": the slats snap fully open on a pure position move. The reference derives _target_tilt_level from the DP's optimistic/unconfirmed state and falls back to _group_tilt_level once the CCU confirms (cover.py:305-313, 322-338, 497-540), so this is a semantic divergence, not a port style choice. The secondary claim also holds, with one qualification the finding omits: the spurious STOP only reaches the wire when Capabilities.SupportsStop is set — which every cover profile does (cover/init.go), so with SupportsStop the reproducer records stopCount=1 on the second command against a stationary blind. Physical wrong movement of a slat on a device that carries the tilt axis keeps this at high.

findings.title: docs/external-clients/mcp.md omits an entire MCP tool family (6 of 25 tools, including 3 write/actuation tools) and states a wrong total
findings.claim: mcp.md:109 states 'Nineteen tools, in two tiers: 16 read tools + 3 write tools' and lists exactly those 19 in the tables at lines 127-144 (16 read) and 152-156 (3 write). The actual server registers 25 tools: internal/north/mcp/tools_alarm.go registers list_alarm_zones (line 70), list_triggered_motion (111), get_security_status (160) unconditionally inside registerReadTools (tools.go:200-204), and arm_alarm_zone (207), disarm_alarm_zone (232), reset_motion (253) inside registerWriteTools (tools.go:461-463, gated correctly on AllowWrites -- no security bug in the gating itself). None of these six names, nor the words 'alarm' (beyond the one documented list_alarm_messages) or 'security' or 'motion', appear anywhere in mcp.md. Section 4 ('Read-only vs. write posture') at mcp.md:249-273 tells operators that flipping allow_writes registers 'the three write tools' (set_datapoint, write_paramset, trigger_program) and frames the decision as 'treat allow_writes: true as you would handing an automation script write access to your home' -- without ever mentioning that the same flag also registers arm_alarm_zone and disarm_alarm_zone (able to arm/disarm the alarm engine) and reset_motion (clears latched motion triggers).

In fact the LLM agent can also arm/disarm the configured alarm zones and reset motion-sensor latches -- capabilities the doc never surfaces, so the operator's risk assessment (and the doc's own 'treat this like handing an automation script write access' framing) is made on incomplete information.

findings.title: An established WebSocket connection never expires: session absolute/idle TTL and bearer-token expires_at are enforced only when a credential is resolved, so a socket keeps its captured role indefinitely
findings.claim: The upgrade handler captures the identity once (`if id, ok := auth.IdentityFrom(r.Context()); ok { c.SetIdentity(id) }`, internal/north/rest/ws/handler.go:149-151) and nothing re-resolves it. Every later command is gated on that snapshot (internal/north/rest/ws/client.go:710 puts `c.Identity()` into the dispatch context; internal/north/rest/ws/commands.go:396-408 checks it against writeCommandRoles). Both credential classes carry a server-side expiry that is checked only at resolve time: (a) sessions — `SessionStore.Lookup` (internal/auth/session.go:145-163) evicts on `now.After(sess.Expires)` (12h SessionTTL, internal/auth/session.go:20) or IdleTTL, and is only ever called from `SessionMiddleware` on an HTTP request (internal/auth/session.go:260); (b) bearer tokens — `sqlite.TokenStore.AuthenticateToken` rejects on `expiresAt.Valid && !time.Now().UTC().Before(expiresAt.Time)` (internal/store/sqlite/tokens.go:215), and is only called from `Middleware.resolve` (internal/auth/chain.go... internal/auth/middleware.go:84) on an HTTP request. The only paths that reach an open socket are explicit revocations: `Hub.CloseBySubject` (internal/north/rest/ws/hub.go:154) and `Hub.CloseByToken` (hub.go:181), invoked from Logout, ChangeOwnPassword, UpdateUser, DeleteUser and DELETE /auth/tokens/v2/{fingerprint}. The background sweep that does handle expiry — `startSessionPurge` -> `SessionStore.PurgeExpired` (cmd/openccu-loom/session_purge.go:55, internal/auth/session.go:227) — deletes rows from memory and SQLite and never touches the hub. The socket itself is unbounded in time: writePump pings every 30s (client.go:41) and readPump only requires a frame within 60s (client.go:45), so a client that answers pings holds the connection forever. hub.go:139-140 states the property outright ('for as long as the socket lives, which is unbounded for a client that answers pings') but only draws the revocation conclusion from it, not the expiry one.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator logs into the SPA at 09:00 and leaves the tab open; the browser's WebSocket to /api/v1/events stays connected. At 21:00 the 12h session expires — every REST call from that tab now answers 401 and the SPA shows the login screen — but the socket is still registered in the hub and still dispatches `paramset.put`, `alarm_panel.disarm`, `programs.execute`, `sysvars.set` under the operator identity captured at 09:00. The same holds for a stolen session cookie used to open one socket, and for an API token created with an explicit `expires_at`: after the expiry timestamp the token is refused on every HTTP request while the WebSocket it opened keeps full command authority until the daemon restarts. The documented bounded lifetime of both credential classes is therefore not enforced on the WS command plane at all.
findings.verified_by: code trace: handler.go:143-151 (capture, never re-resolved) -> client.go:702-715 (dispatch uses the snapshot) -> commands.go:396-408 (role gate reads the snapshot); expiry enforcement points session.go:145-163 and sqlite/tokens.go:215 are reachable only from SessionMiddleware/Middleware.resolve on an HTTP request; grep for CloseBySubject/CloseByToken shows only explicit-revocation callers (credential_revocation.go:58/72, handlers/admin_tokens.go); session_purge.go has no hub reference.
findings.fix_sketch: Give the client a credential deadline: store the session's Expires (and the token's ExpiresAt) alongside the identity at upgrade and have writePump's existing 30s ping ticker close the connection once it passes, or have the hourly PurgeExpired sweep call a new Hub.CloseExpired that drops any client whose captured credential is no longer resolvable. Pin it with a boot-order-style test that opens a socket, advances the clock past the TTL, and asserts the next command is refused.
findings.verify_reasoning: Re-derived and I could not find the compensating re-validation. The identity is captured once at upgrade (handler.go:143-151) and the comment there concedes it: 'the raw credential is not retained, so it cannot be re-resolved here'. Every later command reads that snapshot through the dispatch context (client.go:702-715 -> commands.go:396-408 role gate). Both expiry checks are unreachable from the socket: SessionStore.Lookup has exactly one caller in non-test code, SessionMiddleware (grep -> internal/auth/session.go:261 only), and TokenStore.AuthenticateToken is called only from the HTTP middleware and from the voluntary in-band reauth op (ws/client.go:329) — a client that never sends reauth is never re-checked. grep for Expires/expiry/deadline across internal/north/rest/ws/ finds only frame-level write deadlines; the socket itself is unbounded (pingInterval 30s / readTimeout 60s, client.go:40-45) and a hijacked connection escapes http.Server's IdleTimeout. The purge sweep touches memory + SQLite only (session.go:224-...); it has no hub reference. The /events route sits behind the protected router (router.go:1365-1366), so both credential classes reach it, including a Bearer-token machine client whose token carries an explicit expires_at — the strongest form of the bug, since that expiry is an operator's deliberate bound and it is simply not enforced on this plane. Severity stays high rather than critical because the attacker must already hold a valid credential at upgrade time; nothing about the gate is bypassable from an unauthenticated position.

findings.title: CUxD entity unique_ids gained a CCU-serial prefix with no migration, no republish and no retained-message cleanup, so every CUxD entity in Home Assistant is orphaned and duplicated on upgrade
findings.claim: 1) `needsCentralPrefix` gained a `strings.HasPrefix(address, "CUX")` branch (internal/routingkey/uniqueid.go:118, added in 3914578d / release 0.61.3), so `GenerateUniqueID` now prepends the central id for every CUxD address (uniqueid.go:145-147). 2) The MQTT discovery builder feeds that through `scopedUniqueID` → `routingkey.CanonicalUniqueID(serial, chAddr, param, "")` (internal/north/mqtt/discovery.go:503, canonical.go:61-63), so the payload's `unique_id` changes from `loom_cux2801001_1_state` to `loom_<serial10>_cux2801001_1_state` — measured, see verified_by. 3) The discovery TOPIC does not change: nodeID/objectID come from `PathData.DiscoveryNodeID`/`DiscoveryObjectID` (internal/north/mqtt/discovery.go:489-490 → internal/model/naming/pathdata.go:404-413 and :426-431), which are built from central slug + address + channel + parameter and never touch the unique_id. 4) Nothing clears the stale payload. `RunDiscoveryOrphanCleanupOnce` (internal/north/mqtt/retain_cleanup.go:684) compares retained TOPICS against what the build declared, and the topic is unchanged, so the config is not an orphan. The one sweep written for exactly this shape — same topic, changed id — is `RunUnscopedDiscoveryCleanupOnce` (retain_cleanup.go:966), and its gate is `strings.HasPrefix(body.UniqueID, "loom__")` (retain_cleanup.go:932/937/1036); the pre-0.61.3 CUxD id is `loom_cux…`, which does not match (measured). 5) The same id also changes on REST and WebSocket: `generic.DataPoint.CanonicalUniqueID` (internal/model/generic/payload.go:53), `handlers/custom_data_points.go:157,172`, `ws/device_trigger.go:104`, `ws/optimistic_rollback.go:97` all call the same routingkey helpers. 6) `physicalDeviceIdentifier` (internal/north/mqtt/discovery.go:1300-1306) consults the same predicate, so the HA device-block `identifiers` for a CUxD device changes from `openccu-loom_cux2801001` to `openccu-loom_<central-slug>_cux2801001` as well — a second, independent registry key. 7) The published client-side migration cannot repair it: `migrate_unique_id` in docs/external-clients/ha-unique-id-migration.md returns None for any key already starting with `loom_`, which every pre-0.61.3 CUxD key does (measured).
findings.failure_scenario: An operator running 0.61.2 (or any 0.6x/0.5x build) with CUxD devices — the usual Sonos/exec/system-info bridges, plus every CUxD-backed switch — upgrades to 0.61.4. The daemon republishes the identical retained discovery topics with a new `unique_id` inside. Home Assistant keys its entity registry on unique_id, so the old entities stay registered under ids nothing publishes any more (permanently `unavailable`, and restored from the retained config on every HA restart), while a full set of duplicates appears beside them with `_2` entity_id suffixes. Every dashboard card, automation and script that names the old entity_id is now pointed at a dead entity, and the operator has to clear the retained topics by hand or delete and re-add the entities one by one. The same break hits the REST/WS `unique_id` field the HA drop-in integration stores.
findings.verified_by: Reproducer at /tmp/claude-1000/-home-markus-Dokumente-GitHub-openccu-loom/1a822723-58a2-4e8f-9fea-bf6674f96b75/scratchpad/audit/repro/E6-upgrade-compat (copies internal/routingkey into a standalone module and re-implements the v0.61.2 predicate beside it). Plus the code trace above.
findings.fix_sketch: Extend the boot-time same-topic sweep to cover this class: broaden `payloadCarriesUnscopedUniqueID` into a general "the retained payload's unique_id is not the one this build would emit for this topic" check (the builder can recompute the expected id from the topic's node_id/object_id), so the stale config is cleared before `PublishInitialSnapshot` republishes. Alternatively ship a one-shot id-migration list (old→new) that the sweep consumes, and add the CUxD rewrite rule to docs/external-clients/ha-unique-id-migration.md so the drop-in client's registry migration runs a second pass.
findings.verify_reasoning: Shared mechanism verified from source and measured. git log -L on uniqueid.go:105-125 shows the `strings.HasPrefix(address, "CUX")` branch was added in 3914578d (0.61.3) and nothing else in that commit compensates (its only retain_cleanup.go change is the unrelated discoveryNodeIDBelongsTo node-id segment fix). Measured in the throwaway worktree with the repo's own package: CUX2801001:1/STATE -> `loom_11a0001234_cux2801001_1_state` scoped=true, VCU1234567:1 unchanged; the pre-0.61.3 form is `loom_cux2801001_1_state` (the CUX address simply missed needsCentralPrefix). The specific consequence claims each hold: (1) the discovery TOPIC is independent of the unique_id — node_id/object_id come from naming.PathData (discovery.go:489-490, pathdata.go:404-413/426-431) and were not touched — so the retained config is overwritten in place; (2) neither sweep catches it: RunDiscoveryOrphanCleanupOnce compares topics, and the one sweep written for exactly this class (same topic, changed id) gates on unscopedUniqueIDMarker = "loom_"+"_" = `loom__` (retain_cleanup.go:929-937,1036), which the old `loom_cux…` id does not match; (3) physicalDeviceIdentifier consults the same predicate (discovery.go:1300-1306) so the HA device-block identifier changes too — a second, independent registry key; (4) the same id changes on REST/WS through routingkey.CanonicalUniqueID (canonical.go:61-63). The claimed HA-side outcome (old entity orphaned, duplicate created) is not my measurement, but it is the project's own stated model of HA in the doc-comment of the sweep that exists for this class: "Home Assistant keys its registry on unique_id, so the corrected payload creates a second entity beside the stale one instead of replacing it" (retain_cleanup.go:946-951). I lowered critical->high only for scope: it hits installs with CUxD devices, and the damage is orphaned HA registry entries (manually repairable), not destroyed daemon data. Within a CUxD install the impact is total for that device class. One escalation the finding understates: scopedUniqueID now WITHHOLDS every CUxD entity while the CCU serial is unresolved (discovery.go:1462-1465), so a central whose serial never resolves loses all CUxD entities permanently, not transiently.

findings.title: The CUxD central-scoping is a declared Go-vs-Python routing-key divergence that no golden fixture pins and no contract document records, so a client that rebuilds the key emits an id the daemon never publishes
findings.claim: 1) internal/routingkey/uniqueid.go:28-35 states the CUX branch is "a deliberate multi-CCU divergence from the single-per-central Python reference (which does not scope CUxD)". 2) The cross-repo guard is a two-sided fixture pin: `tests/contract/routing_key_contract_test.go:14-30` asserts Go == fixtures, and `script/routing_key_parity.py` (header, lines 5-22) asserts Python == fixtures, so that Go == Python. `grep -i cux tests/contract/testdata/routing_key/*.json` returns nothing — no fixture case carries a CUxD address, so the divergence is invisible to both halves of the guard and `make routing-key-parity` stays green while Go and the reference disagree. 3) CLAUDE.md requires a deliberate divergence to be recorded in notes/parity/by_design.md; the routing-key entry there (notes/parity/by_design.md:75-116, BD-Identity-RoutingKeyNamespaces) still says internal/routingkey "mirrors the shared routing-key contract bit-for-bit and is locked by a golden-fixture test", and `grep -in cux notes/parity/by_design.md` finds only unrelated cuxd_backend / throttle-pool rows. 4) The published external-client contract still enumerates the scoped address classes without CUxD: docs/external-clients/ha-unique-id-migration.md ("the CCU serial … for the address classes whose addresses repeat across CCUs: hub roots (sysvar/program/install_mode), internal addresses (INT000*), and virtual-remote channels") and its `migrate_unique_id` reference implementation. 5) That same document specifies the client behaviour: it consumes the payload's `unique_id` when present and "rebuilds the key from the raw fields when it is absent (e.g. before the CCU serial is known)". The rebuild follows the document, so for a CUxD data point it yields `loom_cux2801001_1_state` while every daemon surface now says `loom_<serial10>_cux2801001_1_state`.
findings.failure_scenario: A drop-in client author implements or maintains the routing key against the published contract (or against the Python reference, which the parity script treats as the source of truth). Every CUxD data point rebuilds to a key the daemon never emits, so the client's registry entry for a CUxD entity is orphaned and its value updates route to nothing — and the two guards that exist to catch exactly this (the golden fixtures and make routing-key-parity) both pass, because no CUxD case is in the fixture set.
findings.verified_by: Code trace + `grep -i cux` over tests/contract/testdata/routing_key/, script/routing_key_parity.py, notes/parity/by_design.md and docs/external-clients/ (all negative). The client-side half (that a real client rebuilds per this document) is stated by the document itself; I could not read the client repo, which is outside this tree.
findings.fix_sketch: Add CUxD cases to tests/contract/testdata/routing_key/unique_id_golden.json, teach script/routing_key_parity.py to expect (and assert) the divergence rather than parity for that class, record the divergence under notes/parity/by_design.md → BD-Identity-RoutingKeyNamespaces, and update docs/external-clients/ha-unique-id-migration.md + ha-drop-in-identity-and-scoping.md with the new scoped class and the second-pass registry rewrite.
findings.verify_reasoning: Every leg re-checked, including the one the finder could not: I read the Python reference directly. aiohomematic/model/support.py:484-509 generate_unique_id scopes ONLY the four hub pseudo-addresses, INT000* and VIRTUAL_REMOTE_ADDRESSES — there is no CUX branch — so Go and the Python source of truth now genuinely disagree for every CUxD address, exactly as uniqueid.go:28-35 declares. The guard really is blind to it: script/routing_key_parity.py's own header (lines 5-22) states the construction is Go==fixtures + Python==fixtures => Go==Python, and it replays only the fixture cases; `grep -ril cux tests/contract/testdata/routing_key/` returns nothing, so `make routing-key-parity` stays green across the divergence. The by_design.md entry required by CLAUDE.md is absent and, worse, actively contradicts the code: BD-Identity-RoutingKeyNamespaces (notes/parity/by_design.md:98-106) still claims internal/routingkey "mirrors the shared routing-key contract bit-for-bit and is locked by a golden-fixture test"; the only CUX hits in that file are unrelated BIN-RPC/throttle rows. The published contract likewise still enumerates the scoped classes as hub roots + INT000* + virtual remotes (ha-unique-id-migration.md:44-54) and asserts the client's rebuild is "bit-identical to the daemon's" (:164-167) — false for CUxD as of 0.61.3 — while migrate_unique_id returns None for any key starting with `loom_`, so no client-side pass repairs it either.

findings.title: A central row stored before the 0.59.1 name allowlist boots anyway — the post-overlay config validation is a Warn, so the CCU silently receives no push events, contradicting the release note
findings.claim: 1) Since 0.59.1 a central name must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$` (pkg/hmtypes/central_name.go:21,29-40); CHANGELOG 0.59.1 promises it is "enforced at config load, in the admin API, in the store and in the onboarding wizard", and the commit message of 89c39556 promises an install that already carries such a name "now fails to start with a message naming it". 2) Centrals adopted through the SPA/wizard live only in the SQLite `centrals` table — the HA add-on documents exactly this (packaging/ha-addon/openccu-loom/DOCS.md:70: "All other daemon settings (centrals, MQTT, auth, Matter) are configured" in the UI). 3) On boot the DB tier replaces `cfg.Centrals` wholesale without validating: `Store.layerCentrals` (internal/configstore/store.go:736-758) reads the rows, maps them via `RowToCentralConfig`, and assigns `cfg.Centrals = out` — no call to `ValidateCentralName` anywhere on that path (grep for ValidateCentralName/IsValidCentralName: only setup.go:213, admin_centrals.go:194/247, config.go:2090, centrals_store.go:132, xmlrpc_server.go:318). 4) `Store.OverlayInto` (store.go:274-300) and `Store.Effective` (store.go:321-338) never call `Validate()` either. 5) The one check that would catch it is `cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_boot.go:223-225`, immediately after OverlayInto — and its error is `logger.Warn("configstore.overlay.validate", …)`; execution continues with the invalid config. (The YAML-tier check at cmd/openccu-loom/main.go:106 → internal/config/config.go:1798 → :1997 → :2090 does hard-fail, but a DB-tier-only central is not in `cfg.Centrals` at that point.) 6) `internal/store/sqlite/centrals_store.go:132` validates only on WRITE, so a row written before 0.59.1 is never re-checked. 7) The consequence is the exact failure the allowlist exists to prevent: the callback router rejects the segment — `routeFromPath` returns ("", false) when `!hmtypes.IsValidCentralName(rest)` (internal/central/rpcserver/xmlrpc_server.go:306-321) — so every XML-RPC push for that central is dropped at the door.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator adopted a CCU from discovery as `CCU Wohnzimmer` (or any name with a space, dot or umlaut) on 0.55–0.59.0, when nothing rejected it; the row sits in the `centrals` table. They upgrade to 0.61.4. The daemon starts cleanly, REST and the SPA show the central, /health is green — and the CCU never delivers a single push event, so no value ever changes. The only trace is one `configstore.overlay.validate` line at WARN in the log. The release note told them this configuration would refuse to start with a message naming it.
findings.verified_by: Code trace through configstore/store.go:736-758 → daemon_boot.go:218-225 → rpcserver/xmlrpc_server.go:306-321, plus an exhaustive grep for the two validator entry points showing no call on the DB read path.
findings.fix_sketch: Validate central names where the DB tier materialises them: call `hmtypes.ValidateCentralName` in `layerCentrals` and drop (or park) the offending row with an error-level log and a /health component, rather than admitting it. Better still, add a one-shot startup repair that renames such a row to its sanitised form and records the rename in the audit log, since a silently unroutable CCU is worse than a renamed one — and surface it in the SPA, because a WARN line is not a repair path.
findings.verify_reasoning: REPRODUCED END TO END on the running daemon; every step of the finder's chain holds, and the operator-visible consequence is if anything worse than described. I renamed the persisted central row from `ccu-v4` to `CCU Wohnzimmer` directly in $S/run/V4/data/openccu-loom.db (a Go helper over modernc.org/sqlite, since no sqlite3 CLI is present), emptied `centrals:` in the YAML so only the DB tier carries it, and restarted. RESULT: the daemon STARTED AND STAYED UP. Its only complaint was one WARN: `configstore.overlay.validate err="config: centrals[0].name: central name \"CCU Wohnzimmer\": only letters, digits, \"-\" and \"_\" are allowed ..."`. GET /api/v1/health then answered HTTP 200 `"status":"healthy"` with `CCU Wohnzimmer/central` healthy and `CCU Wohnzimmer/CCU Wohnzimmer-HmIP-RF` healthy note "recovery completed". The callback URL it advertised to the CCU was `http://127.0.0.1:18510/RPC2/CCU Wohnzimmer`. A POST of a valid XML-RPC `event` to `http://127.0.0.1:18510/RPC2/CCU%20Wohnzimmer` answered `404 not found` -- WITH NO LOG LINE AT ANY LEVEL (the daemon ran at level=debug). And the payoff: firing /set_value on the simulator control port left the data point at `"value":null,"observed":false,"source":"unobserved"` both before and after, whereas the same DP under the valid name had read `value:4.5, observed:true, source:"live"`. So the daemon presents 41 devices, a green /health and a green interface while EVERY data point is permanently unobserved. Code chain re-derived independently: configstore/store.go:736-758 layerCentrals assigns `cfg.Centrals = out` from the rows with no ValidateCentralName anywhere on that path; cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_boot.go:222-224 downgrades the post-overlay `cfg.Validate()` failure to logger.Warn and continues (the OverlayInto error one line above is correctly Error -- the asymmetry is the bug); rpcserver/xmlrpc_server.go:306-321 routeFromPath returns ("",false) for any segment failing hmtypes.IsValidCentralName. The 0.59.1 CHANGELOG promise that such an install 'now fails to start with a message naming it' is false for the DB tier. Severity high is correct and defensible as critical: silent total data loss on the south-bound plane with every health surface reporting green.

findings.title: The live config-file watcher checks 7 hardcoded restart-required fields against restart.go's 53 rules and logs an unconditional success line, so a hand-edited config.yaml reports 'reloaded' for settings that were silently ignored
findings.claim: 1) The watcher is installed on every ordinary deployment: cmd/openccu-loom/main.go:113-127 loads the file and calls `daemonServeWithReload(ctx, cfg, effectiveConfig, …)`, and only an empty config path disables it. 2) internal/config/watcher.go:171-184 — once the handler returns nil, the watcher unconditionally does `w.current.Store(next)` and logs `config.watch.reloaded` at Info; the only negative signal is `config.watch.handler_rejected`, which `hotReloadHandler` never produces. 3) `hotReloadHandler` hot-applies only Logging and MQTT, and its restart-required punch-list (cmd/openccu-loom/reload.go:179-213) is exactly seven explicit comparisons: DataDir, Locale, Callback, North.REST.Listen, North.REST.PublicURL, North.REST.OpenAPIValidateEnabled(), CentralsModifiedInPlace. 4) internal/config/restart.go's `restartRules()` — the project's own single source of truth, which internal/north/rest/handlers/admin_config.go:137-144 explicitly says exists because the two lists drifted before — carries 53 `Path:` entries covering alarm.*, north.matter.*, north.discovery.*, north.mcp.*, north.webhook.*, north.rest.auth.*, north.rest.csrf_*, north.ui.*, backup.* and more; none of those groups appears anywhere in reload.go. 5) The function's own doc comment (reload.go:41-46) states that `north.rest.cors` and `locale, auth, oidc` are in the restart-required bucket where 'any change in these fields logs and is ignored'. For CORS, auth and OIDC that is false — no comparison for them exists in the body, so nothing logs. 6) The gap is a drift, not a design: `git log --oneline v0.55.0..HEAD -- cmd/openccu-loom/reload.go` shows 4 commits, none touching the punch-list, while internal/config/restart.go grew by +121/-1 lines over the same range.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator upgrading from 0.55.x-0.60.x runs the daemon the normal way (`openccu-loom --config config.yaml`), so the watcher is live. They hand-edit the file to set `alarm.enabled: false` for maintenance, or to flip `north.rest.auth.basic_enabled: false` after a lockdown decision, or to change the CORS allow-list. Within the poll interval the log says `config.watch.reloaded` and nothing else — no `daemon.reload.restart_required` warning, because no comparison for those fields exists. The alarm engine, the auth gate and the CORS middleware are all still the ones built at boot, and the operator's only evidence says the change was applied.
findings.verified_by: Independently re-verified every step after a sub-agent first reported it: read main.go:108-127, watcher.go:170-184 and reload.go:28-50 + :175-220 directly; counted `grep -c 'Path:' internal/config/restart.go` = 53; `grep -in 'oidc|locale|rate_limit|ccu_data|reliability|persistence' internal/config/restart.go` = 0 matches, and no rule-group name from restart.go appears in reload.go.
findings.fix_sketch: Replace the hand-written block with `config.RestartRequiredDiff(prev, next)` — the same table admin_config.go:690 already uses — logging one `daemon.reload.restart_required` warning per returned path, and special-case only the two areas actually hot-applied (Logging, MQTT). Fix the doc comment's CORS/auth/oidc claim in the same change.
findings.verify_reasoning: REPRODUCED ON THE RUNNING DAEMON. With the file watcher live (the daemon was started as `openccu-loom run --config <path>`, which is the only ordinary deployment shape -- cmd/openccu-loom/main.go:126 calls daemonServeWithReload unconditionally with the resolved path), I hand-edited the live config file to make TWO changes that internal/config/restart.go explicitly rules as restart-required: `north.matter.enabled` false->true (restart.go:163) and `north.rest.auth.basic_enabled` true->false (restart.go:404). Within one watcher tick the log said exactly two things: `daemon.reload.applied hot_reloaded_fields=0 restart_required_fields=0` and `config.watch.reloaded path=...` -- BOTH AT INFO, and NO `daemon.reload.restart_required` warning for either field. Neither change took effect: GET /api/v1/matter/exposable still answered 503 'north.matter.enabled is false in the daemon config', and GET /api/v1/devices without credentials still answered 401 while with credentials it answered 200. So the operator's only evidence says 'reloaded, zero restart-required fields' for two settings that were silently ignored. Mechanism confirmed exactly as stated: internal/config/watcher.go:173-185 stores the new config and logs `config.watch.reloaded` at Info the moment the handler returns nil, and cmd/openccu-loom/reload.go's hotReloadHandler returns a non-nil error only on an MQTT swap failure (reload.go:148), so the `config.watch.handler_rejected` branch is effectively unreachable. reload.go:179-213 is exactly seven hand-written comparisons (DataDir, Locale, Callback, North.REST.Listen, North.REST.PublicURL, North.REST.OpenAPIValidateEnabled, CentralsModifiedInPlace) against restart.go's 53 `Path:` entries (grep -c confirms 53), and a grep of restart.go for oidc|locale|rate_limit|ccu_data|reliability|persistence returns 0. The finder's doc-comment sub-claim is also accurate on inspection: the comment at reload.go:41-46 lists `north.rest.cors` and `locale, auth, oidc` as fields whose change 'logs and is ignored', and while Locale IS compared, CORS, auth and OIDC have no comparison in the body at all -- they are ignored silently. Severity high stands: a hand-edited config.yaml is a documented deployment path and the feedback the operator receives is affirmatively wrong, not merely absent.

findings.title: restart.go carries no rule for six boot-time-only areas including the OIDC client secret, so the SPA's save response and the restart-pending banner report 'no restart needed' for changes that never take effect
findings.claim: 1) `config.RestartRequiredDiff` has exactly two production consumers (grep, excluding tests): internal/north/rest/handlers/admin_config.go:690 `restartRequired := len(config.RestartRequiredDiff(base, candidate)) > 0`, which is what the SPA's section-save response reports, and cmd/openccu-loom/restart_pending_provider.go:42, which drives the persistent restart-pending banner. They are the operator's only signal. 2) `grep -in 'oidc|locale|rate_limit|ccu_data|reliability|persistence' internal/config/restart.go` returns zero matches against its 53 `Path:` entries. 3) Each of those areas is nevertheless wired once at boot. OIDC: `buildOIDCClient` (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_north.go:599) is called only from `buildOIDCRest` (daemon_north.go:586), called only from the once-per-boot mount literal at daemon_rest_mount.go:355, so the client — and the client_secret it captured — lives for the process. The sub-agent traced the other five to single boot call sites (locale into the label/MQTT/Matter/alarm wiring; ccu_data via loadCCUArchive at daemon.go:252; reliability inside ccu_wiring.go:749/755 per-central bring-up; persistence.values_cache/.history via daemon_infra.go:116/136/148; north.rest.rate_limit via buildRateLimitConfig at daemon_north.go:741-750, which returns nil when disabled and so installs no middleware at all — the identical 'empty list installs no middleware' shape restart.go already rules for on CORS). 4) The existing guard cannot catch it: tests/contract/config_restart_required_test.go cross-checks restartRules() against the REST schema's own badges only, not against config.ClassifyFields' full leaf set or configstore.AllSections().
findings.failure_scenario: An operator on 0.61.4 rotates a leaked OIDC `client_secret` through the SPA's Auth → OIDC editor, the documented way to change it. The PUT answers `restart_required: false` and the restart-pending banner stays dark, so they believe the daemon now uses the new secret. The OIDC client built at boot keeps presenting the old — possibly compromised — secret until something unrelated restarts the daemon. The same blind spot silently defers a locale change, a `reliability.command_retry_initial_delay` tuning made to rescue a flaky BidCos-RF interface, and turning on `north.rest.rate_limit` after an abuse incident — each reported as applied.
findings.verified_by: Independently re-verified the load-bearing steps after a sub-agent first reported it: `grep -rn RestartRequiredDiff` (two production consumers, as stated), the zero-match grep over restart.go, and the buildOIDCClient → buildOIDCRest → daemon_rest_mount.go:355 single call chain. The five non-OIDC boot call sites are as the sub-agent traced them; I spot-checked the call-site uniqueness but did not re-read each wiring function end to end.
findings.fix_sketch: Add restart.go rules for north.rest.auth.oidc (a block rule over the whole OIDCConfig, mirroring the existing CCU / HA-ingress block rules), locale, ccu_data.{translations_path,easymode_path}, reliability.*, persistence.values_cache/.history and north.rest.rate_limit. Then add a completeness contract test that fails when a configstore.Section or a boot-wired cfg leaf has neither a restartRules() entry nor an explicit 'genuinely live' allowlist entry.
findings.verify_reasoning: MEASURED with a Go test driving the exact function the SPA's save response and the restart-pending banner both read. $S/wt/_scratch_v4/e6_7_test.go calls config.RestartRequiredDiff(base, candidate) on a config.Default() pair differing in one field: `north.rest.auth.oidc.client_secret` -> [], `oidc.enabled` -> [], `oidc.issuer` -> [], `locale` -> []. The two controls behaved correctly: `north.matter.enabled` -> [north.matter.enabled], `north.rest.auth.basic_enabled` -> [north.rest.auth.basic_enabled]. So an operator rotating a leaked OIDC client secret through the SPA gets `restart_required: false` and a dark restart-pending banner. The two production consumers are as claimed and are the operator's only signal: internal/north/rest/handlers/admin_config.go:690 (`restartRequired := len(config.RestartRequiredDiff(base, candidate)) > 0`, the section-save response) and cmd/openccu-loom/restart_pending_provider.go:42 (the banner). The rules are exact-path, not prefix-scoped (RestartRule.Path plus a per-rule Differs closure, restart.go:24-35), so the neighbouring `north.rest.auth.ccu` / `.ha_ingress` / `.basic_enabled` / `.bearer_enabled` rules cannot incidentally cover the OIDC block. And the OIDC client really is boot-frozen: buildOIDCClient has exactly one caller, buildOIDCRest (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_north.go:586), which has exactly one caller, the router-mount literal at cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_rest_mount.go:355, executed once per boot; hotReloadHandler hot-applies only Logging and MQTT, so nothing rebuilds it. Severity high with the finder's `security` category is right: the failure mode is a credential the operator believes rotated that is still being presented. I verified OIDC and locale directly by measurement; the other four areas the finding lists (ccu_data, reliability, persistence, north.rest.rate_limit) I confirmed only as absent from restart.go's rule set, not by re-tracing each boot call site.
