findings.title: A `north.rest` config-section row written by v0.4.0..v0.25.x carries `basic_enabled:false`/`bearer_enabled:false`, which today's tri-state gates read as an explicit "scheme off", so HTTP Basic and Bearer auth die silently on upgrade.
findings.claim:
Chain, every step traced in HEAD:

(1) `config_sections` rows are gated only by `ConfigSectionSchemaVersion` (internal/store/sqlite/config_sections.go:21). Its own doc comment says "Bump this whenever the serialisation shape changes so that rows written by an older daemon are treated as stale and dropped on boot". It has been `1` since it was introduced in 3982e861 (migration 020, 2026-06-15, shipped in v0.4.0) and `git log -S'ConfigSectionSchemaVersion = '` returns only that one commit. `WipeOutdatedSections` (config_sections.go:186-194) deletes only rows whose `schema_version != 1`, so every row written from v0.4.0 onward survives forever.

(2) The `north.rest` row is the whole `config.NorthREST` sub-tree: `marshalSection` -> `case SectionREST: json.Marshal(cfg.North.REST)` (internal/configstore/store.go:644-645). It is written on first boot by `SeedSectionsFromConfig` (store.go:696; no-op once any row exists) and by every SPA save of the REST section. `SeedSectionsFromConfig` and the same `case SectionREST: json.Marshal(cfg.North.REST)` already existed at `b1d314dd^` (verified with `git show b1d314dd^:internal/configstore/store.go`, lines 517 and 468-469).

(3) Until b1d314dd (v0.26.0, 2026-07-04) the fields were `BasicEnabled bool \`json:"basic_enabled"\`` and `BearerEnabled bool \`json:"bearer_enabled"\`` — no `omitempty`, no default assignment anywhere in `applyDefaults` (verified: `git show b1d314dd^:internal/config/config.go` lines 1045-1047, and grep for those identifiers in that revision returns only the struct fields). The commit message itself states they "existed in the config schema and SPA editor but were never read". So the marshalled row unconditionally carried `"basic_enabled":false,"bearer_enabled":false` for every operator who had not set them in YAML — which is everyone, because the keys governed nothing.

(4) b1d314dd changed them to `*bool` with `omitempty` and made them live gates: `BasicAuthEnabled()`/`BearerAuthEnabled()` = `orDefault(x, true)` (internal/config/config.go:1503-1523). nil -> enabled, explicit false -> scheme rejected.

(5) At boot the stored row is layered onto the config: daemon_boot.go:197 (wipe, no-op at version 1) -> :206 (seed, no-op, row exists) -> :218 `OverlayInto` -> `applySection` `case SectionREST: overlaySection(raw, &cfg.North.REST)` (internal/configstore/store.go:575) -> `json.Unmarshal(raw, dst)` (internal/configstore/overlay.go:29). `stripForeignFields` removes only `north.rest.listen`, `auth.users`, `auth.tokens` and the nested oidc/ccu/ha_ingress sub-trees (store.go:118-122 + foreignRelPaths); `auth.basic_enabled` is not in that set, so it survives and lands as a non-nil pointer to false.

(6) Effect: `gatedAuthMiddleware` (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_north.go:77-88) hands `auth.NewMiddleware` a nil UserStore AND a nil TokenStore; `buildAuthStores` (daemon_north.go:103) skips `wsHub.SetTokenStore`; `wireREST` skips the same at daemon_rest.go:228. `applyDefaults` is not re-run after the overlay (daemon_boot.go only calls `cfg.Validate()`, and only as a warning), so nothing repairs the value.

No migration, no compat shim and no log line exists for this: `grep -rn basic_enabled` finds only the config struct, the docs table and the 0.26.0 CHANGELOG entry, which documents the semantic change but says nothing about existing rows. `warnOnDormantOnboarding` (daemon_north.go:241) only warns in the single case "an API token is the only configured credential".
findings.failure_scenario: An installation first started on any release from v0.4.0 through v0.25.x has a `config_sections` row `('north.rest', {... "auth":{"basic_enabled":false,"bearer_enabled":false, ...}}, schema_version=1)`. The operator upgrades to v0.26.0 or later (including HEAD 0.61.4). The daemon starts, `/health` is green, the SPA login still works (session cookies have no gate). But every `Authorization: Basic ...` and every `Authorization: Bearer <api-token>` request now returns 401: `hmcli`, the Node-RED contrib, the openccu-loom-client, any REST/WS automation, and the inbound-webhook/MCP callers that authenticate with an API token. WS upgrades authenticated by token are rejected too (the hub never receives the token store). Nothing in the log says why. The operator's only recovery is to notice the two unchecked boxes in Settings -> north.rest and re-save the section. The same happens on a fresh daemon that restores a backup archive taken on one of those releases, since the restored DB carries the row and goose migrates it forward untouched.
findings.verified_by: Code trace of all six steps above against HEAD (34b0f4c9) plus the two historical revisions (b1d314dd, b1d314dd^, 3982e861), and a reproducer at $S/repro/F6/authgate/main.go which replays the exact old and new struct shapes: `stored row {"enabled":true,"listen":":8119","auth":{"basic_enabled":false,"bearer_enabled":false,"session_enabled":false,...}}` / `before overlay: basic=true bearer=true` / `after overlay: basic=false bearer=false`, with the control (a row written by HEAD) omitting both keys and leaving the gates enabled. Historical facts established with `git show b1d314dd^:internal/config/config.go`, `git show b1d314dd^:internal/configstore/store.go`, `git log -S'ConfigSectionSchemaVersion = '` (single commit), and `git describe --contains 3982e861` -> 0.4.0~34 / `git tag --contains b1d314dd` -> v0.26.0 for the exposure window.
findings.fix_sketch: Bump `ConfigSectionSchemaVersion` to 2 — that is exactly what the constant is documented for, and `WipeOutdatedSections` then drops the stale rows on the next boot so the YAML/compiled-in defaults apply until the operator re-saves. If dropping every section row is judged too blunt, add a goose migration that removes the `basic_enabled`/`bearer_enabled` keys from the stored `north.rest` payload (`json_remove(value_json, '$.auth.basic_enabled', '$.auth.bearer_enabled')` guarded on the daemon_version stamp being absent), restoring nil = enabled. Either way add a contract test that decodes a pre-0.26-shaped `north.rest` payload and asserts both gates resolve to enabled, and make the ratchet explicit: a field that moves from unread to read must bump the section schema version.
findings.verify_reasoning: I refused the finder's reproducer and re-established both halves from the repository itself. PREMISE (did those releases really write basic_enabled:false?): yes, proven by running the historical marshal path, not a reconstruction. `git show b1d314dd^:internal/config/config.go:1045-1047` shows `BasicEnabled bool` / `BearerEnabled bool` with json tags and no omitempty, and `git grep BasicEnabled b1d314dd^` returns ONLY those struct lines - nothing ever assigned them, so applyDefaults could not have made them true. I then checked out b1d314dd^ into its own worktree and ran that revision's real marshalSection(SectionREST, config.Default()): it emits `{"auth":{"basic_enabled":false,"bearer_enabled":false,...}}` verbatim. SeedSectionsFromConfig has written all sections on first boot since aa55e3f7 (0.1.0), and stripUnmanagedFields at that revision removed only listen/users/tokens. EXPOSURE WINDOW: ConfigSectionSchemaVersion has been 1 since 3982e861 (0.4.0) and `git log -S` returns that single commit, so WipeOutdatedSections never drops those rows; migration 020's DEFAULT 0 wipes only pre-020 rows, and a wipe just re-seeds the same false payload from the then-current daemon. No migration after 020 rewrites config_sections payloads. HEAD: the fields are `*bool,omitempty` with BasicAuthEnabled()/BearerAuthEnabled() = orDefault(x, true) (config.go:1504-1523); foreignRelPaths for north.rest strips only listen, auth.users, auth.tokens and the nested oidc/ccu/ha_ingress sub-trees (store.go:118-122,161-178) - auth.basic_enabled is not among them; daemon_boot.go:197-224 wipes, seeds, overlays and never re-runs applyDefaults. EFFECT, run against HEAD's own applySection: the old payload leaves basic=false bearer=false where the default was true, and a HEAD-written control row omits both keys and keeps them enabled. Consumers: gatedAuthMiddleware passes nil stores (daemon_north.go:77-88), buildAuthStores skips wsHub.SetTokenStore, and auth.Middleware with nil stores attaches no Identity so Require answers 401 - it fails CLOSED, not open, so this is a silent availability break for every Basic/Bearer client (hmcli, Node-RED, openccu-loom-client, token-authenticated WS), not an auth bypass. Severity stays high on that basis.

findings.title: A CCU adopted at runtime through the REST API gets its background-job scheduler cancelled the moment the HTTP request finishes, so none of its per-central jobs ever run.
findings.claim: handlers.CreateCentral passes the request context into the service: `svc.Put(r.Context(), row)` (internal/north/rest/handlers/admin_centrals.go:209; UpdateCentral does the same at :270). That context reaches the lifecycle's Put, which calls `l.orch.adoptCentral(ctx, cc)` (cmd/openccu-loom/central_adopt.go:829). adoptCentral registers the standard jobs and then starts the unit with the SAME context: `unit.Start(ctx)` (central_adopt.go:469) -> `u.Scheduler.Start(ctx)` (internal/central/central.go:628) -> `ctx, s.stopFunc = context.WithCancel(ctx); s.runCtx = ctx; go s.runJob(ctx, j)` (internal/scheduler/scheduler.go:193-201). net/http cancels r.Context() as soon as the handler returns, so every job goroutine of that central exits immediately. The jobs lost are the whole StandardJobs bundle registered at cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_jobs.go:43-150: central.health_heartbeat, hub program/sysvar/inbox/service-message/alarm-message/system-update/install-mode refresh, hub connectivity, BidCos duty-cycle, last-event-age, the reconcile pass and the firmware jobs. The per-interface ping probe survives because it is a raw goroutine started by the bring-up manager on its own parentCtx (internal/central/adapter/ccu_wiring.go:1049, and the explicit //nolint:contextcheck note at central_adopt.go:497), which is exactly why the CCU still looks connected.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator adds a second CCU in the SPA (or accepts a discovered one). Measured on a clean daemon: POST /api/v1/centrals at 13:11:38 returned 201 and logged central.adopt.live; six minutes later the new central's health components were still frozen at their adopt-time samples (runtime1/central 13:11:38, runtime1/runtime1-HmIP-RF 13:11:44), no runtime1/scheduler component had ever been created, and GET /api/v1/system/ccu reported {'runtime1': available=false} while the boot central heartbeat-refreshed every 60 s and reported available=true. The CCU pings fine and serves devices, but its programs, system variables, service messages, install mode, connectivity aggregate, firmware check and system_health metric never refresh, and the operator's dashboard shows the CCU as unavailable - until the daemon is restarted, after which the same CCU works normally.
findings.verified_by: measurement on a clean daemon (evidence in $S/repro/G1/EVIDENCE.md section 1) plus the full code trace above
findings.fix_sketch: adoptCentral must not hand a request-scoped context to Unit.Start. Give the orchestrator a long-lived, teardown-bounded context (the same parentCtx the bring-up manager already uses) and pass that to unit.Start, keeping the caller's ctx only for the store write and the CCU probes.
findings.verify_reasoning: Reproduced live, twice, in two independent daemon runs, and the blast radius is wider than the finding states in one direction and narrower in another. Adopting a CCU through POST /api/v1/centrals returns 201 and brings the south-bound up correctly -- devices load, names load, and push events keep arriving: I fired LEVEL=0.42 on the simulator and the runtime-adopted central's data point updated within 3 s. What never happens is the entire scheduler plane. The `<central>/scheduler` health component -- which the central.health_heartbeat job creates on its first 60 s tick -- never appears; `<central>/central` and `<central>/<iface>` stay frozen at their adopt-time samples and decay to `unknown` at +90 s; GET /system/ccu reports available=false from then on, permanently; the diagnostics central_scores entry sits at 0. In 20 minutes of debug log the ONLY recurring activity for a runtime-adopted central is `xml-rpc.ping` every 15 s -- a raw goroutine the bring-up manager runs on its own daemon-lifetime parentCtx (central_adopt.go:497 //nolint:contextcheck) -- while the boot-adopted central in the same process logs hub.program_refresh / hub.sysvar_refresh / hub.install_mode_refresh / hub.connectivity_refresh / devicedetails.refresh every 30-60 s. So the dead set is the whole StandardJobs bundle: central.health_heartbeat, central.check_connection, central.refresh_client_data, central.reconcile, central.firmware_check / _delivery_check / _updating_check, hub.connectivity_refresh, hub.bidcos_interfaces_refresh, hub.metrics_refresh, hub.last_event_age_refresh, hub.program_refresh, hub.sysvar_refresh, hub.inbox_refresh, hub.service_messages_refresh, hub.alarm_messages_refresh, hub.system_update_refresh, hub.install_mode_refresh and devicedetails.refresh.<central>. Programs and sysvars ARE present for the adopted CCU because the initial hub load runs during bring-up -- they are simply frozen at their adopt-time values forever. RECOVERY: nothing recovers it short of a daemon restart. A second PUT is a no-op (`central.adopt.skip_already_live`, central_adopt.go:820-826). The operator's obvious repair -- toggling the CCU off and on in the SPA -- goes through removeCentral + adoptCentral and is EQUALLY dead: I measured it, and 100 s after the re-enable the re-adopted central was frozen again with no scheduler component. Only restarting the daemon fixes it: after restart the same central got `runtime2/scheduler healthy` on a 60 s heartbeat and its hub jobs actually ran. The mechanism the finder and E1-2 name is exact: svc.Put(r.Context(), row) -> adoptCentral -> unit.Start(ctx) -> Scheduler.Start(ctx) -> job goroutines parented on the request context, which net/http cancels when the handler returns. High rather than critical only because device values keep flowing; every periodic, hub and health surface for that CCU is dead until restart.

findings.title: HTTP Basic auth runs a bcrypt cost-12 verification on every single request with no cache, so the whole REST API is ~300x slower under Basic than under Bearer and any unauthenticated caller can burn a CPU core per request.
findings.claim: Every request re-authenticates from scratch. MemoryUserStore.AuthenticateBasic (internal/auth/auth.go:336-356) runs bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword at bcryptCost = 12 (auth.go:293) for a known user and a dummy compare at the same cost for an unknown one (:343). sqlite.UserStore.AuthenticateBasic does the same (internal/store/sqlite/users.go:205 dummy, :211 real) and additionally issues an `UPDATE users SET last_seen_at` per successful request (:214). The two are chained (auth.ChainedUserStore, wired at cmd/openccu-loom/ccu_auth_wiring.go:74), so a credential that misses the SQLite store costs TWO cost-12 verifies. Nothing caches the verdict between requests. north.rest.rate_limit.enabled defaults to false (example.config.full.yaml:165, config default), and the brute-force limiter is mounted only on POST /auth/login (internal/north/rest/router.go:713-716), so nothing bounds the work an anonymous caller can request on any other path.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured on one daemon, same 131-operation GET sweep, only the Authorization header changed: with Bearer the whole sweep finished in seconds (per-request 3-15 ms); with Basic the identical requests took 1.8-4.6 s each (GET /info 3.80/4.54/4.62 s under Basic vs 4.6/19.6 ms with no auth at all). A single bcrypt cost-12 verify measured on the same box was 2.1-2.8 s under load - i.e. essentially the entire request time is the KDF. Requests with a WRONG password cost the same (4.58/5.02/5.27 s) and so do requests naming a user that does not exist (3.96/2.62 s), so an unauthenticated attacker sending Basic headers to any endpoint saturates the CPU with a handful of concurrent connections. For legitimate users, every Basic-auth client (curl scripts, the Node-RED nodes, CI, the documented `curl -u` examples) pays a full password KDF plus one SQLite write per API call.
findings.verified_by: measurement ($S/repro/G1/EVIDENCE.md section 4: sweep timings with Basic vs Bearer vs anonymous, plus an in-repo bcrypt cost-12 micro-benchmark) plus the code trace above
findings.fix_sketch: Cache the Basic verdict keyed on a salted hash of the presented credential for a short TTL (or mint a session on first success and let the client reuse it), and gate repeated failures per source IP the way POST /auth/login already is. Keeping cost 12 for the one-off login is right; paying it per request is not.
findings.verify_reasoning: Measured and worse than the finding argues in the one place it matters, with one supporting claim refuted. Same daemon, same endpoint, only the Authorization header changed: anonymous 2.5-8 ms, Bearer 2.4-3.2 ms, Basic with the correct password 0.72-1.03 s, Basic with a wrong password 1.6-3.0 s, Basic naming an unknown user 1.7-1.9 s. A cost-12 bcrypt verify measured in isolation on the same box: 1.5-1.7 s wall, 0.80 s CPU (7.97 s user for 10 verifies). So the ~300x Basic-vs-Bearer ratio is real; the ABSOLUTE numbers in both the finding and my run are inflated roughly 4-6x by the co-running audit agents (load average 13-16 on 4 cores) and would be ~250-350 ms per verify on an idle box -- still two to three orders of magnitude above a normal request. The wrong-password path costs two verifies because ChainedUserStore tries the SQLite store (dummy compare on ErrNoRows, users.go:203) and then the memory store (real compare, auth.go:343-352), and YAML-seeded users are bcrypt-hashed at boot (daemon_north.go:90-99), so there is no cheap path. Basic is ON by default (AuthConfig.BasicAuthEnabled -> orDefault(nil, true), config.go:1516). REFUTED SUB-CLAIM: the finding says the brute-force limiter is mounted only on POST /auth/login. It is not -- auth.GuardBasicAuth(d.LoginRateLimit) is mounted router-wide at router.go:615-616 and charges failed Basic verifications against the same per-IP buckets. But the conclusion survives, because that guard sits INSIDE AuthResolve (r.Use order: AuthResolve at :606, GuardBasicAuth at :616, the per-identity RateLimit at :630), so the KDF has already been paid by the time any limiter can answer. I measured exactly that: 12 concurrent wrong-password requests -> six 401 and six 429, and ALL TWELVE took ~14.5 s, i.e. every throttled request still burned its bcrypt; 12 HTTP requests consumed ~48 CPU-seconds and saturated four cores for 15 s. Sequentially the limiter never engages at all -- ten wrong-password requests in a row all returned 200/401 with no 429, because the bucket refills at 1/s and each attempt takes 2-7 s, i.e. the attack is slowed only by the work it causes. And it reaches endpoints that need no credentials: GET /api/v1/health is public and answered 200 after a full 2-7 s bcrypt whenever a Basic header was attached. north.rest.rate_limit.enabled defaults to false (config.go:1216-1219) and would not help anyway for the same ordering reason. High stands: an unauthenticated caller can exhaust the CPU of a default install through a public endpoint, and every documented `curl -u` / Node-RED / CI client pays a full password KDF (plus one `UPDATE users SET last_seen_at` for SQLite users, users.go:214) on every single API call.

findings.title: A device going unreachable never produces a device.availability_changed broadcast, because the availability announcement sits behind the visibility gate that suppresses UNREACH
findings.claim: EventBridge.dispatchLive (eventbridge.go:1174-1197) fans a value change to WS inline and hands the rest to publishValueChangedMQTT. The per-device availability announcement - the only producer of hmevent.DeviceLifecycleEvent{Subtype: AVAILABILITY_CHANGED} for a single device (the other producer, adapter/device_availability.go:53, is the interface-wide forced-availability path) - is the LAST statement of publishValueChangedMQTT (eventbridge.go:1437 -> refreshDeviceAvailability at :1455 -> events.Publish at :1481). That function returns early at eventbridge.go:1330 when buildPublishEvent reports the parameter as globally suppressed, and the gate it consults (eventbridge.go:1549 -> filter.Adapter.VisibleForChannel -> visibility.Registry.IsAllowedForChannel, registry.go:130) rejects exactly UNREACH, STICKY_UNREACH and CONFIG_PENDING, which are listed in hiddenParameters (internal/store/visibility/rules.go:174-196) and are precisely the three parameters isReachabilityParameter (eventbridge.go:913-917) treats as availability-carrying. The fallback written for this case - dispatchLive's `if b.mqtt == nil` branch at eventbridge.go:1178-1182, whose comment says 'the WebSocket device-lifecycle plane and the Matter reachability forward exist in a deployment without MQTT too' - is dead in production: mqttSupervisor.Start allocates a stable Wiring even when MQTT is disabled (cmd/openccu-loom/mqtt_supervisor.go:306-318), so b.mqtt is never nil in the daemon. The WS emitter itself is wired and healthy (ws/device_lifecycle.go:140-150): 25 device.availability_changed frames were emitted at boot, all from ordinary parameters whose first observation seeded the availability cache.
findings.failure_scenario: Fired UNREACH=true on VCU2737768:0 through the simulator control port. REST GET /api/v1/devices immediately reported the device as available:false, and firing UNREACH=false flipped it back to true. Over the entire daemon lifetime (273 buffered events, replayed with since=0) not one device.availability_changed frame carries seq > 100; every one of the 25 is from boot. A WebSocket client - the Node-RED contrib, an external client, any SPA view driven by the device-lifecycle plane - subscribes to the declared device.availability_changed broadcast and therefore never learns that a device died or recovered; it keeps rendering the device as online until something re-reads REST. By the same early return the retained MQTT availability topic (bridge.PublishAvailability, reached from the same refreshDeviceAvailability) is not republished on the UNREACH edge either, so with MQTT enabled a Home Assistant entity would stay 'available' after the device stopped answering - traced in code, not observed, since MQTT was off in this run.
findings.verified_by: measurement + code trace. Live: $S/repro/G2/listen3.log (UNREACH true/false on VCU2737768 -> only datapoint.value_changed), $S/repro/G2/replay_all.json (full 273-event buffer; no device.availability_changed above seq 100), REST availability before/after. Trace: eventbridge.go:1178-1182/1330/1437/1455/1481/1549, rules.go:174-196, mqtt_supervisor.go:306-318, device_lifecycle.go:140.
findings.fix_sketch: Move refreshDeviceAvailability out of publishValueChangedMQTT and call it from dispatchLive unconditionally (before the MQTT branch), so it runs regardless of the visibility verdict and of whether MQTT is wired; the visibility gate must decide what is *published as an entity*, never whether the daemon notices a device went offline. Pin it with a test that fires UNREACH through the real bridge and asserts the DeviceLifecycleEvent arrives with MQTT disabled.
findings.verify_reasoning: Observation and named mechanism both hold, and I pinned the mechanism with a differential experiment rather than by reading alone. Trace: dispatchLive (eventbridge.go:1174) publishes to WS inline, then - because b.mqtt is non-nil - hands the rest to publishValueChangedMQTT, whose early return at eventbridge.go:1330-1334 fires when buildPublishEvent reports the parameter globally suppressed; the only per-device producer of DeviceLifecycleEvent{AVAILABILITY_CHANGED} is refreshDeviceAvailability, called as the LAST statement of that same function (eventbridge.go:1437 -> events.Publish at :1481-1489). The gate is filter.Adapter.VisibleForChannel -> visibility.Registry.IsAllowedForChannel (eventbridge.go:1549), and UNREACH / STICKY_UNREACH / CONFIG_PENDING - exactly the three names isReachabilityParameter (eventbridge.go:913-919) treats as availability-carrying - are all in hiddenParameters (rules.go:172-195). Differential proof: PUT /api/v1/visibility/unignore {patterns:['UNREACH']} makes the gate pass, and the identical UNREACH true/false stimulus then emits device.availability_changed on device.VCU2822385.lifecycle for both edges. Removing the suppression removes the defect - that is the mechanism, not a hypothesis. The dead-fallback sub-claim also holds: mqttSupervisor.Start with MQTT disabled still calls ensureWiring(nil) (mqtt_supervisor.go:302-318), which allocates the process-stable *mqtt.Wiring, and daemon_infra.go:205 assigns exactly that to si.mqttWiring, which daemon.go:267 hands to NewEventBridge - so b.mqtt is never nil in the daemon and the 'no MQTT' branch at eventbridge.go:1176-1182 (whose comment claims the WS lifecycle plane and Matter reachability forward still work without MQTT) is unreachable in production. The one part I did not measure is the MQTT consequence: with a broker attached the retained availability topic hangs off the same refreshDeviceAvailability behind the same early return, so it is not republished either - traced in source only, MQTT was off in my run as in the original.

findings.title: MASTER paramset writes are gated by the MASTER data-point-creation whitelist, so almost every parameter the read surfaces offer is rejected as 'hidden' and the WS config-session can never be saved
findings.claim: ParamsetsDomain.PutParamset calls checkVisibility (paramsets.go:142 -> :453) which asks VisibilityGate.IsAllowedForChannel per parameter and returns hmerr.ErrParameterHidden for the first miss, rejecting the whole write (paramsets.go:465-468). For a MASTER paramset that gate resolves to visibility.Registry.IsAllowedForChannel (registry.go:130-137) -> ParameterDecider.computeIgnoredMaster (decider.go:275-283) -> checkMasterParameterIgnored, i.e. the relevantMasterParamsetsByChannel / relevantMasterParamsetsByDevice whitelist (rules.go:16-19, :49ff). That whitelist exists to decide which MASTER parameters are *created as data points* ('Without a whitelist match, MASTER DPs default to NoCreate so unlisted devices don't surface ~25 configuration entities', decider.go comment) - it is not an authorization list. Reusing it as a write gate makes every MASTER parameter outside it unwritable, while every read surface (paramset.get MASTER, paramset.description, config.session.open, the config export) still hands out the full CCU paramset. VisibleValues (paramsets.go:475ff) exists precisely so 'a read surface can offer exactly what the write surface accepts', and the session/read paths do not use it.
findings.failure_scenario: Live, over WS: config.session.open on VCU2128127:4 (HmIP-BSM SWITCH_VIRTUAL_RECEIVER) offers 10 MASTER parameters; staging any of them and calling config.session.save fails with internal_error 'put_paramset: parameter "POWERUP_JUMPTARGET": parameter is hidden and may not be written'. Repeated across 7 channels of 5 device types (VCU2128127:0 ARR_TIMEOUT, VCU2128127:1 DBL_PRESS_TIME, VCU1769958:0 ARR_TIMEOUT, VCU3609622:1 ADAPTIVE_REGULATION, VCU8537918:4 LOGIC_COMBINATION) - every single one rejected. The REST twin behaves identically: PUT /api/v1/devices/VCU2128127:4/paramsets/MASTER with a valid X-Edit-Token returns 403 'Parameter hidden'. Control: TEMPERATURE_OFFSET on VCU3609622:1 (in climateMasterParameters) returns 202, and GLOBAL_BUTTON_LOCK on channel 0 (in the nil/0 whitelist) passes the gate too - so exactly the whitelist decides. Net effect: the channel-configuration feature (session-based MASTER editing, master_profiles.apply, paramset.put MASTER) can display and stage a channel's configuration but can write only the handful of parameters the HA-entity whitelist happens to name; an operator's save always fails with an internal error.
findings.verified_by: measurement + code trace. Live WS session transcript and REST 403/202 contrast recorded in this run; trace paramsets.go:142/453-468, registry.go:130-137, decider.go:194-283, rules.go:16-19.
findings.fix_sketch: Stop using the MASTER data-point-creation whitelist as the write gate: for MASTER, validate against the channel's paramset description (writable OPERATIONS bit) instead, or drop the gate for MASTER entirely and keep it for VALUES. If some MASTER parameters really must stay unwritable, filter them out of every read surface via VisibleValues so open/description/export and the write gate agree, and reject only the offending parameter rather than the whole paramset.
findings.verify_reasoning: Observation and named mechanism both hold. No prerequisite was skipped: the edit lock was acquired and presented (proved by the 423 when omitted), the paramset key and channel address were the ones the session itself returned, and neither the expert flag on ui-schema nor any config option changes the verdict. Mechanism verified in source AND by a differential experiment. Source: ParamsetsDomain.PutParamset (paramsets.go:141) calls checkVisibility (:453-470) which returns hmerr.ErrParameterHidden on the first parameter the gate rejects, rejecting the whole write; the gate is always non-nil in production (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon.go:619 .SetVisibilityGate(visReg)); Registry.IsAllowedForChannel (registry.go:130-137) -> ParameterDecider.computeIgnoredMaster (decider.go:274-283) -> checkMasterParameterIgnored (decider.go:336-367), which is the MASTER *data-point-creation* whitelist (relevantMasterParamsetsByChannel rules.go:16-19, relevantMasterParamsetsByDevice rules.go:50ff) and whose step 3 default-denies every unlisted parameter. The climate result is the exact positive control: precisely the climateMasterParameters set passes on HmIP-BWTH ch1. Differential proof of the mechanism: PUT /api/v1/visibility/unignore {central_name:'ccu-v10', patterns:['POWERUP_JUMPTARGET:MASTER@HmIP-BSM:4']} -> applied_count 1, after which the identical PUT returns 202 while LOGIC_COMBINATION on the same channel still 403s. That is the matchesUnIgnore escape at decider.go:280 and it isolates the whitelist as the sole decider. Two corrections to the finding's wording, neither changing the verdict: (a) the session is not 'never' saveable everywhere - whitelisted parameters do save, so the accurate statement is 'every parameter outside the DP-creation whitelist', which on the two switch channels I measured is 100% of what the session offers; (b) an admin-only escape hatch exists (centrals[].visibility.un_ignore / PUT /visibility/unignore, grammar PARAMETER:PARAMSET@MODEL:CHANNEL), so the defect is bypassable per parameter by an expert - it is not a prerequisite the auditing agent skipped, since the shipped default rejects everything the read surface offers.

findings.title: A dead CCU never flips any north-bound availability surface: REST, MQTT and Matter keep reporting every device online indefinitely
findings.claim: The InterfaceClient never leaves ClientStateConnected when the CCU disappears. `StateMachine.IsConnected` (internal/client/state_machine.go:133) returns true for both Connected and Reconnecting, and the recovery coordinator runs its own loop without driving the client state machine: with the CCU's TCP port closed the daemon logged `recovery.failed ... tcp probe 127.0.0.1:18350: dial tcp ... connection refused` every ~15 s while `evaluate_central_state` (internal/central/central.go:1350) kept printing `all_connected:true, any_connected:true`, flapping the central only between running and degraded. Because no ClientStateChangedEvent with To in {Disconnected, Reconnecting, Failed, Stopped} is ever published, `WireDeviceAvailability` (internal/central/adapter/device_availability.go:67-77) — whose own doc comment says it exists so 'HA / REST / SPA stop showing stale online entities after a CCU-side disconnect' — never runs its force-unavailable branch. Every downstream surface therefore keeps the stale value.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured: godevccu on 127.0.0.1:18350 SIGKILLed at 13:21; at 13:25 `ss` confirmed the port closed, and the daemon answered GET /api/v1/interfaces with `connected: true`, GET /api/v1/devices with `available: true` for all 4 devices, published retained `openccu-loom/ccu-g3/ccu-g3-HmIP-RF/<addr>/availability = online` for all 4 devices, and GET /api/v1/matter/endpoints with `reachable: true` on both bridged endpoints — while GET /api/v1/health reported the interface and the central `unhealthy` and GET /api/v1/system/ccu reported `available: false`. A user whose CCU is powered off or rebooting sees every Home Assistant entity available with frozen values and every Matter accessory online, forever; only the health page tells the truth.
findings.verified_by: measurement against the running daemon (logs $S/run/G3/logs/daemon-chaos.log; REST/MQTT/Matter captures) plus code trace of the four files named above
findings.fix_sketch: Drive the client state machine from the recovery coordinator: on a failed reconnect probe transition Connected -> Reconnecting (and after N failures -> Failed) so ClientStateChangedEvent fires and WireDeviceAvailability's existing branch runs. Separately, stop counting Reconnecting as connected in the surface that feeds GET /api/v1/interfaces.connected. Pin it with a boot-order-style e2e test that kills the simulated CCU and asserts devices[].available == false and the retained availability topic == offline.
findings.verify_reasoning:
MEASURED AND REPRODUCED. Daemon 0.61.4 (own instance, REST :19400, MQTT :19430, Matter :19440) against godevccu on :19450-19452. Simulator SIGKILLed at 13:42:42; ports confirmed closed. For 19 min 5 s (62 consecutive 10 s poll samples, 13:42:58 -> 14:01:47) GET /api/v1/interfaces reported connected:true, GET /api/v1/devices reported available:true for both devices, GET /api/v1/matter/endpoints reported reachable:true for both bridged endpoints, the retained MQTT topics openccu-loom/ccu-v13/ccu-v13-HmIP-RF/<addr>/availability stayed 'online', the retained per-DP payloads kept "available":true, and openccu-loom/ccu-v13/hub/connectivity/ccu-v13-HmIP-RF stayed 'true'. Not one of those surfaces emitted a single message after the kill. The surfaces that DO tell the truth: GET /api/v1/system/ccu available:false within seconds, and GET /api/v1/health -> 503 unhealthy (every interface component unhealthy triggers the all-interfaces-down rule in health.ServiceAvailability). 

THE 'NEVER' IS STRUCTURAL, NOT A TIMING WINDOW. I checked every slower path the brief named. (a) The per-interface connection checker runs every 15 s (connectionCheckerInterval, ccu_wiring.go:62); it publishes ConnectionLostEvent, which only marks data-point value SOURCES stale (values_source_lifecycle.go:69) and degrades health -- it never touches the client state machine. (b) The recovery coordinator's heartbeat is 60 s (DefaultHeartbeatInterval) and only re-grants one attempt to an exhausted interface. (c) The attempt cap is 8 (DefaultMaxRecoveryAttempts); reaching it moves the CENTRAL to Failed, never the client. (d) callbackFreshness is 180 s; it only feeds the same ConnectionLostEvent. Over the 19 min the daemon logged 140 recovery.trigger / 24 recovery.started / 23 recovery.failed, EVERY failure at stage tcp_checking ('tcp probe 127.0.0.1:19450: dial tcp: connect: connection refused'). The eight-stage pipeline is Cooldown -> TCP_CHECKING -> RPC_CHECKING -> WARMING_UP -> STABILITY_CHECK -> RECONNECTING -> DATA_LOADING (ccu_wiring.go:915-957), and the ONLY production code that moves a live client out of ClientStateConnected is InterfaceClient.Reconnect (interface_client_orchestration.go:145-156), wired as the RECONNECTING stage -- unreachable while the CCU is down, because TCP_CHECKING fails first. So the force-unavailable branch of WireDeviceAvailability (device_availability.go:71-80) fires only on a recovery that is already succeeding, i.e. exactly when the devices are about to come back. The wiring is inverted, not slow.

SINGLE-WRITER CHAIN VERIFIED: Device.SetForcedAvailability has exactly one production caller (device_availability.go:46) driven only by ClientStateChangedEvent; DeviceLifecycleSubtypeAvailabilityChanged has two publishers, that one and eventbridge.go:1487 which fires only on an inbound wire value (none arrive from a dead CCU); Matter Reachable hangs off that same lifecycle event (daemon_matter.go:3277-3283); GET /interfaces connected is literally ClientState()==Connected (coordinators/client.go:51-56).

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE FINDING, neither of which rescues it. (1) The cited code fact is wrong: state_machine.go:133 is IsAvailable, and IsConnected (line 137-141) returns state==Connected ONLY -- it does not treat Reconnecting as connected. The surfaces stay true because the state never leaves Connected at all, not because Reconnecting is miscounted. (2) I could not confirm the coordinator's suggested refinement that a 'ping_pong_verification' option exists and flips this in ~3 min when enabled: `grep -rn 'ping_pong_verification|PingPongVerification'` over internal/config and the whole tree returns nothing at HEAD 34b0f4c9. There is no such config field, so there is no opt-in that changes the outcome; I am not asserting that refinement.

findings.title: A graceful shutdown never publishes `<base>/bridge/status = offline`, so every HA entity stays available after a normal daemon stop
findings.claim: `Bridge.AnnounceOnline` (internal/north/mqtt/bridge.go:874) publishes the retained `online` marker on `<base>/bridge/status`, and every HA-Discovery payload the daemon emits references that topic in `availability` with `availability_mode: all` (e.g. internal/north/mqtt/discovery.go:515-522, discovery_aggregate.go:380-387, alarm_discovery.go:73-80). There is no counterpart: `grep -rn 'AnnounceOffline'` over the whole tree returns nothing, and the only caller side is `_ = bridge.AnnounceOnline(ctx)` in cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_north.go:717. The `offline` value therefore exists only as the broker-side MQTT Last Will, which a broker discards when the client sends a clean DISCONNECT — exactly what a graceful shutdown does.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured on one broker with a subscriber attached to '#': SIGTERM at 12:41:07 produced `openccu-loom/security/availability offline` and `openccu-loom/alarm/<zone>/availability offline` but NO `openccu-loom/bridge/status` message at all, leaving the retained value at `online`; SIGKILL at 12:46:12 produced `openccu-loom/bridge/status offline` (the broker's LWT). So after `systemctl stop openccu-loom`, a Home Assistant add-on stop or a `docker stop`, all ~84 discovered entities stay `available` in Home Assistant showing their last values, indefinitely, instead of going `unavailable`.
findings.verified_by: measurement — MQTT stream $S/run/G3/mqtt-stream.txt lines at 12:41:07 (SIGTERM, no bridge/status) vs 12:46:12 (SIGKILL, bridge/status offline)
findings.fix_sketch: Add `Bridge.AnnounceOffline(ctx)` that publishes the retained `offline` payload on `b.topics.BridgeStatus()` and call it from the daemon's MQTT teardown before the client disconnects. Add a plane round-trip test asserting the topic carries `offline` after a graceful Stop.
findings.verify_reasoning: MEASURED, both halves, on my own broker + daemon. A graceful SIGTERM publishes no message at all on <base>/bridge/status, leaving the retained value at 'online'; a SIGKILL makes the broker publish the Last Will 'offline' on the same topic. The code matches exactly: the CONNECT carries Will{Topic: buildLWTTopic(cfg), Payload: 'offline', Retain: true} (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_north.go:661-665) and Bridge.AnnounceOnline (internal/north/mqtt/bridge.go:874) is the only writer of that topic; there is no AnnounceOffline anywhere in the tree (`grep -rn AnnounceOffline .` returns nothing), and the shutdown path mqttSupervisor.teardown (cmd/openccu-loom/mqtt_supervisor.go:640-661) goes straight to lifecycle.Stop, i.e. a clean DISCONNECT, which by MQTT spec makes the broker discard the will. Every HA-Discovery payload the daemon emits lists that topic first in an availability_mode:'all' list (verified in the live payloads on my broker), so after a clean stop all three availability sources for a device entity remain online: bridge/status retained 'online', the per-device availability topic retained 'online', and the per-DP payload's "available":true. The Security & Safety plane is the exception and does the right thing -- openccu-loom/security/availability was published 'offline' at the instant of SIGTERM.

findings.title: The HA-discovery orphan sweep deletes retained configs the daemon is still driving, so the published entity set differs between two runs on the same fleet
findings.claim: `RunDiscoveryOrphanCleanupOnce` is fired from the post-central-snapshot hook (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_southbound.go:599-645) and evicts every retained `homeassistant/.../config` under the central's node-id namespace that is not present in `Bridge.declared` at that moment (internal/north/mqtt/retain_cleanup.go:684-790). `declared` is only written by a successful publish (internal/north/mqtt/bridge.go:1937), and the hub-plane publisher that declares sysvars / programs / install-mode / message counters / system metrics is serial-gated and re-Started later on CentralSouthboundReadyEvent (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_southbound.go:66-69). The sweep therefore races the hub declare pass, and anything not yet declared is deleted from the broker; the pass is one-shot per central per boot, so nothing re-publishes it within that run.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured eviction counts across six boots against the same 4-device fleet: 15, 1, 42, 0, 1, 0. In the first boot the log line `mqtt.discovery_orphan_cleanup central=ccu-g3 evicted=15` (12:19:22) was followed by exactly 15 HA entities that never appeared on the broker for the remaining 20 minutes of that run: `homeassistant/sensor/ccu-g3_sysvars/{alarmlevel,energytoday,lastmotion}/config`, `homeassistant/switch/ccu-g3_programs/{1000,1001,1002}/config`, `homeassistant/button/ccu-g3_programs/{1000,1001,1002,1003}_execute/config`, `homeassistant/sensor/ccu-g3_central/install_mode_hmip/config`, `homeassistant/sensor/ccu-g3_messages/{service,inbox}/config`, `homeassistant/sensor/ccu-g3_system/connection_latency/config`, `homeassistant/update/ccu-g3_system/system_update/config`. They only reappeared after a daemon restart. A third boot evicted 42 configs. In Home Assistant this deletes the corresponding entities (and every automation/dashboard reference to them) on an arbitrary subset of restarts.
findings.verified_by: measurement — six boots, eviction counts from the daemon logs, retained-topic set diff $S/run/G3/mqtt-topics-run1.txt vs $S/run/G3/mqtt-topics-run2.txt; the precise ordering that produces a large eviction is PLAUSIBLE (I could not force it on demand)
findings.fix_sketch: Do not run the discovery orphan sweep off the device snapshot. Gate it on the hub-discovery ready signal (the same CentralSouthboundReadyEvent debounce the hub publisher uses) so `declared` is complete before the comparison, and/or make the sweep a diff against the topics the current build *can* declare rather than the ones it happens to have published already.
findings.verify_reasoning:
The eviction is GENUINELY WRONG -- it retracts HA-Discovery configs the daemon published seconds earlier in the SAME boot and is still driving -- and the mechanism is sharper than the finding states. Root cause: RunDiscoveryOrphanCleanupOnce takes a broker 'snapshot' by SUBSCRIBING to homeassistant/# for a window (default 2 s, north.mqtt.retain_cleanup_window_ms) and its collector IGNORES THE RETAINED FLAG -- the handler signature is func(topic string, _ []byte, _ bool) (internal/north/mqtt/retain_cleanup.go:710-712, snapshotRetained at :437-490). Every LIVE publish the daemon itself makes during that window is therefore treated as a retained orphan candidate. Bridge.publishDiscovery writes b.declared[topic] only AFTER client.Publish returns (bridge.go:1917-1937), while the broker has already fanned the message out to the sweep's own subscription, so the handler's `_, declared := b.declared[topic]` check loses the race for anything published inside the window. Proof that this is not a leftover-from-a-previous-build story: G3's boot 1 ran against a broker started 37 s earlier with an EMPTY retained store, and still logged inspected:83 evicted:15.

DIRECT DOCUMENTARY PROOF from the G3 capture (which I re-derived independently from the raw stream, not from the finding's prose): in daemon-run3, at 12:47:23-24 the daemon published 60 per-device configs plus 23 hub-plane configs (programs 8, sysvars 5, messages 3, central 2, connectivity 1, system 4); the sweep snapshot closed at 12:47:26.616 with inspected:107 evicted:42; and at 12:47:26 the stream carries empty-payload retractions on EXACTLY those hub node ids (programs 15, sysvars 10, system 6, messages 5, central 4, connectivity 2 = 42). Publish and retract are 2 s apart, same boot, same bridge. Damage is durable: the hub discovery pass is one-shot per boot, and G3's run1 retained set captured 17 minutes after its evicted:15 sweep contains only 9 hub configs where the following run's contains 23 -- 14 hub entities gone for the life of that daemon. In Home Assistant an empty retained config deletes the entity and every automation/dashboard reference to it.

WHY THE COUNT VARIES ACROSS IDENTICAL BOOTS: it is purely whether the hub-plane publish burst falls inside the sweep's snapshot window, which is a race between two independent timelines. I ran six boots of the same daemon against the same 2-device fleet and the same broker: evicted 0,0,0,0,0,0 with inspected 53 every time -- in all six the hub burst landed ~3 s BEFORE the window opened (hub configs at 13:47:10, window 13:47:13.2-15.2), so everything was already in `declared`. G3's boots landed the other way. A seventh boot with retain_cleanup_window_ms raised to 15000 also evicted 0, because the wider window pushed the sweep-slot queue out past the hub burst instead of over it. So the nondeterminism is real and the finding's own 15/1/42/0/1/0 spread is the signature, but the sweep is not 'usually destructive' -- it is destructive exactly when the two bursts overlap.

I did NOT confirm the coordinator's suggested refinement that 'the orphan sweep's 45 s timer fires during the initial publish': I measured the discovery sweep opening 3-4 s after the post-central-snapshot hook on a default window and ~29 s after it on a 15 s window (slot contention with the raw sweep and the unscoped scrub), never on a 45 s timer, and there is no 45 s constant in the sweep path. The trigger is SetPostCentralSnapshotHook (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_southbound.go:598-645), not a fixed timer.

findings.title: Every ALARM system variable is modelled with a string value instead of a bool, because the CCU reports value:"" for the ALARM type and parseSysvarValue falls through to StringValue
findings.claim: Measured on both live CCUs: SysVar.getAll returns `"value": ""` for EVERY variable of type ALARM - 15 of 15 on OttoGo, 23 of 23 on KearneyGo, e.g. {"id":"10639","name":"DutyCycle-Alarm","type":"ALARM","value":"","valueName0":"nicht ausgelöst","valueName1":"ausgelöst"}. This is the CCU's own behaviour, not a transient: `cat /www/api/methods/sysvar/getall.tcl` emits `sv.Value()`, and a read-only ReGa walk over ID_SYSTEM_VARIABLES with ValueSubType()==istAlarm shows value=[] varType=4 (string) while the real state sits in AlState(). Go side: hub_wiring.go:1137 -> upsertSysvar -> parseSysvarValue(hmenum.HubValueTypeAlarm, `""`). In that function (hub_wiring.go:1856-1893) the `case Logic, Alarm:` arm at line 1871 only matches "true"/"1"/"false"/"0"; "" matches neither, control leaves both switches and line 1893 returns hmtypes.StringValue(""), true. Verified by executing the real function in the worktree: inferSysvarType=ALARM, parseSysvarValue -> ok=true kind=string string="" (a LOGIC "false" in the same run correctly yields kind=bool). upsertSysvar then calls existing.OnValue(StringValue("")) (hub_wiring.go:1212). The MQTT publisher passes val.Unwrap() through sysvarStateForMQTT (hub_mqtt_publisher.go:762/886), which returns the raw "" because the sysvar has no ValueList, while hub_discovery.go:237-252 declares the same entity as a binary_sensor with payload_on "true" / payload_off "false" and device_class problem. The reference stack does not do this: aiohomematic's parse_sys_var routes ALARM through to_bool(), and to_bool("") returns the bool False (aiohomematic/support/__init__.py:116-137).
findings.failure_scenario: An operator has a CCU alarm variable (on this CCU: Heizungsausfall, S_Rauchmelder_Status, S_Wassermelder_Status, DutyCycle-Alarm, RF-Gateway-Alarm, WatchDog-Alarm, 38 across the two machines). OpenCCU-Loom publishes an MQTT discovery payload declaring a binary_sensor with device_class problem and payload_on/payload_off "true"/"false", then publishes the empty string on its state topic on every hub refresh. Home Assistant shows the entity as unknown and it never turns on or off - the smoke/water/heating-failure alarm is silently dead on every north-bound plane. REST /sysvars likewise reports type ALARM with value "".
findings.verified_by: live SysVar.getAll on both CCUs + read-only ReGa probe of ValueSubType()==istAlarm + the CCU's own getall.tcl + executing parseSysvarValue in the worktree ($S/repro/G4/EVIDENCE.md §1, out/*.SysVar.getAll.json, scripts/probe_alarm_sysvar.fn)
findings.fix_sketch: In parseSysvarValue, treat an ALARM/LOGIC payload of "" as false (or return ok=false so the model keeps ValueKindNone rather than a string), and never let the ALARM arm fall through to the StringValue fallback. Better still, source the ALARM state from AlState() - extend the get_alarm_messages / sysvar-description ReGa script to emit it - since sv.Value() is structurally empty for OT_ALARMDP objects.
findings.verify_reasoning: Measurement and mechanism reproduce exactly; the failure_scenario over-states the affected set. Re-measured with my own raw JSON-RPC client (no repo transport): SysVar.getAll returns value:"" for 15/15 ALARM entries on OttoGo and 23/23 on KearneyGo, while LOGIC entries in the same responses carry "true"/"false". This is CCU behaviour, not a request defect: I read /www/api/methods/sysvar/getall.tcl off the device and it emits `sv.Value()` for the value field, and a read-only ReGa walk over ID_SYSTEM_VARIABLES shows every istAlarm variable with Value()=[] and VarType()=4 (string). Mechanism proven by executing the real production functions against the real captured payload (v9_alarm_sysvar_test.go): declared ALARM -> inferSysvarType=ALARM -> parseSysvarValue returns ok=true kind=string unwrap="" (the same run parses LOGIC "false" to kind=bool false), so upsertSysvar calls OnValue(StringValue("")). Consequence chain holds: hub_discovery.go BuildSysvarDiscovery renders a non-extended ALARM sysvar as a binary_sensor with payload_on "true" / payload_off "false" / device_class problem; wireOneSysvar publishes val.Unwrap() through sysvarStateForMQTT, which returns the raw value unchanged because an ALARM sysvar has no ValueList - so the state topic carries the empty string, which matches neither payload, and the HA entity has no reachable ON or OFF state. aiohomematic's reference behaviour is confirmed as claimed: parse_sys_var routes ALARM through to_bool, and to_bool("") returns False (support/__init__.py:116-137). WHAT IS OVER-STATED: the failure_scenario names DutyCycle-Alarm, RF-Gateway-Alarm and WatchDog-Alarm and totals 38 variables across the two CCUs. Those are isInternal:true, and hub_wiring.go:1121 skips internal sysvars unless the operator sets include_internal_sysvars or an INTERNAL marker. With default config the affected set is 3 on OttoGo (Heizungsausfall, S_Rauchmelder_Status, S_Wassermelder_Status) and 2 on KearneyGo (Alarm_1SV, SysvarAlarm) - 5, not 38. Severity stays high because the surviving 3 are exactly the operator's smoke / water / heating-failure alarms, and because opting into internal sysvars widens it back to 38. ALSO UNVERIFIABLE READ-ONLY: no ALARM sysvar on either CCU is currently triggered (AlState()==0 for all 38), so I cannot show what a triggered one reports; the demonstrated defect is that the normal, untriggered state is unrepresentable on the north-bound plane.

findings.title: Assigning a channel to a system variable is impossible on real CCUs: resolveChannelISEID calls Interface.getIseIDByAddress, which the CCU does not implement, and maps the 401 to ErrSysvarChannelUnknown -> 422
findings.claim: Live: `Interface.getIseIDByAddress {"interface":"HmIP-RF","address":"00245A49949662"}` -> `json-rpc error 401: method not found (Interface.getIseIDByAddress)` on OttoGo (firmware 3.89.8.20260719). The CCU's method directory has no such file: `ls /www/api/methods/interface/` lists 56 .tcl files and getiseidbyaddress.tcl is not one of them; the CCU's only ISE-ID lookup is Device.getReGaIDByAddress (which answers "18470" for the device address and "noDeviceFound" for a channel address). Go side: hubJSONRPCWriter.resolveChannelISEID (hub_wiring.go:2127-2146) issues exactly that call; the client wraps a JSON-RPC fault as *hmerr.JSONRPCError (internal/client/transport/jsonrpc/client.go:342), so the `errors.As(err, &rpcErr)` branch at hub_wiring.go:2130 fires for EVERY address and returns hub.ErrSysvarChannelUnknown. Both callers are on the operator path: CreateSysvar (hub_wiring.go:2040, whenever spec.Channel != "") and UpdateSysvar (hub_wiring.go:2191, whenever spec.Channel is non-nil and non-empty). The REST handlers translate that sentinel into 422 with the detail "channel_address does not resolve to a device channel" (internal/north/rest/handlers/hub.go:577 and :671). Clearing an assignment still works (*spec.Channel == "" short-circuits to channelParam "-1" without a lookup, hub_wiring.go:2185-2189); only setting one is dead. Note the same method backs CcuBackend.GetIseIDByAddress (internal/client/backends/ccu_extended.go:957), which therefore always errors too.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator creates or edits a system variable in the SPA and picks a channel for the Kanalzuordnung (e.g. 00245A49949662:1). The daemon answers 422 'channel_address does not resolve to a device channel' for every address on the CCU, including addresses it has itself just loaded into the model and is rendering in the picker. The feature cannot be used at all on real hardware, and the error blames the operator's input.
findings.verified_by: live JSON-RPC call (401 method not found) + `ls /www/api/methods/interface/` on the CCU + code trace of the error mapping to 422 ($S/repro/G4/EVIDENCE.md §3, out/ccu_methods_files.txt)
findings.fix_sketch: Resolve the channel ISE-ID from data the daemon already has: Device.listAllDetail returns every channel's `id` next to its `address` and loadDeviceNames already builds that IseAddressMap (hub_wiring.go:604-634) - invert it instead of round-tripping to a method the CCU does not expose. Keep the JSON-RPC path only as a fallback, and stop mapping a 401 'method not found' onto a validation error that blames the address.
findings.verify_reasoning: I specifically tried to refute this as a malformed-request artefact and could not. The method is genuinely absent, not mis-called: I issued Interface.getIseIDByAddress in the exact shape the Go code sends ({"address":"..."} only, hub_wiring.go:2129), then with the interface parameter added, then as Device.getIseIDByAddress and Channel.getIseIDByAddress - all four return `401 method not found (<name>)` on an authenticated session that answers Interface.listInterfaces and Device.getReGaIDByAddress correctly in the same session, so it is neither a session nor a permission nor a parameter-shape problem. The CCU's own dispatch table settles it: `find /www/api -iname "*iseid*"` returns nothing on either CCU, and the interface namespace lists 56 .tcl files with no getiseidbyaddress.tcl. Both CCUs agree (same firmware 3.89.8.20260719). The CCU offers no channel->ise-id lookup at all over JSON-RPC: Device.getReGaIDByAddress answers "18470" for the device address 00245A49949662 but "noDeviceFound" for the channel address 00245A49949662:1. Consequence chain verified end to end: hubJSONRPCWriter is the production sysvar mutator (constructed at hub_wiring.go:158); jsonrpc.Client wraps every CCU fault as *hmerr.JSONRPCError (client.go:342), so the errors.As branch at hub_wiring.go:2130 fires for every address and returns hub.ErrSysvarChannelUnknown; CreateSysvar takes that path whenever spec.Channel != "" (hub_wiring.go:2039-2045, before any create call is issued, so the sysvar is not created at all) and UpdateSysvar whenever spec.Channel is non-nil and non-empty (hub_wiring.go:2185-2194); both REST handlers map that sentinel to 422 with detail "channel_address does not resolve to a device channel" (handlers/hub.go:577-581 and :670-677); and the SPA really sends the field on both paths (SysvarList.svelte:213 on edit, :319 on create). Clearing an assignment still works because *spec.Channel == "" short-circuits to "-1" without a lookup - only setting one is dead. Severity stays high: the feature is 100% unusable on real hardware and the error message blames the operator's input.

findings.title: The MQTT plane topic round-trip guards compare declarations against a reimplementation of the publisher's topic set, so a publisher-side topic change is undetected
findings.claim: TestSecurityPlaneTopicsRoundTrip (security_topics_roundtrip_test.go:38) collects the declared side from the real discovery builders, but builds the 'published' side in securityPublishedTopics (security_topics_roundtrip_test.go:125-143) as a hand-written mirror: a literal key list {state,alarm,problem,health,last_alarm,last_fault,event,fault} fed through securityStateTopic plus securityClassTopic/securityZoneTopic. It never observes internal/north/mqtt/security_reconcile.go, which is the code that actually enqueues the writes (security_reconcile.go:48-67). Measured: changing security_reconcile.go:54 from `p.enqueueJSON(securityStateTopic(base, "problem"), ...)` to `p.enqueueJSON(base+"/security/problems", ...)` — i.e. the publisher writing a different topic than discovery declares — left TestSecurityPlaneTopicsRoundTrip green (0.117s) AND the whole internal/north/mqtt package green (18.3s). The same mirror shape is used by hub_topics_roundtrip_test.go (hubPublishedTopics), alarm_topics_roundtrip_test.go (alarmPublishedTopics), device_topics_roundtrip_test.go and addon_update_topics_roundtrip_test.go; the alarm one at least restates its topics literally instead of calling the shared helper, the security one calls the same helper on both sides for every state topic.
findings.failure_scenario: A refactor of security_reconcile.go / hub_mqtt_publisher.go drops or respells one publish call. Home Assistant creates the entity from the retained discovery config and it stays unavailable (or unknown) forever — exactly the `security/class_smoke` vs `security/class/smoke` defect these guards were written for after it shipped. CI is green on every PR, and the plane's own publish tests are green too because they assert the publisher writes what the publisher writes.
findings.verified_by: mutation in $S/wt: internal/north/mqtt/security_reconcile.go:54 topic renamed; `go test ./internal/north/mqtt/ -run TestSecurityPlaneTopicsRoundTrip` ok, `go test ./internal/north/mqtt/` ok; mutation reverted
findings.fix_sketch: Derive the published set by driving the real publisher (construct the AlarmMQTTPublisher/SecurityPublisher against a recording client, run reconcile, collect the topics it enqueues) instead of restating it. If a full publisher rig is too heavy, at minimum stop calling the same topic helper on both sides — the security plane's state topics currently move in lockstep by construction.
findings.verify_reasoning: The MQTT *PlaneTopicsRoundTrip guards do not observe the publisher. securityPublishedTopics (security_topics_roundtrip_test.go:125-143) and hubPublishedTopics (hub_topics_roundtrip_test.go:183-209) are hand-written sets built by calling the same topic helpers the discovery side calls; the guard's own doc comment concedes this ('deliberately derived from the same builders the publisher uses, so a rename on either side keeps both in step'). The published half therefore moves in lockstep with the declared half by construction, and the one divergence the guard exists to catch — publisher writes topic X, discovery declares topic Y — is exactly the divergence it cannot express. I reproduced the weakness on two planes, so it is a family weakness, not one bad guard. IMPORTANT CORRECTION to the finder's evidence: the specific mutation they ran (security 'problem') IS caught, by a different guard they did not run — tests/contract/security_mqtt_plane_test.go drives the real publisher and observes real publishes, and it failed with 'no publish observed for topic openccu-loom/security/problem'. The finder scoped their run to internal/north/mqtt and so reported a hole that is in fact plugged at that spot. I therefore re-ran the experiment on a security topic that no observation test pins ('health', renamed to 'engine_health'): internal/north/mqtt AND the entire tests/contract package both stayed green. Same for the hub plane: diverging the publisher's own topic resolver (Inbox.MQTTTopics, internal/model/hub/inbox.go:242) from the discovery declaration left the hub guard, the whole mqtt package, internal/model/hub and internal/central/adapter all green. So the guard genuinely does not bite; the suite compensates for some security-plane topics by accident of a separate contract test, and for none of the hub plane. Severity stays high: the uncovered topics are real (security/health, security/last_fault, the hub inbox aggregate), and the failure mode is the shipped 'entity appears in Home Assistant and stays unavailable forever' defect.

findings.title: TestEveryRegistryWalkerHasAnAdoptSeam only recognises the literal `for … := range <Registry>.List()` form, so hoisting the call into a local hides the walker entirely
findings.claim: rangesOverRegistryList (registry_walker_adopt_seam_test.go:336-347) requires rng.X to be a *ast.CallExpr resolving to (*central.Registry).List; anything else is not a walker. Measured: rewriting internal/security/service.go:169 from `for _, u := range s.reg.List() {` to `units := s.reg.List()` + `for _, u := range units {` — a behaviour-preserving edit — removes internal/security.Service.Start from the walker set. With the adopt seam ALSO removed (svc.AttachCentral(name) deleted from cmd/openccu-loom/security_wiring.go:89), the guard passes (ok, 69s) while a runtime-adopted CCU never enters the Security & Safety domain. Without the hoist the same seam deletion FAILS the guard, so the hoist is the whole difference. The instrumented run shows the guard sees only 7 walkers in the entire tree, and the anti-vacuity floor is `len(walkers) < 5` — with one walker hidden it is still 6, so the floor does not compensate. Registry.Names() (internal/central/central_registry.go:271) is a second invisible traversal form and is already used in 15+ production call sites.
findings.failure_scenario: The defect class CLAUDE.md calls the second-largest the daemon has produced (13 hand-found instances) returns: a subsystem subscribes to every central present at boot, a CCU adopted at runtime is permanently silent on that plane until restart, and the guard that exists to make this loud never sees the walk because it was spelled with a temporary or with Names().
findings.verified_by: two mutations in $S/wt: (a) seam deletion alone -> FAIL with the walker named; (b) seam deletion + `units := s.reg.List()` hoist -> ok. Both reverted.
findings.fix_sketch: Detect the walk by data flow rather than syntax: flag any function that calls (*central.Registry).List or .Names and reaches events.Subscribe with a value derived from the result, regardless of where the range sits. Cheaply approximated by also matching a range whose X is an identifier assigned from List()/Names() in the same function body.
findings.verify_reasoning: rangesOverRegistryList (tests/contract/registry_walker_adopt_seam_test.go:336-347) requires the range expression to be, syntactically, a *ast.CallExpr resolving to (*central.Registry).List. Both halves of the claim reproduce exactly. Half (a), the negative control: deleting svc.AttachCentral(name) from cmd/openccu-loom/security_wiring.go:89 makes the guard FAIL in 46s, naming internal/security.Service.Start and its file:line and printing the full remediation text — so the guard is real and does bite the plain defect. Half (b): adding a behaviour-preserving hoist on top ('units := s.reg.List()' then 'for _, u := range units') makes the same broken tree PASS in 57.8s. The hoist is the entire difference; nothing else changed. The anti-vacuity floor does not compensate — it is 'len(walkers) < 5' (line 87) and the run stayed above it with one walker hidden, which is why the test reported ok rather than the vacuity error. The Names() half of the claim is also correct: the guard's resolver checks fn.Name() != "List" and there is no reference to Names anywhere in the file, so a Registry.Names() traversal is structurally invisible to it. I checked whether that hole is currently occupied and it is not: the ~18 production Names() call sites are per-request name resolution (internal/north/mqtt/command_subscriber.go:339 resolveCentral), REST/MCP listings and mDNS counts — none is a boot walk that subscribes. So today the Names() form is a latent hole, not an active defect. Severity high: this guards the defect class CLAUDE.md calls the second-largest the daemon has produced (13 hand-found instances), and the evasion is a refactor any developer might perform innocently.

findings.title: The dormant-capability wiring pins assert only that a method name appears somewhere in the package source, so a call that is present but never executed keeps them green
findings.claim: MustFindMethodCall (wiring_helpers.go:101-120) parses the caller path — which for most pins is a whole package DIRECTORY (parseFiles, wiring_helpers.go:37) — and walks the AST for any SelectorExpr whose Sel matches the method name and whose receiver expression string ends with the receiver ident. It never asks whether the enclosing function is reachable, whether the branch runs, or what the call achieves. The ~25 pins in tests/contract/wiring_pins/dormant_capability_wiring_test.go all rest on it. Measured on the archetype: replacing `bridge.AttachACLLister(store)` (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_matter.go:243) with `_ = func() { bridge.AttachACLLister(store) }` — the call present in source, never executed — leaves TestPin_ACLLister_AttachedInDaemon green (0.415s). Every behavioural ACL test (internal/north/matter/endpoint/dispatcher_acl_test.go, im/read_wildcard_acl_test.go, bridge/subscribe_acl_test.go, …) constructs its own dispatcher and lister, so none of them crosses the composition root either. The same limitation applies to the syntactic pin TestPin_BootCentralRemovalMirrorsEveryAdoptHook (tests/contract/wiring_pins/central_boot_removal_test.go:33), which stayed green when I dropped the security detach half from perCentralHooks (cmd/openccu-loom/central_adopt.go:251) — there the effect test in cmd/openccu-loom caught it, and for the ACL pin no such effect test exists.
findings.failure_scenario: The ACL wiring is moved into a helper that the composition root stops calling, or lands behind a config branch that is never taken. endpoint.TopologyDispatcher has no ACL source, CheckACL fails open, and every AccessControl entry a Matter controller wrote is silently unenforced on operational (CASE) reads/writes/invokes — with the pin, the bridge unit tests and the whole suite green.
findings.verified_by: mutation in $S/wt: cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_matter.go:243 turned into a never-invoked closure; `go test ./tests/contract/wiring_pins/ -run TestPin_ACLLister_AttachedInDaemon` ok; reverted
findings.fix_sketch: For the security-relevant pins (ACL above all) add one effect assertion through the real composition root: build the bridge the way daemon_matter.go does and assert an unauthorised CASE read is refused. Where a syntactic pin must stay, at least require the call to sit in a function the composition root reaches, and say in the doc comment that presence, not execution, is what it checks.
findings.verify_reasoning: Both halves confirmed, and the second half makes this more than a cosmetic test weakness. Test half: contract.MustFindMethodCall (tests/contract/wiring_helpers.go:101-120) parses a caller path — for this pin the whole cmd/openccu-loom DIRECTORY — and walks the AST for any SelectorExpr whose Sel matches the method name and whose receiver string ends with the receiver ident. It never asks whether the enclosing function is reachable or whether the call executes. Replacing 'bridge.AttachACLLister(store)' at cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_matter.go:243 with '_ = func() { bridge.AttachACLLister(store) }' — call present in source, never invoked — left TestPin_ACLLister_AttachedInDaemon PASS in 0.12s, and left the ENTIRE tests/contract/... tree (195s) plus tests/contract/wiring_pins (7.8s) plus cmd/openccu-loom (101s) green. Notably TestEveryWiringSetterHasAProductionCaller does not compensate, because the syntactic caller still exists. The ~25 pins in dormant_capability_wiring_test.go all rest on this same helper, so the weakness is the whole pattern, not one pin. Security half, checked independently as instructed: CheckACL genuinely fails open. internal/north/matter/endpoint/dispatcher.go:762-765 reads 'if d == nil || d.acl == nil { return im.StatusSuccess // enforcement not wired — fail open }', and the behavioural table pins that as intended: dispatcher_acl_test.go:88 case 'nil lister fails open' passes fabricIndex=1 (a real CASE fabric) requiring privManage and expects im.StatusSuccess. I ran that subtest and it PASSES. The only production path that populates d.acl is Bridge.AttachACLLister -> bridge.go:665 dispatcher.SetACLLister, i.e. the exact call the mutation neutralised. So losing this one line silently unenforces every AccessControl entry a Matter controller wrote, on all operational CASE reads/writes/invokes, with no test anywhere failing. That is a latent security hole gated by a presence-only assertion, which is why severity stays high rather than dropping to a test-quality note.

findings.title: ENUM-typed binary sensors publish the VALUE_LIST label but declare payload_on/off "true"/"false", so Home Assistant never matches the state and the entity stays `unknown` forever
findings.claim: The per-parameter binary_sensor branch in `Build` writes a fixed boolean payload contract regardless of the wire type: `body["value_template"] = valueJSONValueLowerTemplate` and `body["payload_on"]="true"` / `body["payload_off"]="false"` (internal/north/mqtt/discovery.go:691-705). The raw plane, however, resolves ENUM data points to their VALUE_LIST label before publishing: `internal/central/adapter/eventbridge.go:1806-1808` calls `mqtt.ResolveEnumLabel(value, pd.Type, pd.ValueList)` whenever `pd.Type == hmenum.ParameterTypeEnum`, and `ResolveEnumLabel` (internal/north/mqtt/bridge.go:2005-2014) returns `valueList[idx]`. So the slot state is `{"value":"OPEN"}`, the declared template renders `open`, and neither `payload_on` ("true") nor `payload_off` ("false") matches. Home Assistant's mqtt binary_sensor handles the no-match case at homeassistant/components/mqtt/binary_sensor.py:199-222: it falls into the `else: # Payload is not for this entity` branch, emits an _LOGGER.info("No matching payload found for entity ...") and `return`s without touching `_attr_is_on`. The entity therefore never leaves `unknown`, and the only trace is an INFO-level log line. Fleet measurement over the full 399-device corpus: 43 of 11784 emitted entities are binary_sensors whose descriptor type is ENUM - HMIP-SWDO / HmIP-SWDO-I / HmIP-SWDM / HmIP-SWDM-B2 / HmIP-SCI ch1 STATE (VALUE_LIST [CLOSED,OPEN], device_class window/opening), HmIP-DLP ch3 STATE (device_class door), HM-Sen-RD-O ch1 STATE (VALUE_LIST [DRY,RAIN], device_class moisture) and 36x PROCESS (VALUE_LIST [STABLE,NOT_STABLE], device_class running) on HmIP-MIO16-PCB and HmIP-FWI.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator pairs an HmIP-SWDO window contact and enables MQTT discovery. HA creates `binary_sensor.<name>` with device_class `window`. The daemon publishes `{"value":"CLOSED",...}` / `{"value":"OPEN",...}` on every open/close. HA logs `No matching payload found for entity: binary_sensor.x with state topic: ... template output: 'open'` at INFO (invisible at default log level) and the contact shows `unknown` in the dashboard forever - every automation keyed on it never fires. The same happens for the HM-Sen-RD-O rain detector and for all 36 PROCESS diagnostics.
findings.verified_by: code trace + reproducer. Fleet dump: $S/wt/tests/integration/testdata/discovery_snapshot_openccu-loom.json (produced by TestDiscoverySnapshotDumpAgainstGodevccu with the production publish order and Usage gate mirrored; see $S/repro/J1/worktree_generator.patch), joined against the per-DP descriptor table j1_descriptors.json - 43 hits, listed above. End-to-end reproducer $S/repro/J1/zz_j1_enum_binary_test.go.txt (run in the worktree's internal/central/adapter package) drives one HMIP-SWDO STATE value through the real EventBridge and prints both halves in one run: `STATE slot payload : {"value":"OPEN","available":false,...}` and `payload_on = true / payload_off = false / value_template = {% if value_json is defined and value_json.value is not none %}{{ value_json.value | lower }}{% endif %}`. HA side read from /home/markus/Dokumente/GitHub/core (HA 2026.8.2) mqtt/binary_sensor.py:199-222.
findings.fix_sketch: In the binary_sensor branch of Build, when the descriptor is ENUM with a two-entry VALUE_LIST, derive payload_on/payload_off from the list itself (lower-cased, matching the `| lower` template) instead of hard-coding "true"/"false" - e.g. payload_off = lower(valueList[0]), payload_on = lower(valueList[1]); for longer lists map the on-set explicitly. Add a Test*PlaneTopicsRoundTrip-style guard that, for every fleet binary_sensor, asserts the declared payload_on/off is producible by the state the raw plane publishes for that descriptor.

findings.title: north.rest.rate_limit.* and north.rest.tls_cert_file/tls_key_file are bound once at router assembly but carry no restart-required badge, so enabling either security control reports success and changes nothing
findings.claim: Both live in SectionREST (internal/configstore/sections.go:28) and are rendered by the section editor (neither is in configstore.sectionUnmanagedPaths, internal/configstore/store.go:118-123, nor in dedicatedEditorPaths). Rate limit: cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_rest_mount.go:390 `RateLimit: buildRateLimitConfig(cfg)`; buildRateLimitConfig (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_north.go:741-750) returns nil when !rl.Enabled, and internal/north/rest/router.go:629 `if d.RateLimit != nil { r.Use(middleware.RateLimit(*d.RateLimit)) }` — a middleware that was not installed at assembly time can never start running. TLS: cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_rest_mount.go:277-285 builds the CertReloader only `if cfg.North.REST.TLSEnabled()`, and :518-519 `if tlsReloader != nil { restServer.EnableTLS(tlsReloader) }`. mountRESTServer runs once (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon.go:781). restSurfaceRestartRules (internal/config/restart.go:227-269) badges csrf_enabled, csrf_secure, cors, openapi_validate and north.ui.enabled — but neither the rate-limit block nor the two TLS paths, so RestartRequiredFieldPaths() omits them and the PUT answers restart_required:false (internal/north/rest/handlers/admin_config.go:690). The field's own doc comment (internal/config/config.go:1182-1188) adds to the confusion by advertising hot reload: it is the certificate FILE CONTENT that is hot-reloaded, never the paths.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) An operator under a brute-force / scraping load opens Settings -> REST, ticks rate_limit.enabled, sets rps/burst, saves. The UI reports success with no restart badge and no pending-restart banner; the limiter is never installed and every request still passes unlimited. (b) An operator uploads a certificate and sets north.rest.tls_cert_file / tls_key_file expecting the API+SPA to move to HTTPS; the save succeeds with no restart hint and the listener keeps serving plain HTTP, so credentials continue to travel unencrypted while the config surface reports TLS configured.
findings.verified_by: code trace: restart.go restSurfaceRestartRules read in full; buildRateLimitConfig + router.go:629 nil gate; daemon_rest_mount.go TLSEnabled() gate at :281 and EnableTLS at :518; single mountRESTServer call site
findings.fix_sketch: Add restart rules for north.rest.rate_limit.{enabled,requests_per_second,burst} and north.rest.{tls_cert_file,tls_key_file} in restSurfaceRestartRules. For TLS also reword the field comment so the hot-reload claim is scoped to the certificate bytes, not to enabling TLS.
findings.verify_reasoning: Both halves hold, verified against source and by executing the restart table. Rate limit: buildRateLimitConfig (daemon_north.go:741-750) returns nil when !rl.Enabled and router.go:629 installs middleware.RateLimit only `if d.RateLimit != nil` — a middleware absent at assembly can never appear later. TLS: daemon_rest_mount.go:277-286 builds the CertReloader only `if cfg.North.REST.TLSEnabled()` and :518-519 calls EnableTLS only when that reloader exists; the same gate also decides whether handlers.TLSCertService is wired, so even the certificate-upload surface is dead when TLS was off at boot. mountRESTServer runs once (daemon.go:781). restSurfaceRestartRules covers csrf_enabled, csrf_secure, cors, openapi_validate, north.ui.enabled and nothing else: RestartRequiredFieldPaths() reports false for north.rest.rate_limit.enabled/.requests_per_second and for tls_cert_file/tls_key_file, and RestartRequiredDiff(base, tls-configured) == [] while TLSEnabled() == true on the same candidate. Neither path is in sectionUnmanagedPaths/dedicatedEditorPaths, so the section editor renders them. Severity kept at high: unlike J2-2 these are security controls that report applied and are not — an anti-brute-force limiter that never installs, and a config surface that shows TLS configured while the listener stays plain HTTP. The field comment (config.go:1182-1190) does advertise hot reload; it is true only for the certificate bytes, as claimed.
