findings.title: The CCU JSON-RPC login backoff only engages after 10 consecutive rejections and is applied while the login mutex is held, so a rotated CCU password produces 10 back-to-back Session.login attempts and then stalls every JSON-RPC call on that central for up to 60 s each.
findings.claim: Login enforces the accumulated backoff only under `if failCount >= loginMaxFailedAttempts && backoff > 0` (internal/client/transport/jsonrpc/client.go:386-395), so the first 10 rejected logins are issued with no delay at all — contradicting the method's own doc comment ('exponential backoff starting at 1 s, doubling each time ... across up to 10 failures', :360-364) and the const comment on loginMaxFailedAttempts ('the number of consecutive authentication failures after which the client stops retrying login automatically', :90-93); the client never stops, it only starts sleeping. From attempt 11 on, currentBackoff has already saturated at loginMaxBackoff = 60 s (noteLoginFailure, :445-455), and the sleep runs inside Login, which is only reached through loginOrRenew (:575-586) and reloginLocked (:616-631) — both hold c.sessionLoginMu across the call. Every Call therefore serialises behind that 60 s sleep (Call -> acquire on the bounded semaphore :227 -> loginOrRenew :232).
findings.failure_scenario: An operator rotates the CCU WebUI password (or the CCU's session pool fills up — the CCU reports both as the same JSON-RPC error, :403-407). The daemon first hammers the CCU with 10 immediate Session.login attempts, which is what keeps an exhausted session pool exhausted. Afterwards every hub read on that central — sysvars, programs, device names, the SPA's hub views, the ReGa runner — blocks for up to 60 s before failing, one caller at a time, instead of failing fast; a request without a deadline blocks indefinitely long. The 'stops retrying automatically' contract the constant documents never takes effect, so the CCU keeps receiving a rejected login every 60 s forever.
findings.verified_by: Code trace of internal/client/transport/jsonrpc/client.go:86-102 (constants), :365-440 (Login, backoff gate at :386), :445-455 (noteLoginFailure saturating at 60 s), :563-598 (loginOrRenew holds sessionLoginMu across Login), :616-631 (reloginLocked likewise), :226-234 (every Call goes through loginOrRenew).
findings.fix_sketch: Apply the backoff from the first failure (drop the `failCount >= loginMaxFailedAttempts` gate and sleep whenever currentBackoff > 0), and move the wait out of the mutex-held region — record a `nextLoginAttempt` deadline and have Login return hmerr.ErrAuthFailure immediately while the deadline is in the future, so callers fail fast instead of queueing. Either honour the documented 'stop retrying' contract or reword both comments to match the implemented behaviour.
findings.resolution: the login backoff no longer holds the session mutex; a caller arriving during a backoff fails fast

findings.title: Colour changes made outside Matter (hue / saturation / colour temperature) never dirty-mark the ColorControl cluster, so a subscribed controller keeps showing the old colour until brightness or on/off happens to change
findings.claim: The bridge's only proactive-report path for a bridged endpoint is `Bridge.wireMeasurementListenersLocked` (internal/north/matter/bridge/subscribe.go:868-975), which takes the endpoint's Source, type-asserts it to `interfaces.MatterChangeNotifier` (subscribe.go:905-907) and registers ONE callback (`wireMeasurementNotifier`, subscribe.go:983-1006) that calls `mgr.OnAttributeChanged(p)` for the endpoint's reportable paths. For a colour light the Source is `*light.ColorLight` / `*light.ColorTempLight` / `*light.RGBWLight`. None of the three defines `OnMatterValueChanged`; they inherit it through `*Light` -> `*generic.Float`, and `(*generic.Float).OnMatterValueChanged` (internal/model/generic/matter.go:244-249) subscribes to the LEVEL data point ONLY. The colour data points are separate fields that nothing subscribes to: `ColorLight.hue` / `.saturation` (internal/model/custom/light/color.go:25-30), `ColorTempLight.kelvin` / `.colorLevel` (color.go:167-181), `RGBWLight.kelvin` (rgbw.go:66-77). The affected attributes ARE declared reportable - `hsColorServer.MatterReportable()` returns CurrentHue (0x0000) + CurrentSaturation (0x0001) (matter_color.go:526-528), `ctColorServer.MatterReportable()` returns ColorTemperatureMireds (0x0007) (matter_color.go:386-388) - so the paths exist in `endpoint.ReportablePaths` and would be shipped if anything ever marked them dirty. The wrapper cluster servers (`hsColorServer`, `ctColorServer`, `rgbwColorServer`) are plain value structs with no `OnMatterValueChanged`, so the secondary loop at subscribe.go:951-965 that rescues `ElectricalPowerServer`-style sibling notifiers finds nothing either. The file's own compile-time-assertion comment states the gap outright: matter_color.go:29-31 'Colour-attribute (hue / saturation / colour-temperature) change propagation is a separate additive refinement.' Every other custom DP fans its constituent data points in explicitly - Climate (climate/matter.go:57-67), Cover/Blind/Garage (cover/matter.go:55-91), Lock (lock/matter.go:41-50), Siren (siren/matter.go:44-70) - which is what makes this one an omission rather than a design.
findings.failure_scenario: An HmIP-RGBW / HmIP-BSL colour light is bridged to Apple Home or Google Home with an active wildcard subscription. The user changes only the colour - at the wall remote, in the CCU WebUI, from a CCU program, or from the OpenCCU-Loom SPA/MQTT plane. HUE/SATURATION (or COLOR_TEMPERATURE) update in the model, `Float.OnConfirmedUpdate` on LEVEL does not fire, `Manager.OnAttributeChanged` is never called for (endpoint, 0x0300, 0x0000/0x0001/0x0007), and no ReportData carries the new colour. Apple Home / Google Home keep displaying and reporting the previous colour indefinitely - until the user separately changes brightness or on/off, which dirties the full reportable-path set (filterPathsByNotifierCluster falls back to all paths because ColorLight is not itself a MatterClusterServer, subscribe.go:1029-1033) and finally ships the colour that has been stale for hours.
findings.verified_by: code trace: bridge/subscribe.go:868-1006 (single notifier per endpoint) -> internal/model/custom/light/color.go:25-30 and rgbw.go:66-77 (colour DPs are separate fields) -> internal/model/generic/matter.go:244-249 (inherited notifier watches only the LEVEL DataPoint) -> internal/model/custom/light/matter_color.go:386-388,526-528 (the colour attributes are declared reportable). Cross-checked against every other custom DP's OnMatterValueChanged (climate/cover/lock/siren) which all compose their constituent DPs via custom.CombineUnsubs.
findings.fix_sketch: Give ColorLight / ColorTempLight / RGBWLight their own `OnMatterValueChanged` that shadows the embedded Light's and combines it with the colour DPs' notifiers, exactly as Climate does: `custom.CombineUnsubs(l.Light.OnMatterValueChanged(cb), l.hue.OnMatterValueChanged(cb), l.saturation.OnMatterValueChanged(cb))` (and `kelvin` / `colorLevel` for the CT and RGBW variants). Add a wiring pin that publishes a hue-only confirmed update through a real bridge + subscription manager and asserts a ReportData for (0x0300, 0x0000) arrives.
findings.verify_reasoning: Mechanism verified end to end, and the source admits it: matter_color.go:28-31 states 'Colour-attribute (hue / saturation / colour-temperature) change propagation is a separate additive refinement.' The bridge registers exactly one notifier per endpoint (bridge/subscribe.go:983-1005), obtained by asserting the endpoint Source to interfaces.MatterChangeNotifier. ColorLight/ColorTempLight/RGBWLight define no OnMatterValueChanged of their own (grep over internal/model/custom/light/*.go finds none — only the doc comments), so they inherit (*generic.Float).OnMatterValueChanged (internal/model/generic/matter.go:244-249), which wraps the LEVEL DataPoint only. The colour attributes ARE declared reportable (hsColorServer.MatterReportable -> CurrentHue/CurrentSaturation at matter_color.go:526-528; ctColorServer -> ColorTemperatureMireds at :386-388; rgbwColorServer at :743-749), so the paths exist and would ship if anything marked them dirty. Nothing does: the only other OnAttributeChanged call sites are Descriptor.PartsList (bridge/bridge.go:790-797) and BDBI.Reachable (bridge/receive.go:531). The max-interval path does not rescue it — the manager passes nil paths on the keep-alive tick (im/subscription/engine.go:112-125) and reportSubscription then ships an empty ReportData with SuppressResponse (bridge/subscribe.go:369-392), i.e. a heartbeat, not a re-read. The recovery route the finder names also checks out: *ColorLight does not implement MatterClusterID (only the wrapper servers do), so filterPathsByNotifierCluster falls back to the full reportable set (subscribe.go:1027-1040) and the next brightness/on-off change ships the stale colour. Downgraded from high to medium: Matter is opt-in (default off), attribute READS are live so an explicit read or a re-subscribe returns the fresh colour, and the staleness self-heals on the next level/on-off change. Within those bounds the described failure — Apple/Google showing the old colour for hours after a wall-remote or CCU-side colour change — is exactly right.

findings.title: AccessControl.Extension (0x0001) is always encoded as TLV null instead of a list, because the wire writer has no case for []AccessControlExtensionEntry and the []any case it claims to use can never match
findings.claim: `AccessControl.MatterRead(0x0001)` returns `[]AccessControlExtensionEntry{}` when empty (internal/north/matter/cluster/core/access_control.go:264-272) and `[]AccessControlExtensionEntry` with the stored rows when populated; `MatterReadFiltered` returns the same concrete type on the fabric-filtered path (access_control.go:314-330). `defaultAttributeValueWriter` (internal/north/matter/bridge/reply.go:454-1001) type-switches on the dynamic type and has cases for every other list the cluster servers return - []AccessControlEntryStruct (532), []NetworkInterfaceStruct (588), []FabricDescriptorStruct (635), []NOCStruct (663), [][]byte (686), []uint32 (707), []uint16 (727), []NetworkInfoStruct (737), []GroupKeyMapStruct (754), []GroupInfoMapStruct (767), []TargetStruct (785), []DeviceTypeStruct (807), []AccuracyStruct (836) - but NOT []AccessControlExtensionEntry. A Go type switch matches the exact dynamic type, so `case []any:` (reply.go:695, whose comment claims 'used by AccessControl.extension') cannot match a `[]AccessControlExtensionEntry` value. Control therefore falls to `default:` at reply.go:996-1001, which calls `enc.PutNull(tag)`. The comment on the Fabrics case (reply.go:644-647) documents exactly this failure mode for a sibling attribute: 'Without this case the writer falls through to default: and emits TLV null'. The Extension write path is fully implemented and stores per-fabric rows (access_control.go:592-630, decoder at bridge/attribute_value_reader.go decodeExtensionList), so this is a live read-back path, not dead code. The cluster also advertises FeatureMap=0x1 (EXTS) precisely on the grounds that 'we serve Extension (accessControlAttrExtension returns an empty list above)' (access_control.go:272-289) - a claim the wire contradicts. matter.js models Extension as a non-nullable list (packages/model/src/standard/elements/access-control.element.ts), so null is off-schema in both the empty and the populated case.
findings.failure_scenario: A controller (or an interop/conformance run) writes AccessControl Extension entries and reads them back: the write is accepted with Success and the rows are stored in `AccessControl.extensions`, but every subsequent read and every Subscribe report for 0x001F:0x0001 carries TLV null, so the data is permanently unreadable - the feature looks implemented and returns nothing. Independently, every wildcard read/subscribe of the root endpoint - which Apple Home performs right after CASE - carries `null` for a list-typed attribute whose feature bit the same cluster advertises, which is the exact schema inconsistency the neighbouring Fabrics comment blames for an Apple RemoveFabric teardown.
findings.verified_by: code trace + Go type-switch semantics: access_control.go:264-272 / 314-330 return `[]AccessControlExtensionEntry`; reply.go:454-1001 enumerates the writer's cases with no arm for that type; reply.go:695 `case []any` matches only dynamic type []interface{}; reply.go:996-1001 default calls PutNull. Cross-checked every other slice type returned from a MatterRead in internal/north/matter/cluster and internal/model against the writer's case list - this is the only gap.
findings.fix_sketch: Add `case []mattercore.AccessControlExtensionEntry:` to defaultAttributeValueWriter that opens an array and emits one struct per entry with Data at context tag 1 and FabricIndex at 254 (matter.js access-control.element.ts AccessControlExtensionStruct), and fix the stale `case []any` comment. Add a TLV fixture to notes/parity/matter/tlv-wire-fixtures.json covering the empty and the one-entry shape.
findings.verify_reasoning: Verified by experiment, not only by reading. AccessControl.MatterRead(0x0001) returns []AccessControlExtensionEntry both empty (access_control.go:264-272) and populated, and MatterReadFiltered returns the same concrete type (:316-330); endpoint/dispatcher.go:448-469 passes the value through unchanged into im.AttributeValue{Value: v}; im.ReportData.MarshalTLV is always called with the single writer defaultAttributeValueWriter (reply.go:270) - there is no per-cluster writer override anywhere in internal/north/matter. The writer's type switch has no arm for that type, so it falls to default -> enc.PutNull (reply.go:996-1001). I encoded it: with the concrete empty slice AND with a one-entry slice the AttributeDataIB byte stream is `... 24 04 01 18 34 02 18 ...` - byte-identical to an explicit AttributeValue{IsNull:true} - whereas []any{} produces `36 02 18 18` (an empty TLV array). So both the empty and the populated case go on the wire as null. matter.js HEAD (checked directly, commit 4120271): packages/model/src/standard/elements/access-control.element.ts:34-37 declares Extension as `type: "list"` with conformance EXTS and no `quality: "X"`, i.e. non-nullable - so null is off-schema, and the Go cluster advertises FeatureMap=0x1 (EXTS) on the explicit grounds that it serves the list (access_control.go:280-289). The write path is live (access_control.go:592-630 stores per-fabric rows), so read-back is genuinely broken rather than dead code. Severity kept at medium: it is a real wire-schema violation on every root-endpoint wildcard read, but no shipping controller is known to depend on Extension, and the finder's link to the Apple RemoveFabric teardown is an analogy to a different attribute, not an observed effect.

findings.title: A SubscribeRequest with KeepSubscriptions=true still tears down every subscription the peer holds on the same CASE session, contradicting the flag matter.js honours
findings.claim: `registerSubscription` sets `ReplaceSessionDuplicate: fabricIndex != 0 && requestHdr.HasSourceNodeID` (internal/north/matter/bridge/subscribe_dispatch.go:264) - the expression contains no `req.KeepSubscriptions` term, so it is true for EVERY CASE Subscribe regardless of the flag. `subscription.Manager.Subscribe` then runs `if req.ReplaceSessionDuplicate && req.SessionID != 0 { m.CloseSession(req.SessionID) }` (internal/north/matter/im/subscription/manager.go:212-214), and `CloseSession` deletes every subscription whose SessionID matches (manager.go:321-336) and fires the close observer, which drops the bridge routing entry (bridge/subscribe.go:91-104) so no report - not even a keep-alive - can ever be sent for it again. matter.js does the opposite: `InteractionServer.ts:611` gates the peer teardown on `if (fabric !== undefined && !keepSubscriptions)`, and nothing anywhere in the server path cancels an existing subscription when keepSubscriptions is true. The Go code's own SubscribeArgs doc-comment states the correct rule it then violates: 'When false (the default) existing subscriptions on the session are left untouched, which is the correct behaviour for a peer that genuinely intends to hold multiple simultaneous subscriptions with different path sets' (manager.go:518-528). Note the KeepSubscriptions=false teardown is already handled separately and correctly a few lines above (subscribe_dispatch.go:219-237 via ClosePeer/CloseSession), so ReplaceSessionDuplicate adds nothing for that case and only mis-fires for the true case.
findings.failure_scenario: A controller holds two subscriptions with different path sets over one CASE session - e.g. a wildcard subscription plus a narrow high-cadence one, which is what chip-tool produces when two `subscribe` invocations target the same node, and what any client built on matter.js's InteractionClient produces since its subscribe default is keepSubscriptions=true. The second SubscribeRequest silently closes the first: its routing entry is deleted, the engine stops ticking it, and the controller receives no cancellation of any kind. The entities backed by the first subscription freeze at their last reported value until the controller's own MaxInterval watchdog expires and it re-subscribes - and if it re-subscribes on the same session, it loses the other one instead, ping-ponging.
findings.verified_by: code trace: subscribe_dispatch.go:238-265 (flag set unconditionally for CASE) -> im/subscription/manager.go:203-214 (CloseSession on the whole session) -> manager.go:321-336 + bridge/subscribe.go:91-104 (routing entry destroyed). Gold standard read directly: ../matter.js/packages/node/src/node/server/InteractionServer.ts:611-628 clears only under `!keepSubscriptions`; ../matter.js/packages/matter.js/src/cluster/client/InteractionClient.ts:790,840,917 default keepSubscriptions=true.
findings.fix_sketch: Change the flag to `ReplaceSessionDuplicate: !req.KeepSubscriptions && fabricIndex != 0 && requestHdr.HasSourceNodeID`, or drop it entirely since the KeepSubscriptions=false branch above already tears down by (fabric, peer). Add a manager test that admits two subscriptions with different path sets on one SessionID with KeepSubscriptions=true and asserts both stay active.
findings.verify_reasoning: The flag is set with no KeepSubscriptions term: subscribe_dispatch.go:264 `ReplaceSessionDuplicate: fabricIndex != 0 && requestHdr.HasSourceNodeID`, i.e. true for every CASE Subscribe. Manager.Subscribe then runs `if req.ReplaceSessionDuplicate && req.SessionID != 0 { m.CloseSession(req.SessionID) }` (manager.go:211-214) before the quota check, and CloseSession (manager.go:321-336) deletes every subscription whose SessionID matches and calls finishClose, which fires the close observer that the bridge uses to drop the routing entry. The KeepSubscriptions=false branch immediately above (subscribe_dispatch.go:219-237) already tears down by (fabric, peer) via ClosePeer, so the flag adds nothing for the false case and only mis-fires for the true case - and SubscribeArgs' own doc comment (manager.go:518-528) states the rule it violates. Gold standard checked directly at matter.js HEAD (4120271): packages/node/src/node/server/InteractionServer.ts:611 `if (fabric !== undefined && !keepSubscriptions)` guards the whole peer-teardown loop, and nothing else in the server subscribe path cancels an existing subscription; the client default is keepSubscriptions=true in both packages/protocol/src/action/request/Subscribe.ts:45 (`keepSubscriptions ?? true`) and packages/matter.js/src/cluster/client/InteractionClient.ts:790/840/917. The finder's line citations are accurate. Severity medium: a controller that holds one subscription per session (Apple's usual pattern) never trips it, but the behaviour is non-conformant and the second-subscription case degrades silently, with no cancellation sent to the peer.

findings.title: A single AttributeReport whose encoded size exceeds the 2048-byte datagram cap can never be sent, and the resulting send error aborts the whole Subscribe-Initial rather than degrading
findings.claim: `chunkReportData` fills chunks greedily and closes the current chunk when adding an entry breaches the budget, but only if the chunk is non-empty: `if len(body) > budget && (len(current.Reports) > 0 || len(current.EventReports) > 0)` (internal/north/matter/bridge/reply.go:329, mirrored at :348). An entry that alone exceeds the budget is therefore emitted in a chunk of its own at whatever size it needs - the function's doc-comment says so explicitly (reply.go:299-305: 'A single oversized entry (e.g. a Descriptor.PartsList with 1000+ endpoint IDs) cannot be sub-split at this layer - it ships in its own chunk and the receiver decides whether to tolerate the over-sized datagram'). But the receiver never gets the choice: `udp.Listener.Send` hard-rejects the datagram before it reaches the socket - `if len(payload) > MaxDatagramSize { return ErrPayloadTooLarge }` with MaxDatagramSize = 2048 (internal/north/matter/transport/udp/listener.go:33, 242-245). On the Subscribe path that error propagates out of `sendReplyReliable` -> `streamInitialReportChunks` returns err (bridge/subscribe_dispatch.go:407-411) -> `handleSubscribeRequest` returns without ever sending the remaining chunks or the SubscribeResponse (bridge/subscribe.go:803-806), so the subscription is never established and the failure repeats on every retry. The plain Read path fails the same way (bridge/receive_dispatch.go:176). Two attributes can reach that size on a real deployment: (1) Descriptor.PartsList, encoded at exactly 3 bytes per endpoint (`enc.PutUint16` per entry, reply.go:732-736) and enumerated on both EP0 and EP1, with no cap on bridged-endpoint count anywhere in internal/north/matter/endpoint/assembler.go or the eligibility filter - after the AttributeDataIB/path/DataVersion wrapper this crosses 2048 bytes on the order of 650 bridged endpoints (arithmetic from the 3-byte element cost, not measured); (2) OperationalCredentials.TrustedRootCertificates (reply.go:686-693), which is NOT fabric-scoped and concatenates one Matter root certificate (~230-250 bytes) per commissioned fabric, with SupportedFabrics defaulting to 254 (internal/north/matter/cluster/core/operational_credentials.go:386-399).
findings.failure_scenario: On a large multi-CCU installation the bridge assembles enough endpoints that the Aggregator's Descriptor.PartsList AttributeReport alone exceeds 2048 bytes. Every Apple Home / Google Home wildcard Subscribe then dies mid-stream at that chunk with ErrPayloadTooLarge; the controller never receives the SubscribeResponse, times the exchange out and abandons commissioning. Nothing recovers this without reducing the exposed-endpoint count, and the only bridge-side trace is a debug-level `matter.tx.reply` line - /health stays green while the Matter plane is entirely unusable.
findings.verified_by: code trace of the mechanism: reply.go:322-359 (single oversized entry is admitted as its own chunk), transport/udp/listener.go:33+242-245 (hard 2048 reject on Send), bridge/subscribe_dispatch.go:407-411 and bridge/subscribe.go:803-806 (error aborts the Subscribe before the SubscribeResponse), reply.go:732-736 (3 bytes per PartsList entry), no endpoint-count cap found in endpoint/assembler.go or eligibility/eligibility.go. The ~650-endpoint threshold is arithmetic from the exact per-element cost plus the report wrapper, not a measurement.
findings.fix_sketch: Sub-split oversized list attributes at the AttributeDataIB level using the Matter list-chunking form (ListIndex-append AttributeDataIBs, §10.6.1) the way matter.js's AttributeReadResponse emits large lists, so PartsList/TrustedRootCertificates ride across several chunks. As a minimum stop-gap, have chunkReportData return an error (or emit an AttributeStatusIB(ResourceExhausted) for that one path) when a single entry exceeds MaxDatagramSize, so the rest of the report and the SubscribeResponse still ship instead of the whole interaction dying.
findings.verify_reasoning: Mechanism reproduced. chunkReportData closes the current chunk only when it is non-empty (reply.go:329 and :348), so a single entry larger than the budget ships as its own over-budget chunk; udp.Listener.Send rejects any payload > MaxDatagramSize=2048 before touching the socket (transport/udp/listener.go:33, 242-245); sendReplyReliable -> sendReplyOpts writes through exactly that listener (reply.go:133,205), streamInitialReportChunks returns the error (subscribe_dispatch.go:407-411) and handleSubscribeRequest returns before sendSubscribeResponse (subscribe.go:803-806). Measured the threshold rather than trusting the finder's arithmetic: a Descriptor.PartsList AttributeReport encodes to 1236 B at 400 endpoints, 1836 B at 600, 2136 B at 700 and 2736 B at 900, always as a single chunk - so the plaintext crosses 2048 at roughly 683 endpoints and, with the ~32 B of message header + AES-CCM tag added by sendReplyOpts, the effective ceiling is ~670 bridged endpoints. Nothing caps the bridged-endpoint count (no cap in endpoint/assembler.go or the eligibility filter). The TrustedRootCertificates variant needs ~9 commissioned fabrics (SupportedFabrics defaults to 254, operational_credentials.go:386-395), which is reachable but rare. Two refinements to the finder's write-up: the threshold is ~670, not ~650 (immaterial), and the consequence is under-stated - registerSubscription has already admitted the subscription when the stream fails and nothing releases it, so each failed attempt leaves a live record consuming per-fabric quota until the same session re-subscribes. Severity medium: catastrophic when triggered (Matter plane dead, /health green, only a debug log) but it needs an unusually large exposure set.

findings.title: A non-finite float on the south wire is accepted into the model and then breaks every north-bound JSON encoding of the containing collection
findings.claim: The write path rejects NaN/Inf explicitly (internal/parameter/validate.go:147, ErrNaNOrInf) and the BIN-RPC encoder rejects them too (internal/client/transport/binrpc/encode.go:227-231). The read/callback path has no counterpart at any layer. (1) XML-RPC: decode.go:124-132 does strconv.ParseFloat(strings.TrimSpace(s), 64) and returns DoubleValue(f) when err==nil; measured (repro at $S/repro/F5/nan.go): ParseFloat accepts "nan", "NaN", "inf", "+Inf", "infinity" with err==nil (only "1e999" errors). So <double>nan</double> or <double>inf</double> decodes to a DoubleValue. (2) BIN-RPC: decode.go:160-168 computes math.Pow(2, float64(exp)) * float64(mant) / 2^30 with mant/exp read straight off the wire as int32 — a large exp yields +/-Inf, and (mant==0, large exp) yields Inf*0 = NaN; encode.go guards NaN/Inf on the way out, decode.go has no such guard. (3) The value crosses into Go: internal/central/adapter/xmlrpc_caller.go:123-124 (xmlRPCValueToGo -> float64) and internal/central/adapter/wire_value.go:24 (ParamValueFromWire -> hmtypes.FloatValue). (4) A third, string-shaped route reaches the same place: internal/model/generic/coerce.go:123-125 (toFloat64) parses a wire string with the same ParseFloat, so a CCU/CUxD that ships the literal "nan" for a FLOAT parameter lands NaN too. (5) internal/central/adapter/callback_handlers.go:346 calls dp.OnWireValue(goValue); internal/model/generic/datapoint.go:995-1007 -> OnEventAt (datapoint.go:1032+) stores the value with no finiteness or range check — valuesClose(old, NaN) is false so it is even treated as a change and fires the update callbacks. (6) North-bound: internal/north/rest/handlers/write.go:80-84 JSON() sets the 200 header FIRST and then discards the encoder error (`_ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)`); measured: json.Encoder.Encode on a slice containing one NaN returns `json: unsupported value: NaN` and writes 0 bytes, so the ENTIRE response body is empty, not just the offending entry. internal/north/mqtt/bridge.go:1116-1118 PublishSlotState returns the marshal error before publishing, so that data point's retained state topic stops updating for good.
findings.failure_scenario: A CUxD system device (or a Homegear/CCU interface daemon, or any unauthenticated LAN peer reaching the callback listener on :8120 / :8129) pushes ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE = <double>nan</double> for a channel the daemon mirrors. From that moment: POST /api/v1/devices/values:batch (internal/north/rest/handlers/values_batch.go:110-114, which serialises the raw value via toDataPointSummary -> DataPointSummary.Value) answers HTTP 200 with a zero-byte body whenever the batch touches that data point, so the SPA view built on it renders a JSON parse error and every OTHER data point in the same batch is lost as well; the MQTT state topic for that DP never updates again (publish error per event); nothing surfaces the cause because the encoder error is discarded at write.go:83.
findings.verified_by: code trace through the eight file:line steps above + measurement at $S/repro/F5/nan.go (stdlib behaviour of strconv.ParseFloat and json.Encoder.Encode: 'Encode err=json: unsupported value: NaN, bytes written=0')
findings.fix_sketch: Reject non-finite floats where they enter, not where they leave: add a math.IsNaN/IsInf guard to xmlrpc decodeTypedValue's "double" branch and to binrpc readValue's typeDouble branch (error, mirroring encodeDouble), and to generic.toFloat64's string branch. Belt-and-braces: make handlers.JSON encode into a buffer and answer 500 on a marshal error instead of writing a 200 header first and swallowing it.
findings.verify_reasoning: MEASURED END TO END against the live daemon, not inferred. Baseline: POST /api/v1/devices/values:batch for VCU1769958:1 ACTUAL_TEMPERATURE + SET_POINT_TEMPERATURE answered HTTP 200 with 1621 bytes. I then POSTed a plain, UNAUTHENTICATED XML-RPC `event` methodCall carrying `<double>nan</double>` to the daemon's own callback listener at http://127.0.0.1:18510/RPC2/ccu-v4 -- it answered 200 with a normal `<nil/>` response, i.e. the value was accepted. The identical batch request then answered `HTTP=200 bytes=0`: a zero-byte body, and the healthy SET_POINT_TEMPERATURE entry in the same batch was destroyed along with it. `<double>inf</double>` reproduces it identically. The whole decode->store->encode chain is as the finder traced: xmlrpc decode.go:123-131 does strconv.ParseFloat with no finiteness check (ParseFloat accepts "nan"/"inf"), binrpc decode.go:160-168 computes 2^exp * mant / 2^30 with no guard while its own encoder rejects non-finites, and handlers.JSON (internal/north/rest/handlers/write.go:80-84) sets the 200 header FIRST and then discards the encoder error with `_ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)`. Nothing was logged at any level -- I grepped the daemon log after the injection and found no trace of the failure. The blast radius is WIDER than the finding claims in one respect: the single-DP endpoint GET /api/v1/devices/{addr}/channels/{no}/data-points/{param} also answers `HTTP=200 bytes=0`. It is NARROWER in one respect: /api/v1/devices, /api/v1/devices/{addr} and .../channels all keep answering normally (5774 / 2329 / 4944 bytes), because they do not serialise the raw value. TWO SUB-CLAIMS ARE OVER-STATED, neither load-bearing: (a) 'the MQTT state topic for that DP never updates again' -- internal/north/mqtt/bridge.go:1116-1118 returns the marshal error before publishing, so only the NaN event itself is dropped; a subsequent finite value publishes normally. (b) The poisoning is not permanent: I injected `<double>21.5</double>` afterwards and the batch immediately returned to HTTP 200 / 801 bytes. So the window is 'until the next event for that DP', which for a change-driven sensor can be hours. The exposure is real and unauthenticated by default: cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_helpers.go:189-191 returns a nil allowlist unless cfg.Callback.RestrictSourceIPs is set, and rpcserver/listener.go:104-107 treats nil as accept-all, so any LAN host can reach the listener. Severity medium is the right rating -- it needs either a misbehaving CCU/CUxD or a hostile LAN peer, and it self-heals -- but the consequence class (an unauthenticated remote emptying a documented API response with no log line) is real.

findings.title: GET /health reports overall status "unknown" on every healthy daemon about 90 s after boot, because two boot-only components stale-decay and drag the aggregate down.
findings.claim: recordConfigOverlayHealth (cmd/openccu-loom/config_overlay_health.go:31) and recordSecretHealth (cmd/openccu-loom/secret_health.go:28) each record exactly one sample, at boot, and are never called again. internal/health/tracker.go:296-308 (applyStaleLocked) downgrades any component whose last sample is older than DefaultStaleAfter (90 s, tracker.go:83) to StatusUnknown. health.ServiceAvailability - the function the /health handler uses (internal/north/rest/handlers/health.go:56) - ends with `if worst == StatusHealthy && hasUnknown { return StatusUnknown }` (tracker.go:390-391), and Tracker.Overall has the identical rule at tracker.go:338-340. So as soon as those two boot records go stale, a daemon whose every live component is healthy reports "unknown".
findings.failure_scenario: Clean daemon, one CCU, everything working. At boot+25 s GET /api/v1/health returns status "healthy". At boot+2m30s it returns status "unknown" (HTTP still 200) with clean/central, clean/<iface>, clean/scheduler and sqlite all "healthy" and only config.overlay + config.secrets "unknown". Every consumer that reads the status string - the SPA health surface (health.status.unknown -> "Unknown"/"Unbekannt" in assets/ui/src/lib/i18n.ts:1018), an operator dashboard, a watchdog script following docs/admin/observability.md - therefore never sees "healthy" again for the lifetime of the process. The mirror-image consequence is worse: when the master key is missing, recordSecretHealth records config.secrets as UNHEALTHY, and 90 s later that warning silently turns into "unknown" as well.
findings.verified_by: measurement on a freshly booted daemon ($S/repro/G1/EVIDENCE.md section 2) plus the code trace above
findings.fix_sketch: Either re-record the two one-shot components on a cheap periodic job (they are pure in-memory state), or mark them as non-decaying in the tracker (a per-component 'no staleness' flag) so a permanent boot fact is not treated as a missing heartbeat.
findings.verify_reasoning: The mechanism and the observation are exactly right and I reproduced them: daemon booted 13:28:39, GET /api/v1/health `healthy` at +31 s, `unknown` at 13:30:42 (+2 min) and never healthy again, with clean/central, clean/<iface>, clean/scheduler and sqlite all healthy and only config.overlay + config.secrets `unknown` -- both recorded exactly once at boot from cmd/openccu-loom/daemon.go:220-225 and never again. On the disagreement the brief asks me to settle, V4 is right and the finder over-states. (1) The AGGREGATE an operator reads IS degraded, permanently: /health.status is `unknown` forever, GET /diagnostics reports status `unknown` with available:false, and the health SCORE is capped because HealthAdapter.Score counts an unknown component as 0 -- I measured score 66 on a six-component daemon where every live component was healthy, which is a second, quantitative operator-facing lie the finder did not name. (2) But HTTP stays 200 throughout (handlers/health.go:56-59 maps only StatusUnhealthy to 503), and docs/admin/observability.md explicitly tells operators to point probes at the HTTP code and to parse the components array for dashboards -- so the documented monitoring contract is unaffected and no probe flaps. (3) The finder's 'mirror-image consequence is worse' is refuted: applyStaleLocked (tracker.go:298-310) rewrites only Status and leaves LastSample untouched, so a failed overlay keeps its note verbatim in the body, and the Prometheus gauges config_overlay_failed / config_secrets_plaintext are Set once and hold their value (config_overlay_health.go:41-49, secret_health.go:36-43). A missing master key therefore degrades from `unhealthy` to `unknown` on the status axis while the note and the gauge stay correct. (4) The blast radius is also narrower than 'every consumer': the HA/MQTT system_health sensor reads the PER-CENTRAL tracker (daemon_jobs.go:129-137), not the daemon-global one, so it is unaffected, and the SPA ConnectivityLights match named component subsets and stay green. What is genuinely broken is the aggregate status string plus the score/available flags on /health, /diagnostics, the WS system.health command and the MCP surface. Medium, not high.

findings.title: PUT /centrals/{name} silently resets every field the body omits - including `enabled` - and answers 204, so a partial replace takes a working CCU completely offline.
findings.claim: assets/openapi.yaml declares CentralRow with `required: [name, host, interfaces, enabled]` for putCentral. UpdateCentral (internal/north/rest/handlers/admin_centrals.go:230-287) decodes into sqlite.CentralRow and validates only row.Name (:247) and row.Host (:252); the only field protected against the Go zero value is PasswordPlain, via the presence probe in decodeCentralRow (:95-117), whose own doc-comment states the hazard verbatim: 'a partial replace that only flips `enabled` decodes to the Go zero value and destroys the CCU password on disk'. The same reasoning was never applied to enabled, port, json_rpc_port, tls, username, ports, primary_interface, visibility or behavior. The store write `svc.Put(r.Context(), row)` (:270) is an unconditional upsert, and a row with Enabled=false makes the lifecycle tear the central down (central_adopt.go:806-821, removeCentral).
findings.failure_scenario: A REST client (or a generated SDK following the schema loosely) sends PUT /api/v1/centrals/ccu-e2e with {name, host, username, interfaces} to change the username. Measured: HTTP 204 No Content, then GET /api/v1/centrals shows enabled:false with port and json_rpc_port gone, GET /api/v1/system/ccu returns {"entries":[]} and GET /api/v1/devices returns 0 items - the 13 devices, the MQTT/WS/Matter topology and every per-central surface for that CCU are gone, with a 2xx as the only feedback. Recovery needs a second, complete PUT.
findings.verified_by: measurement against the running daemon ($S/repro/G1/EVIDENCE.md section 3) plus the code trace above
findings.fix_sketch: Enforce the schema's required set in UpdateCentral (reject a body without `enabled` / `interfaces` with 400), or make the handler a merge over the stored row - reading the existing record and overlaying only the keys the payload actually carried, the same presence-probe technique decodeCentralRow already implements for password_plain.
findings.verify_reasoning: The observation reproduces EXACTLY on a daemon configured the way the finder's was -- and that configuration is the flaw in the finding. In my run 1 the daemon logged `WARN openapi.spec.read path=assets/openapi.yaml err="no such file or directory"` because buildOpenAPIValidator (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon_north.go:827-837) resolves a BARE RELATIVE path against the process cwd, and I had started the daemon from its data directory. With no validator mounted, `PUT /api/v1/centrals/ccu-v12` carrying {name,host,username,interfaces} returned 204, flipped enabled to false, zeroed port and json_rpc_port, tore the central down, emptied /system/ccu and dropped every device. I then restarted the SAME binary with the SAME config from a cwd where assets/openapi.yaml resolves; the daemon logged `openapi.spec.loaded` and the byte-identical request came back 400 `request body has an error ... Error at "/enabled": property "enabled" is missing`, i.e. the middleware enforces the schema's `required: [name, host, interfaces, enabled]` before the handler ever runs. north.rest.openapi_validate defaults to TRUE (config.go:1153-1160) and the Dockerfile ships the spec at /app/assets/openapi.yaml with WORKDIR /app (Dockerfile:53-55), so the Docker image and both HA add-ons -- the primary shipped deployments -- reject the destructive body. The same re-test also 400s `POST /alarm/zones {"position":1}`, so the finder's sibling G1-rest-live-6 is the same artefact. Now the three sub-questions the brief asked. (a) TRUE: assets/openapi.yaml declares enabled required for putCentral and UpdateCentral (admin_centrals.go:230-287) validates only Name and Host -- the handler itself enforces none of its own documented required set, and the only field protected against the Go zero value is PasswordPlain, whose doc-comment at decodeCentralRow:95-117 names this exact hazard. (b) FALSE as stated: the shipped SPA edit dialog ALWAYS sends `enabled` -- buildRow() sets `enabled: fEnabled` (CentralsAdmin.svelte:385) and toggleEnabled spreads the whole row (`{...row, enabled: !row.enabled}`, :475) -- so no SPA save can disable a CCU by omission. I checked this because the brief asked me to; the coordinator's summary that the SPA omits `enabled` is wrong and I am not repeating it. What buildRow DOES omit is `port`, `ports` and `visibility`, and I measured those being silently destroyed by a SPA-shaped save WITH the validator active (they are optional in the schema, so no middleware can catch them). (c) TRUE: bare 204, no body, no warning; only an INFO `central.remove.live` + `central.disable.live` in the log and an audit row. The damage is permanent -- after a restart the DB tier still wins over the YAML entry, so ccu-v12 stayed disabled. Re-rated from high to medium: the catastrophic variant needs a daemon whose spec file did not resolve AND a client that ignores the documented required set; the variant that bites every deployment is the silent loss of port/ports/visibility on the operator's own edit dialog.
findings.resolution: PUT /centrals/{name} merges on omit for every optional field
findings.status_verified_at: dea785a1 (pre-#606 HEAD); the open two re-checked on 4eecb1e6

findings.title: GET /api/v1/config reports the configured callback ports, not the ports the daemon actually bound, so the dynamic-port modes advertise an address nothing listens on.
findings.claim: ConfigAdapter.SanitizedConfig fills the snapshot straight from the parsed config: `snap.CallbackPorts = hmapi.ConfigPorts{XMLRPC: a.source.Callback.Port, BINRPC: a.source.Callback.BinPort}` (internal/central/adapter/config.go:35-38). Neither value is the effective bind. With `callback.port_range` the XML-RPC listener binds the first free port in the range while Callback.Port keeps the applyDefaults value 8120; with the documented dynamic mode `bin_port: 0` the BIN-RPC listener gets an OS-assigned port while Callback.BinPort stays 0. Nothing else on the REST surface reports the effective port (checked /info, /system/status, /system/ccu, /interfaces).
findings.failure_scenario: Daemon configured with `callback: {port_range: "18110-18140", bin_port: 18150}`. The daemon logs `callback.listen addr=127.0.0.1:18110 port=18110` and announces `http://127.0.0.1:18110/RPC2/ccu-e2e` to the CCU, but GET /api/v1/config returns {"callback_ports":{"xmlrpc":8120,"binrpc":18150}}. An operator debugging 'my CCU pushes no events' opens the firewall for 8120, or a support bundle records 8120 - both point at a port the daemon never bound. With bin_port: 0 the API reports 0.
findings.verified_by: code trace plus observed responses ($S/repro/G1/EVIDENCE.md section 5)
findings.fix_sketch: Feed the callback servers' resolved listener addresses (the same values the rpcserver logs and the init() calls carry) into the ConfigAdapter and report those, falling back to the configured value only before the listeners bind.

findings.title: POST /alarm/zones accepts a body without the spec-required `name` and creates a permanently nameless alarm zone with 201.
findings.claim: assets/openapi.yaml declares the POST /alarm/zones body with `required: [id, name]` and declares 400/422 for validation failures. The handler decodes the body (DecodeJSON, rejecting only unknown fields and malformed JSON) and persists whatever it decoded; no non-empty check on Name exists on the create path. The declared-required `id` is likewise ignored - the server mints its own UUID - which is fine, but leaves `name` as the only operator-facing identifier and it is unvalidated.
findings.failure_scenario: POST /api/v1/alarm/zones with {"position":1} returned 201 and {"id":"ae5be8e4-8f80-4de1-904b-83e9955f8b08","name":"","position":1}; GET /api/v1/alarm/zones then lists a zone with an empty name alongside the real ones. In the SPA's zone list and in every arm/disarm confirm dialog that zone is an unlabelled row the operator cannot tell apart, and alarm arming is one of the surfaces where picking the wrong row has physical consequences. A related looseness in the same area: POST /alarm/codes accepted zones:["zone1"] naming a zone id that does not exist, and PUT /security/sources/{ref} answered 204 for a ref that resolves to no data point.
findings.verified_by: reproducer: negsweep.py case 'missing-required-zone' ($S/repro/G1/neg_results.json), followed by GET /alarm/zones
findings.fix_sketch: Reject an empty name with 422 in the create and update handlers, and validate the zone ids referenced by an alarm code against the zone store.

findings.title: Three read endpoints return a JSON shape the OpenAPI schema forbids: two arrays serialised as `null` and one object declared where an array is returned.
findings.claim: Schema-validating every 200 response of the 131-operation GET sweep against assets/openapi.yaml produced exactly three impossible shapes plus one nullable artefact. (a) GET /incidents declares `type: array` but returns literal `null`: ListIncidents forwards `querier.IncidentsFiltered(...)` (internal/north/rest/handlers/incidents.go:139) / `applyIncidentsFilter(...)` (:142) straight to JSON, and a nil slice marshals as null - note the nil-reader branch three lines above deliberately writes `[]Incident{}` (:129), so the intent is an array. (b) GET /centrals/discovered/ignored has the same defect (declared array, observed null). (c) GET /diagnostics/capture declares `type: object, additionalProperties: true` while ListCaptures returns a slice: `JSON(w, http.StatusOK, svc.List())` (internal/north/rest/handlers/diagnostics_capture.go:141), again with an `[]diagnostics.Summary{}` array in the nil branch (:138). The daemon's OpenAPI middleware validates requests only, so nothing catches response drift.
findings.failure_scenario: A generated client (the project ships openccu-loom-client / -types) types listIncidents as Incident[] and iterates the result; against a daemon with no incidents it receives null and throws instead of showing an empty list. listCaptures is typed as a record and receives an array. The `null`-vs-`[]` pair is the classic shape that only appears on an empty system - i.e. on a fresh install, which is exactly when a new user first opens the view.
findings.verified_by: automated schema validation of every GET response ($S/repro/G1/get_results2.json, entries with schema_error) plus the handler code
findings.fix_sketch: Return an initialised empty slice from the incident and ignored-CCU readers (or wrap with a `if x == nil { x = []T{} }` at the handler), and correct the /diagnostics/capture response schema to the array the handler actually returns.

findings.title: replay_done overtakes the events it acknowledges: control frames and domain frames sit on two independent queues drained by one select, so the resume ack arrives after the first replayed event and reports a seq hundreds ahead of what the client has received
findings.claim: client.replayFrom (client.go:286-302) pushes every replayed event through c.enqueue (the domain queue c.out) and then pushes {op:"replay_done", seq:last} through sendOp -> enqueueCtrl (the control queue c.ctrl). writePump (client.go:597-640) selects over c.out and c.ctrl with no ordering between them, and Go's select picks uniformly among ready cases, so the single control frame is written after roughly the first domain frame instead of after the last. assets/wsapi.json's `resume` block documents the opposite: '{op:"replay_done", seq:N} confirms the replay finished and carries the last-replayed seq'.
findings.failure_scenario: Subscribed with {op:"subscribe",topics:["*"],since:1}. Frame order on the wire: `subscribed` -> event seq=2 -> `{op:"replay_done",seq:258}` -> events seq=3,4,5,...,258. A client that implements the documented protocol either (a) treats replay_done as 'replay complete, everything after this is live' and mislabels ~256 replayed events as live - re-firing automations on every reconnect - or (b) persists replay_done.seq as its resume cursor, as the envelope documentation instructs ('clients store the last received value and pass it back as since'), and on the next reconnect asks for since=258, permanently skipping events 3..257 it never actually processed. Reproduced twice, with 40-frame and unbounded captures.
findings.verified_by: measurement + code trace. Capture in this run (subscribed / seq 2 / replay_done seq 258 / seq 3..): $S/repro/G2/replay_all.json; trace client.go:286-302 and 597-640.
findings.fix_sketch: Send replay_done through the same queue as the replayed events (enqueue a marker on c.out, or serialise both planes onto one ordered channel with a discriminator), so the ack cannot be reordered ahead of the payload it acknowledges.
findings.verify_reasoning: Observation and named mechanism both hold. client.replayFrom (ws/client.go:287-302) pushes every replayed event through c.enqueue onto the buffered domain channel c.out (client.go:193-213) and then pushes {op:'replay_done', seq:last} through sendOp -> enqueueCtrl onto the separate control channel c.ctrl (client.go:264-279). writePump (client.go:598-650) selects over <-c.out, <-c.ctrl and the ping ticker with no ordering constraint; Go's select chooses uniformly among ready cases, so with 146 frames queued on c.out and 1 on c.ctrl the single control frame can be - and in my capture was - written first. That contradicts assets/wsapi.json's own resume block ('after the replay completes, the daemon sends ... {op:"replay_done", seq:N} confirms the replay finished and carries the last-replayed seq'), docs/integrations/rest-ws.md:111 and ADR 0022:35. Both client consequences the finding names are real given the documented contract: a client treating replay_done as the live boundary mislabels every replayed event, and a client persisting replay_done.seq as its cursor skips 2..146 on the next reconnect.

findings.title: A BOOL system variable whose value arrives as a JSON boolean is dropped entirely: no value on REST/WS/MCP, permanently observed:false, and no hub.sysvar_changed when it flips
findings.claim: parseSysvarValue (hub_wiring.go:1856-1894) first tries json.Unmarshal into a string; on failure its comment says it falls back to 'bare numeric / bool shape' but the fallback only tries json.Number (:1863-1868) and returns (zero, false) for anything else. A JSON boolean therefore never parses, so upsertSysvar's `if pv, pok := parseSysvarValue(...); pok { existing.OnValue(pv) }` (hub_wiring.go:1221) is skipped, Sysvar.observed stays false (model/hub/sysvar.go:465-493) and no value is ever recorded. The LOGIC/ALARM branch at :1871-1877 that would map true/false is unreachable for this shape because it operates on the already-decoded string.
findings.failure_scenario: godevccu's SysVar.getAll returns {"name":"Presence","type":"BOOL","value":true}. The daemon reports that sysvar on WS sysvars.list, REST GET /api/v1/sysvars and MCP list_sysvars with observed:false and the `value` key entirely absent, while every other sysvar (FLOAT 0, ENUM 0, STRING "") carries its value - so a client sees a system variable that exists but has no state, and cannot tell it from a genuinely never-read one. Changing it on the CCU (SysVar.setBool Presence=false) produced no hub.sysvar_changed broadcast at all, while the same experiment on a FLOAT sysvar (TargetTemperature 21.5 -> 23.5) did broadcast within one refresh cycle. Whether a production CCU returns bare booleans or quoted strings here I could not verify without hardware; the code's own comment claims it accepts the bare bool shape, and the project's own simulator - which every integration and e2e run uses - emits it.
findings.verified_by: measurement + code trace. Raw godevccu SysVar.getAll capture vs the daemon's WS/REST/MCP output in this run; trace hub_wiring.go:1856-1894 and :1221.
findings.fix_sketch: In parseSysvarValue, add a json.Unmarshal into bool alongside the json.Number fallback (and normalise it to "true"/"false" before the type switch), so LOGIC/ALARM sysvars decode from either the string or the bare JSON shape. Add a table test covering value: true, "true", 1, "1" for HubValueTypeLogic.

findings.title: hub.install_mode_changed is broadcast on every install-mode poll with a byte-identical payload, so a 'changed' event fires every 30 s forever and floods the replay buffer
findings.claim: loadInstallMode (hub_wiring.go:1703-1725) polls Interface.getInstallMode per data point, applies dp.OnState(...) and then calls unit.Hub.PublishInstallModeRefreshed() unconditionally, outside any change check. PublishInstallModeRefreshed (internal/central/coordinators/hub.go:971-985) publishes one hmevent.InstallModeChangedEvent per install-mode data point regardless of whether OnState changed anything. The WS hub re-broadcasts each one as hub.install_mode_changed (ws/hub_events.go:307-315) and the MQTT hub publisher subscribes to the same event (adapter/hub_mqtt_publisher.go:609), so both planes carry the noise.
findings.failure_scenario: Over one 28-minute run with a single interface and install mode off the whole time, the replay buffer holds 63 hub.install_mode_changed events, all with the identical payload {"central":"ccu-g2","enabled":false,"remaining_s":0}, one per 30 s poll - together with hub.metrics_changed they are 156 of the 273 events the daemon emitted (57 % of the entire event stream on an idle system). Consequences: every WS client and SPA view re-renders on a non-event; the 1024-entry replay buffer documented in assets/wsapi.json fills with no-ops, so a client reconnecting after a longer outage gets replay_lost far sooner than the declared capacity suggests; with MQTT enabled the same no-op is republished to the broker every 30 s.
findings.verified_by: measurement + code trace. 63 identical frames in $S/repro/G2/replay_all.json; trace hub_wiring.go:1723, coordinators/hub.go:971-985, ws/hub_events.go:307.
findings.fix_sketch: Have dp.OnState report whether the state actually changed and publish only for the data points that did (or diff enabled/remaining_s against the last published tuple in PublishInstallModeRefreshed). The same question is worth asking for the hub.metrics_changed gauge push, which republishes last_event_age_seconds every 30 s with a value that differs only in the fourth decimal.

findings.title: 18 of the 136 commands assets/wsapi.json declares answer 'unknown_command' in every build of the daemon, and the by_design table that is supposed to explain them is stale in both directions
findings.claim: system.commands on a running daemon returns 118 commands; assets/wsapi.json declares 136. The 18 missing ones - addon_update.check, addon_update.install, ccu.device_statistics, ccu.throttle_stats, central.connectivity, central.info, central.reconcile, central.system_health, change_history.clear, change_history.list, incidents.clear, incidents.get, incidents.list, paramset.copy, paramset.form_schema, service_messages.disable, service_messages.suppressed, service_messages.unsuppress - are all registered behind a non-nil provider in RegisterExtendedCommands (internal/north/rest/ws/commands_extended.go:339-415), and the composition root passes nil for every one of those providers (cmd/openccu-loom/ws_adapters.go:153-190, the trailing comment lists them). The existing guards (tests/contract/wsapi_schema_test.go) compare the schema against the router.Register call sites in source, which exist - they cannot see that production never supplies the provider, which is the bracketing shape CLAUDE.md calls out. notes/parity/by_design.md:975-989, the document that is supposed to make this legible, is wrong in both directions: it lists CacheClearer/ccu.cache_clear and FirmwareRefresher/firmware.refresh as dormant although both are wired and answer live, and it omits incidents.list, incidents.get, paramset.form_schema, service_messages.suppressed, service_messages.unsuppress and addon_update.check/install entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: assets/wsapi.json is the pinned client contract (the Node-RED contrib pins it as spec/ and drift-tests against it). An external client that implements the published catalogue - a monitoring integration calling incidents.list, a diagnostics view calling ccu.throttle_stats, a config UI calling paramset.form_schema - gets {"code":"unknown_command"} from every deployment of the shipped binary, with nothing in the schema marking those entries as unavailable. Measured by diffing the declared set against system.commands and then invoking all 18 individually.
findings.verified_by: measurement + code trace. Live diff declared-vs-registered plus 18 individual calls, all unknown_command; trace commands_extended.go:339-415, ws_adapters.go:153-190, by_design.md:975-989.
findings.fix_sketch: Mark the dormant commands in assets/wsapi.json with an explicit availability flag (and let system.commands stay the runtime truth), refresh the by_design table to match what is actually wired, and add a black-box contract test that boots the daemon and asserts that every command the schema declares as available is present in system.commands.
findings.verify_reasoning: The count and the observation are exactly right; the explanation overreaches on 2 of the 18. 16 of them are unconditionally dormant in every build: cmd/openccu-loom/ws_adapters.go:153-190 hard-codes nil for ChangeHistory, ChangeHistoryClearer, Central, ThrottleStats, DeviceStatistics, IncidentClearer, ExtendedHub and ParamsetReader (with a trailing comment naming them), and omits IncidentLister and UISchema from the config literal entirely, so RegisterExtendedCommands' non-nil guards (commands_extended.go:338-412) never fire. There is no build tag anywhere in internal/north/rest/ws. But addon_update.check and addon_update.install are NOT in that class: ws_adapters.go:162 passes AddonUpdater: w.addonUpdater, which daemon.go:413 sets from wireAddonUpdate -> addonupdate.NewCapabilityProbe().Supported() (addon_update_wiring.go:29-33). That is a genuine runtime capability gate - on a CCU add-on install with the firmware installer present those two commands ARE registered - and wsapi.json's own description for both says 'Unregistered (unknown command) on platforms without the self-update capability'. So both 'unregistered in every build of the daemon' and 'with nothing in the schema marking those entries as unavailable' are false for those two. The correct statement: 16 declared commands are unregistered in every build; 2 more are capability-gated and already documented as such. Everything else in the finding stands and I verified it: the guard tests/contract/wsapi_schema_test.go extracts literal strings from router.Register(...) call sites via the AST (extractRegisteredWSCommands, :140-198), so it structurally cannot see a nil provider - the bracketing shape CLAUDE.md names; and notes/parity/by_design.md's 'ws-rest-split' dormant table is stale in both directions - it lists CacheClearer/ccu.cache_clear and FirmwareRefresher/firmware.refresh as dormant while ws_adapters.go wires both (measured answering live above), and it omits incidents.list, incidents.get, paramset.form_schema, service_messages.suppressed, service_messages.unsuppress and addon_update.check/install.
findings.resolution: by_design's dormant-command table corrected in both directions; the authoritative list is the stub test
findings.status_verified_at: dea785a1 (pre-#606 HEAD); the open two re-checked on 4eecb1e6

findings.title: MCP read tools silently return an empty list for an unknown central_name instead of an error, so an assistant is told the CCU has no devices
findings.claim: The central-scoped MCP read tools filter client-side without validating the name: registerListDevices (tools.go:241-255) does `want := strings.TrimSpace(in.CentralName)` and skips every device whose central differs, with no check that `want` names a registered central; list_programs, list_sysvars, list_rooms, list_functions, list_service_messages, list_alarm_messages and list_inbox follow the same shape. The WS twins resolve the name through centralHub (ws/commands_default.go:562-571) and return bad_request 'ws: unknown central: X', so the two planes disagree about the same mistake.
findings.failure_scenario: list_devices{central_name:"NO-SUCH-CCU"} returns {"devices":[]}, and list_programs / list_sysvars / list_rooms return the same empty envelopes, while WS sysvars.list / programs.list / inbox.list with the same name return bad_request. An LLM agent that mistypes or hallucinates a central name (or uses a name from a stale config) is handed a well-formed 'you have no devices / no programs / no system variables' answer and will report it to the user as fact. This is the failure mode the MCP surface is least able to recover from, because an empty success is indistinguishable from a real empty inventory.
findings.verified_by: measurement + code trace. Live MCP tools/call results for NO-SUCH-CCU vs the WS twins in this run; trace tools.go:241-255, ws/commands_default.go:562-571.
findings.fix_sketch: Resolve central_name against the registry in the shared MCP helper and return an isError result naming the known centrals when it does not match, mirroring the WS ErrCentralUnknown path.
findings.resolution: list_rooms and list_functions validate central_name like their siblings
findings.status_verified_at: dea785a1 (pre-#606 HEAD); the open two re-checked on 4eecb1e6

findings.title: Only JSON-RPC error 400 is treated as a stale CCU session, so a backend that signals expiry with any other code makes every hub refresh and every operator command fail for a full 90-second freshness window instead of re-logging in
findings.claim: jsonrpc.Client.callOnce recovers a stale session only for the single hard-coded code ccuAccessDeniedCode = 400 (client.go:112-115, :337-341); any other JSON-RPC error is wrapped as a plain hmerr.JSONRPCError and surfaced to the caller. Proactive upkeep is loginOrRenew (client.go:563-593) gated by hasFreshSession, whose window jsonSessionAge is 90 s (client.go:104-106), so once the CCU-side session dies the client keeps sending the dead id until its own window elapses. The repo already knows: tests/integration/jsonrpc_test.go:179-186 carries a TODO to map godevccu's -32001/-32002 to ErrAuthFailure.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured against godevccu over a 30-minute daemon run: 39 Interface.getInstallMode, 39 SysVar.getAll, 39 Program.getAll, 16 ReGa.runScript, 9 Interface.listInterfaces and 5 Device.listAllDetail calls failed with 'json-rpc error -32002: Session expired or invalid', in bursts of one to three consecutive 30 s refresh cycles, each burst ending exactly 90 s after it began. Every burst logs 'scheduler: job failed' for hub.sysvar_refresh / hub.program_refresh / hub.install_mode_refresh / hub.connectivity_refresh / devicedetails.refresh, and operator-facing commands issued inside a burst fail outright: WS backup.status, backup.trigger, groups.list, groups.create, sysvars.usage, device.rename and device.rename_channel all returned internal_error with the same -32002 text. A direct probe of the simulator shows why the session dies at all: Session.renew answers `true` (which the client reads as 'renewed in place', per its own comment citing renew.tcl) but the old id is invalid on the very next call, so each renew kills the session for the next 90 s. I could not verify whether production CCU firmware ever reports expiry with a code other than 400 - on that firmware the retry path would mask this - so the user-visible blast radius on real hardware is unproven; against the project's own simulator, which every integration and e2e run uses, it is total for the affected calls.
findings.verified_by: measurement + code trace. Daemon log timeline of json-rpc op.end outcomes ($S/run/G2/daemon.log), direct simulator probe $S/repro/G2/ttl_probe.py + ttl_probe.log; trace client.go:104-115, :337-341, :563-593.
findings.fix_sketch: Classify session expiry by error semantics rather than one magic number: treat 400 plus the -32001/-32002 family (and an empty/invalid-session message) as a stale session, re-login and retry once, exactly as the 400 path already does. Separately, decide whether Session.renew's contract is 'same id' (then godevccu is wrong and should be fixed upstream) or 'new id' (then the client must adopt the returned session).
findings.resolution: closed by the 0.62.0 / 0.63.0 fix waves; confirmed still closed on re-verification
findings.status_verified_at: dea785a1 (pre-#606 HEAD); the open two re-checked on 4eecb1e6

findings.title: Removing a central at runtime leaves 13 retained MQTT topics behind, including one HA discovery config that becomes a permanently-unavailable entity
findings.claim: `removeCentral` calls `o.bringUp.RemoveCentral(name)` (cmd/openccu-loom/central_adopt.go:566) — which runs the central's full southbound teardown — before it calls `o.sbDeps.hubMQTT.RetractCentral(unit)` (line 595). `RetractCentral` builds the connectivity retract items by iterating `u.Clients.List()` (internal/central/adapter/hub_mqtt_publisher.go:202-216), so once the teardown has drained that registry the connectivity binary_sensor is never retracted. The raw-plane hub state topics (`hub/programs/<id>/state`, `hub/programs/<id>/execute_available`, `hub/sysvars/<name>/state`, `hub/update`) have no retract path at all — `RetractCentral` only clears discovery configs.
findings.failure_scenario: Reproduced twice, identical result: adopt `ccu-g3b` via POST /api/v1/centrals (145 MQTT topics appear), then DELETE /api/v1/centrals/ccu-g3b. All 13 REST/Matter/health/metrics surfaces drop the central and 132 of 145 topics are cleared, but these 13 survive as retained messages: `homeassistant/binary_sensor/ccu-g3b_connectivity/ccu-g3b-hmip-rf/config`, `openccu-loom/ccu-g3b/hub/programs/{1000..1003}/{state,execute_available}`, `openccu-loom/ccu-g3b/hub/sysvars/{AlarmLevel,EnergyToday,TargetTemperature}/state`, `openccu-loom/ccu-g3b/hub/update`. Home Assistant keeps a `binary_sensor` for the removed CCU's interface forever; its state topic is never written again, so it sits `unavailable` and cannot be removed except by hand-clearing the retained topic.
findings.verified_by: measurement — two adopt/remove cycles, retained-topic snapshot after each removal; code trace of central_adopt.go:566/595 and hub_mqtt_publisher.go:202-216
findings.fix_sketch: Snapshot the interface list (or build the connectivity retract items) before `bringUp.RemoveCentral`, and extend `RetractCentral` to clear the central's retained hub raw-plane state topics too. A regression test can assert that the retained topic set under both `homeassistant/` and `<base>/<central>/` is empty after a DELETE.
findings.resolution: central removal retracts the raw hub-plane state topics as well as the discovery configs
findings.status_verified_at: dea785a1 (pre-#606 HEAD); the open two re-checked on 4eecb1e6

findings.title: north.mqtt fields declared `restart_required: false` never reach the running bridge — the save reports success and changes nothing until a restart
findings.claim: GET /api/v1/config/schema declares `north.mqtt.topic_base`, `north.mqtt.raw_enabled` and `north.mqtt.discovery_enabled` with `restart_required: false`, and PUT /api/v1/config/sections/north.mqtt answers `{"restart_required": false, ...}`. The live `Bridge` reads these from its own immutable `BridgeConfig` (`b.cfg.RawEnabled` / `b.cfg.HADiscoveryEnabled` / `b.topics`, internal/north/mqtt/bridge.go:83 and the ~25 gate sites that read them), which the section save does not update; the DB overlay is only re-read by `applyDefaults` at boot.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured: PUT north.mqtt with `topic_base: "loomtest"` -> HTTP 200 with `restart_required: false`; over the next 45 s the daemon published 0 topics under `loomtest/` and continued publishing under `openccu-loom/`. PUT with `raw_enabled: false, discovery_enabled: false` -> HTTP 200, `restart_required: false`; over the next 70 s the daemon kept publishing raw-plane topics. After a restart the same stored values did take effect (GET /api/v1/config then reported `features: {ha_discovery: false, raw_topics: false}` and `homeassistant/*` publishing stopped). An operator who renames the topic base or turns the discovery plane off from the SPA gets a success toast, no restart hint, and a daemon that keeps doing the old thing.
findings.verified_by: measurement — MQTT stream $S/run/G3/mqtt-cfg.txt before/after each PUT and across the following restart
findings.fix_sketch: Either propagate a north.mqtt section save into the live bridge (rebuild BridgeConfig + TopicBuilder and re-announce), or mark these three fields `restart_required: true` in `config.ClassifyFields` so the schema, the SPA and the PUT response all tell the operator the truth.
findings.resolution: not worked in #606: a north.mqtt section save still reports restart_required:false and reaches no running bridge. cmd/openccu-loom/reload.go and internal/north/rest/handlers/admin_config.go are untouched.
findings.status_verified_at: dea785a1 (pre-#606 HEAD); the open two re-checked on 4eecb1e6

findings.title: `north.mqtt.raw_enabled: false` is ignored by the alarm and Security & Safety planes, which keep publishing raw topics
findings.claim: Every device/hub publisher gates on `if !b.cfg.RawEnabled { return nil }` (about 25 sites in internal/north/mqtt/bridge.go). The alarm and security publishers do not: `PublishAlarmState` (internal/north/mqtt/alarm_publisher.go:683), `PublishAlarmAvailability` (:689), `RetractAlarmTopic` (:698) and `PublishAlarmEvent` (:703) carry no RawEnabled check, and internal/north/mqtt/security_publisher.go contains no `RawEnabled` reference at all — only the discovery halves gate, on `HADiscoveryEnabled` (:517, :661, :671).
findings.failure_scenario: Measured with `raw_enabled: false` persisted and applied at boot (GET /api/v1/config reported `raw_topics: false`): after the restart at 13:12:57 the `homeassistant/*` plane went silent as expected, but the daemon still published retained `openccu-loom/security/{availability,state,alarm,problem,health}` and `openccu-loom/security/class/smoke` — 6 topics, repeatedly. An operator who disables the raw plane (e.g. to keep a shared broker clean, or because only HA Discovery is wanted) still gets the alarm/security raw plane written to their broker.
findings.verified_by: measurement — topics published after 13:12:57 in $S/run/G3/mqtt-cfg.txt while GET /api/v1/config reported raw_topics false; code trace of alarm_publisher.go / security_publisher.go
findings.fix_sketch: Add the `if !b.cfg.RawEnabled { return nil }` gate to the alarm and security publish methods, matching every other raw-plane publisher, and extend the existing `Test*PlaneTopicsRoundTrip` guards with a raw-disabled case.
findings.resolution: CLOSED AS A DECISION: raw_enabled governs the raw topic plane and deliberately does not silence the state topics an entity discovery payload names (by_design BD-MQTT-RawGateCoversRawTopicsOnly)

findings.title: /api/v1/health can never report `healthy` more than 90 s after boot: two boot-only components decay to `unknown` forever
findings.claim: `Tracker.applyStaleLocked` (internal/health/tracker.go:298-309) downgrades any component whose last sample is older than `staleAfter` to `StatusUnknown`, and `DefaultStaleAfter` is 90 s (:82); the daemon never passes `WithStaleAfter`. `config.secrets` and `config.overlay` are each recorded exactly once, at boot, by `recordSecretHealth` / `recordConfigOverlayHealth` (cmd/openccu-loom/daemon.go:221 and :224 — the only call sites) and are never re-recorded. `Tracker.Overall` (:318-342) returns `StatusUnknown` whenever any component is unknown and nothing is worse, so from 90 s after boot the aggregate can never be `healthy` again, and `Tracker.IsAvailable()` (:596) is permanently false.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured on a fully healthy daemon: 31 s after boot GET /api/v1/health returned `{"status":"healthy", ...}`; from then on it returns `unknown` (or `degraded` when something else is degraded). Final reading with every real component green — `ccu-g3/ccu-g3-HmIP-RF healthy, ccu-g3/central healthy, ccu-g3/scheduler healthy, matter healthy, matter.bridge healthy, mqtt healthy, sqlite healthy` — the aggregate was `unknown`, solely because `config.overlay` and `config.secrets` had gone stale. Any operator dashboard or uptime check that alerts on `status != healthy` fires permanently on every deployment.
findings.verified_by: measurement — GET /api/v1/health at boot+31 s vs boot+3 min vs boot+25 min across four daemon runs; code trace of tracker.go:82/298/318 and daemon.go:221-224
findings.fix_sketch: Give one-shot components a latched status that staleness does not decay (e.g. a `Sticky` sample flag, or re-record them on the health heartbeat), or exclude them from `Overall`'s unknown-propagation. Add a test that boots the daemon, advances the clock past staleAfter and asserts the aggregate is still healthy.
findings.verify_reasoning:
NOTE ON IDS: my fourth assignment was the /api/v1/health finding, which G3 filed as G3-lifecycle-chaos-7 (G3-lifecycle-chaos-4, the runtime-central-remove leftovers, was not in my brief). The mechanism and the observation are exactly as claimed and I reproduced them; what does not hold is the 'high' rating, so this is PARTIAL with a re-rate, agreeing with V4.json.

WHAT IS REAL, MEASURED ON A FULLY HEALTHY DAEMON WITH A LIVE CCU: booted 13:53:34; GET /api/v1/health returned status 'healthy' at t+10 s through t+60 s; config.overlay and config.secrets flipped to 'unknown' at 13:55:10 (t+96 s, i.e. the 90 s staleAfter plus poll granularity); from 13:55:45 (t+131 s) the aggregate read 'unknown' whenever nothing else was degraded, and it never read 'healthy' again for the rest of the run. Mechanism confirmed in code: health.DefaultStaleAfter = 90 s (internal/health/tracker.go:82), applyStaleLocked rewrites ANY component older than that to StatusUnknown (:298-309), ServiceAvailability returns StatusUnknown when worst==Healthy && hasUnknown (:388-392), and recordSecretHealth / recordConfigOverlayHealth have exactly one call site each, cmd/openccu-loom/daemon.go:221 and :224, with no timer and no second caller -- so the decay is permanent by construction, not merely long.

WHAT DOES NOT SUPPORT 'high'. (1) HTTP stays 200 the entire time (only StatusUnhealthy maps to 503, handlers/health.go:56-59), so liveness/readiness probes and load-balancer draining are unaffected -- I measured http=200 on every one of the 20 polls after the decay. (2) The signal is not lost, only its positive pole: applyStaleLocked rewrites Status and leaves LastSample untouched, so the note travels forever ('database sections applied' vs the failure branch's 'database config sections not applied: <err>'), and the Prometheus config_overlay_failed gauge is set once and holds -- a real overlay or secret failure is still distinguishable and still alerts. (3) Degraded and Unhealthy both outrank Unknown in both collapse functions, so no genuine outage is masked; during my CCU-kill run the same endpoint correctly went 503. (4) The blast radius is one operator-facing status token: the SPA Diagnostics view renders it through statusVariant(), where 'unknown' maps to the muted badge (assets/ui/src/routes/Diagnostics.svelte:386-390) -- a grey 'unknown' chip, not an error state. The concrete damage is that the natural monitoring probe 'alert when status != healthy' fires permanently on every deployment -- a false positive that trains operators to ignore the check. That is real and worth fixing, but it is alert noise in the safe direction, with no data loss, no availability impact and no masked failure. Medium.

findings.title: GET /api/v1/config and /api/v1/config/effective report the configured callback port, not the effective bound one
findings.claim: `ConfigAdapter.SanitizedConfig` fills `snap.CallbackPorts` from `a.source.Callback.Port` / `a.source.Callback.BinPort` (internal/central/adapter/config.go:35-38) — the parsed config, never the port the listener actually bound. With `callback.port_range` set, `applyDefaults` rewrites `Callback.Port` to the 8120 default (documented on `CallbackConfig`), so the reported value is a port nothing listens on. The same applies to `bin_port: 0`, the genuinely dynamic BIN-RPC mode, which would be reported as 0.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured with `callback.port_range: "18310-18319"`: the daemon logged `callback.listen addr=127.0.0.1:18310 port=18310` and `ss` confirmed it listening on 18310, while GET /api/v1/config returned `"callback_ports": {"xmlrpc": 8120, "binrpc": 18320}` and GET /api/v1/config/effective returned `callback.port: 8120` next to `callback.port_range: "18310-18319"`. An operator opening a firewall or diagnosing 'the CCU sends no events' from the API reads 8120 and opens the wrong port; the daemon-side value that the CCU was actually told is 18310.
findings.verified_by: measurement — `ss -ltnp` + the daemon's own `callback.listen` log line vs the two REST payloads; code trace of internal/central/adapter/config.go:35-38
findings.fix_sketch: Feed the rpcserver's effective bound ports into the ConfigAdapter (the same value that is re-advertised in every `init()`), and report those. Keep the configured value only under a separate field if it is still wanted.
